docs.title: The Question
docs.text: Does 1 Peter 3:18-20 teach that Jesus, between His death and resurrection, went to some realm and preached to dead people or imprisoned spirits? If so, this would contradict the teaching that the dead are unconscious.

docs.title: Verse 18
docs.text:
"For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:"

Key phrase: "quickened by the Spirit" - Christ was made alive (quickened) BY the Spirit - This establishes the Spirit as the agent of the action that follows

docs.title: Verse 19
docs.text:
"By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison;"

Critical phrase: "By which" (Greek: en hō) - This refers back to "the Spirit" in verse 18 - It was BY THE SPIRIT that the "going" and "preaching" occurred

The preaching was done BY THE SPIRIT, not by Christ in person going somewhere between death and resurrection.

docs.title: Verse 20
docs.text:
"Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water."

Key phrase: "in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing" - The disobedience occurred during Noah's time - This was during the 120-year period when the ark was being built (Genesis 6:3) - This is WHEN the preaching happened

docs.title: What the Passage Actually Says
docs.text:
1. Christ was made alive by the Spirit (v.18)
  2. By that same Spirit, he went and preached (v.19)
  3. The preaching was to those who were disobedient in Noah's day (v.20)
  4. The disobedience was while the ark was being prepared (v.20)

docs.title: How Did Christ Preach to Noah's Generation?
docs.text:
1 Peter 1:10-11 provides the answer:

"The Spirit of Christ which was in them [the prophets] did signify..."

The Spirit of Christ was IN the Old Testament prophets. Christ preached THROUGH Noah by His Spirit.

2 Peter 2:5 confirms Noah was a preacher:

"Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness"

Genesis 6:3 confirms the Spirit was striving:

"My spirit shall not always strive with man... yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years."

docs.title: The "Spirits in Prison"
docs.text:
Who are these spirits that are now "in prison"?

Option 1: The fallen angels of Genesis 6 - 2 Peter 2:4: "angels that sinned... cast down to hell... chains of darkness" - Jude 6: "angels which kept not their first estate... reserved in everlasting chains" - Genesis 6:1-4: "sons of God" (angels in Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7) took human wives - These angels are now in "prison" awaiting judgment

Option 2: The disobedient humans of Noah's day - They rejected Noah's preaching - They are now in the "prison" of death (Sheol/Hades) - Awaiting resurrection and judgment

Either interpretation is consistent with the text: The preaching happened DURING Noah's time, not between Christ's death and resurrection.

docs.title: Context: Suffering for Righteousness (3:13-17)
docs.text:
Peter is encouraging believers who are suffering for doing good. His point:

  1. Christ suffered for doing right (v.18) - "the just for the unjust"
  2. Noah also suffered rejection for doing right - he preached 120 years while building the ark
  3. Yet both were vindicated - Christ was raised; Noah and his family were saved

Peter uses Noah as an example of: - Faithful preaching despite rejection - Suffering minority (only 8 saved) - Ultimate vindication through water (baptism parallel)

docs.title: What About 1 Peter 4:6?
docs.text: "For for this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit."

docs.title: The Interpretation
docs.text:
This does NOT mean the gospel was preached to people after they died.

"Them that are dead" = people who are NOW dead, but who WERE preached to while alive.

Context (v.5): "judge the quick and the dead" - both living and dead will be judged Meaning: The gospel was preached to these people (who are now dead) so that they could be saved.

Why Peter says this: Some might wonder why bother preaching to people who will die anyway. Peter answers: even though they died ("judged according to men in the flesh"), they will "live according to God in the spirit" - they will be raised.

This is consistent with the state-of-the-dead teaching: The dead are unconscious NOW, but the gospel was preached to them while they were ALIVE, and they await resurrection.

docs.title: Why This Passage Cannot Mean Christ Preached to Dead People
1. It Would Contradict the State of the Dead
docs.text:
• The dead "know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
  • "In that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:4)
  • "There is no work, nor device, nor knowledge... in the grave" (Ecclesiastes 9:10)

How could unconscious beings receive preaching?

docs.title: 2. It Would Make Christ a Liar
docs.text:
• Luke 23:43: "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise"
  • If Jesus was in paradise with the thief, He wasn't in some prison preaching
  • Jesus told Mary on resurrection Sunday: "I am not yet ascended to my Father" (John 20:17)
  • He was in the tomb, not preaching somewhere

docs.title: 3. It Would Make No Theological Sense
docs.text:
• If Christ preached to dead people, offering them salvation after death:
  • Why only the generation of Noah?
  • What about all other generations?
  • This would undermine the urgency of the gospel while alive

docs.title: 4. The Grammar Points to Noah's Time
docs.text:
• "By which" links back to "the Spirit"
  • "When... in the days of Noah" specifies WHEN the preaching occurred
  • The text says the preaching was while the ark was being prepared

docs.title: Traditional Reading (Problematic)
docs.text:
1. Christ died
  2. His spirit went to a place of imprisoned spirits
  3. He preached to them (offering salvation? announcing doom?)
  4. Then rose again

Problems: - Contradicts unconsciousness of death - No clear purpose for the preaching - Grammatically forced reading

docs.title: Consistent Reading (Preferred)
docs.text:
1. Christ was made alive by the Spirit (v.18)
  2. By that same Spirit, Christ went and preached through Noah (v.19)
  3. He preached to those who are now imprisoned spirits (v.20a)
  4. They were disobedient while Noah was building the ark (v.20b)

Support: - Consistent with 1 Peter 1:11 - Spirit of Christ in prophets - Consistent with 2 Peter 2:5 - Noah was a preacher - Consistent with Genesis 6:3 - Spirit striving 120 years - Consistent with state-of-the-dead teaching - Makes logical sense in Peter's argument about suffering for righteousness

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
1 Peter 3:18-20 does NOT teach that Christ preached to dead people between His death and resurrection.

Rather, it teaches that Christ, by His Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of that generation who rejected the message and are now "spirits in prison" awaiting judgment.

This interpretation: - Is consistent with the grammar ("by which") - Is consistent with the timeline ("in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing") - Is consistent with 1 Peter 1:11 (Spirit of Christ in prophets) - Is consistent with 2 Peter 2:5 (Noah as preacher of righteousness) - Is consistent with the state-of-the-dead teaching (the dead are unconscious)

docs.title: Kerusso (G2784) - "Preached"
docs.text: Greek: κηρύσσω (kēryssō) Meaning: To herald, to proclaim as a public crier

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The verb describes the action of "heralding" or publicly announcing important messages with formality and authority. According to Strong's: "to herald (as a public crier), especially divine truth (the gospel)."

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
• "The public proclamation of the gospel and matters pertaining to it"
  • Made by John the Baptist, Jesus, the apostles, and other teachers
  • Used 61 times in KJV: "preach" (51x), "publish" (5x), "proclaim" (2x)

docs.title: Significance for This Study
docs.text: This is the word for public proclamation - what Noah did for 120 years while building the ark. 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah "a preacher (kerux, the noun form) of righteousness."

docs.title: Pneuma (G4151) - "Spirit" / "Spirits"
docs.text: Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma) Meaning: Breath, wind; spirit (human, angelic, or divine)

docs.title: Primary Meanings
docs.text:
1. The Holy Spirit - The third person of the Godhead
  2. Human spirit - The vital principle, rational soul
  3. Supernatural beings - Angels, demons, or spirits
  4. Disposition - The influence that governs the soul

docs.title: Usage in KJV (385 times)
docs.text:
• "Spirit" (111x) - usually Holy Spirit
  • "Holy Ghost" (89x)
  • "spirit" (47x) - evil spirits
  • "spirit" (49x) - human spirit

docs.title: Significance for This Study
docs.text:
In 1 Peter 3:18-19, "pneuma" appears twice: 1. v.18: "quickened by the Spirit" - referring to the Holy Spirit 2. v.19: "spirits in prison" - referring to either fallen angels or departed humans

The connection "by which" links the Spirit of v.18 to the action of preaching to the spirits of v.19.

docs.title: Phylake (G5438) - "Prison"
docs.text: Greek: φυλακή (phylakē) Meaning: Guard, guarding; prison, place of confinement

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The term encompasses both the act of guarding and the place of confinement. Can mean: 1. Guard/Watch - Active vigilance 2. Prison - Place where captives are confined (most common - 36 of 47 uses) 3. Time period - A watch of the night

docs.title: Etymology
docs.text: Derived from phylassō (G5442), meaning "to keep, observe, guard."

docs.title: Usage in KJV (47 times)
docs.text:
• "prison" (36x)
  • "watch" (6x)
  • "imprisonment" (2x)

docs.title: Significance for This Study
docs.text:
The "spirits in prison" are in a place of confinement or restraint. This matches: - 2 Peter 2:4 - angels in "chains of darkness" - Jude 6 - angels in "everlasting chains under darkness"

Whether these are fallen angels or human dead, they are confined awaiting judgment.

docs.title: Poreuomai (G4198) - "Went"
docs.text: Greek: πορεύομαι (poreuomai) Meaning: To go, to traverse, to travel, to journey

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The word describes purposeful movement - "to take one's way, betake oneself, set out, depart."

docs.title: Usage in KJV (154 times)
docs.text:
• "go" (117x)
  • "depart" (11x)
  • "walk" (9x)

docs.title: Significance for This Study
docs.text:
The "going" in v.19 is connected to the Spirit of v.18 by "by which" (en hō). The question is: WHEN did Christ "go" and preach?

The text specifies: "when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing" (v.20).

This was not a journey between death and resurrection, but a "going" by the Spirit through Noah during the 120-year preparation period.

docs.title: Related: Kerux (G2783) - "Preacher"
docs.text: Greek: κῆρυξ (kērux) Meaning: A herald, public messenger, preacher

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
This is the noun form of kerusso. 2 Peter 2:5 uses this word to describe Noah:

"saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher (kerux) of righteousness"

This confirms that Noah was a herald/proclaimer of God's message to his generation.

docs.title: En Hō (ἐν ᾧ) - "By Which"
docs.text: This prepositional phrase in v.19 is crucial. It connects back to "the Spirit" in v.18.

docs.title: Grammatical Analysis
docs.text:
• En = "in, by, with" (preposition)
  • Hō = "which" (relative pronoun, dative masculine/neuter singular)

The antecedent (what "which" refers to) is "Spirit" (pneumati) - the closest appropriate noun.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
"By which [Spirit]" - The Spirit by whom Christ was quickened is the same Spirit by whom He went and preached.

This is consistent with 1 Peter 1:11: "the Spirit of Christ which was in them" (the prophets).

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Greek Term Meaning Significance Kerusso To herald, proclaim Noah proclaimed God's message for 120 years Pneuma Spirit Links v.18 to v.19; Christ worked by His Spirit through Noah Phylake Prison, confinement The disobedient are now confined awaiting judgment Poreuomai To go, journey The "going" was by the Spirit during Noah's time En hō By which Connects the Spirit to the action of preaching Kerux Herald, preacher Noah was "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Pet 2:5)

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The Greek vocabulary supports the interpretation that Christ, BY HIS SPIRIT, preached THROUGH NOAH to those who are now "spirits in prison." The word study reveals:

  1. The preaching (kerusso) was public proclamation - what Noah did
  2. The "Spirit" (pneuma) is the agent of the action
  3. The "prison" (phylake) is where the disobedient are NOW confined
  4. The "going" (poreuomai) was by the Spirit, during Noah's time
  5. "By which" (en hō) grammatically links back to the Spirit

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What does 1 Peter 3:18-20 mean when it says Christ "went and preached unto the spirits in prison"? Does this contradict the teaching that the dead are unconscious?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text:
1 Peter 3:18-20 does NOT teach that Jesus preached to dead people between His death and resurrection. Rather, it teaches that Christ, by His Spirit, preached through Noah to those who rejected the message and are now "spirits in prison" awaiting judgment.

The passage is consistent with the state-of-the-dead teaching that the dead are unconscious. The preaching occurred during Noah's time (while the ark was being prepared), not after these people had died.

docs.title: 1 Peter 3:18-20
docs.text: "For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit: By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison; Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water."

docs.title: 1. "By Which" Links to the Spirit
docs.text: The phrase "by which" (en hō) in verse 19 connects back to "the Spirit" in verse 18. The Spirit by whom Christ was made alive is the same Spirit by whom He went and preached.

docs.title: 2. The Spirit of Christ Worked Through the Prophets
docs.text:
1 Peter 1:10-11 establishes this principle:

"The Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ..."

Christ's Spirit was IN the Old Testament prophets. The Spirit worked through them to deliver God's message.

docs.title: 3. Noah Was "A Preacher of Righteousness"
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:5 explicitly states:

"saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly"

Noah preached to his generation for 120 years while building the ark (Genesis 6:3). Christ, by His Spirit, preached through Noah.

docs.title: 4. The Disobedience Was "In the Days of Noah"
docs.text:
Verse 20 is specific: the spirits were "disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing."

This is WHEN the preaching happened - during the 120-year period before the flood, not between Christ's death and resurrection.

docs.title: 5. God's Spirit Was Striving with Man
docs.text:
Genesis 6:3 confirms:

"My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years."

God's Spirit was striving (through Noah's preaching) with the antediluvian world.

docs.title: 6. Peter's Own Explanation: 1 Peter 4:5-6
docs.text:
This is the strongest single argument for the interpretation. Just one chapter later, in the same letter, Peter explains what he means by preaching to the spirits in prison. Same author, same letter, same topic -- this is the highest-authority cross-reference available.

1 Peter 4:5-6 "Who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead. For for this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit."

The verb tense is decisive. "Was the gospel preached" (εὐηγγελίσθη, euēngelisthē) is aorist passive -- a completed past action. The gospel was preached (past) to people who are now dead. Peter is not describing ongoing preaching to dead people. He is describing past preaching to people who have since died.

The pattern matches 1 Peter 3:19-20 exactly:

1 Peter 3:19-20 1 Peter 4:6 Who was preached to? "Spirits in prison" "Them that are dead" When preached to? "In the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing" Past tense (aorist) -- when alive Current state? "In prison" (dead, fate sealed) "Dead" Who preached? Christ "by the Spirit" (through Noah) "The gospel was preached" (passive) Purpose? Warning before the flood "That they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit"

Peter describes the same reality in both passages: people who received preaching while alive but who are now dead. In 3:19-20 he specifies which group (Noah's generation) and when (while the ark was being built). In 4:6 he explains the purpose: so they could be fairly judged, having heard the message.

If 1 Peter 3:19 described a post-mortem descent to preach to imprisoned angels, then 1 Peter 4:6 would need to describe a different event entirely -- which would mean Peter raised the topic of "preaching to the dead" twice in the same short letter with two completely different meanings. The simpler reading: both passages describe the same thing, and 4:6 clarifies 3:19.

docs.title: Who Are the "Spirits in Prison"?
docs.text:
Given Peter's own explanation in 4:5-6, these are the disobedient humans of Noah's generation:

  • Those who rejected Noah's preaching during the 120-year period
  • They are now (from Peter's perspective) dead -- "spirits in prison"
  • They await judgment, having rejected the message while alive
  • Peter's language in 4:6 ("them that are dead") confirms he is describing humans, not angels

"In prison" describes their current state (dead, fate sealed), not their state at the time they were preached to. This is the same as "reserved unto judgment" (2 Peter 2:4, 9) -- Peter uses the same vocabulary across both epistles to describe those whose fate is sealed but whose final judgment is still future.

Some identify the "spirits" as fallen angels, but this creates a problem with 1 Peter 4:6: if 3:19 describes preaching to imprisoned angels, then 4:6 ("the gospel was preached to them that are dead") becomes disconnected from 3:19 -- and Peter would have introduced two different "preaching to dead/imprisoned beings" events in the same short letter without distinguishing them.

docs.title: Why This Passage Cannot Mean Preaching to the Dead
1. Contradicts the State of the Dead
docs.text:
• "The dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5)
  • "In that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:4)
  • "No work, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave" (Ecclesiastes 9:10)

Unconscious beings cannot receive or respond to preaching.

docs.title: 2. Jesus Was in the Tomb
docs.text:
• Matthew 12:40: Jesus would be "three days and three nights in the heart of the earth"
  • John 20:17: On resurrection Sunday, Jesus said, "I am not yet ascended to my Father"
  • Jesus was not traveling to some prison to preach

docs.title: 3. No Second Chance Theology
docs.text:
• "It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Hebrews 9:27)
  • If the dead could receive the gospel, the urgency of evangelism would be undermined
  • Why only preach to Noah's generation and not all the dead?

docs.title: 4. The Grammar Specifies Noah's Time
docs.text:
• "By which" connects to "the Spirit"
  • "When... in the days of Noah" specifies WHEN
  • "While the ark was a preparing" gives the timeframe

docs.title: Peter's Point in Context
docs.text:
Peter is encouraging believers who suffer for righteousness (3:14-17). His argument:

  1. Christ suffered unjustly - "the just for the unjust" (v.18)
  2. Noah also suffered rejection - he preached 120 years with only 8 believing
  3. Both were vindicated - Christ was raised; Noah was saved through water
  4. Believers will also be vindicated - the baptism parallel (v.21)

The passage is about faithful witness despite rejection, not about preaching to the dead.

docs.title: Parallel Passages
docs.text: Passage Teaching 1 Peter 4:5-6 Peter's own explanation: "the gospel was preached to them that are dead" -- aorist tense confirms preaching happened while alive 1 Peter 1:10-11 Spirit of Christ was IN the prophets 2 Peter 2:4-5 Angels in chains; Noah a preacher of righteousness Genesis 6:3 God's Spirit striving for 120 years Hebrews 11:7 Noah "condemned the world" by his faithful witness

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
1 Peter 3:18-20 teaches that:

  1. Christ was made alive by the Spirit (v.18)
  2. By that same Spirit, He went and preached through Noah (v.19)
  3. He preached to those who are now imprisoned spirits (v.19)
  4. They were disobedient during Noah's time while the ark was being built (v.20)

This is confirmed by: - 1 Peter 4:5-6 -- Peter's own same-letter explanation: "the gospel was preached to them that are dead" (aorist = past, while alive). Same pattern, same author, same letter. - The teaching that Christ's Spirit worked through the prophets (1 Peter 1:11) - The explicit statement that Noah was a preacher (2 Peter 2:5) - The grammar and timeline of the passage itself ("in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing")

The "spirits in prison" received their preaching when they were alive, during Noah's 120-year ministry. They rejected the message, died in the flood, and now await judgment. Christ preached to them not in person after His death, but by His Spirit through Noah while they were still living. Peter confirms this interpretation himself in 4:5-6, where the aorist tense and purpose clause make clear that the preaching occurred before death, not after.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What does 2 Peter 2:4 actually teach about "the angels that sinned"? What does the text state, and how should we interpret ambiguous phrases?

docs.title: The Verse
docs.text: "For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;"

docs.title: Methodological Approach
docs.text: Following proper hermeneutics: 1. Examine what the text ACTUALLY STATES 2. Use Scripture to interpret Scripture - find biblical parallels 3. Avoid importing Greek mythology or extra-biblical sources 4. Acknowledge what is genuinely ambiguous 5. Do not force connections without textual warrant

docs.title: The Key Interpretive Parallel: Revelation 12
docs.text: Before assuming what "cast down" and "chains of darkness" mean, we must examine how Scripture elsewhere describes fallen angels.

docs.title: Revelation 12:7-12
docs.text: 12:7 And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, 12:8 And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven. 12:9 And the great dragon was cast out... he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. 12:10 ...the accuser of our brethren is cast down... 12:12 ...the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
In Revelation 12, Satan and his angels are: - "Cast out" of heaven - "Cast down" to earth - Yet remain active with "great wrath" (v.12-17)

This provides a biblical framework for understanding 2 Peter 2:4: - "Cast down" does NOT necessarily mean imprisoned - Angels can be "cast down" yet still active - "Reserved unto judgment" = "knoweth he hath but a short time"

docs.title: Direct Statements in 2 Peter 2:4
docs.text:
1. There are angels that sinned
  2. God did not spare them
  3. God cast them down (Greek: tartaroo)
  4. God delivered them into chains of darkness
  5. They are reserved unto judgment

docs.title: What the Text Does NOT State
docs.text:
1. WHEN these angels sinned
  2. WHAT their specific sin was
  3. WHO specifically these angels are
  4. Whether they are inactive/imprisoned

docs.title: Reinterpreting Through Revelation 12
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:4 Revelation 12 Meaning "cast them down" "cast out... cast down" Expelled from heaven "chains of darkness" Active with "great wrath" Spiritual state, not physical prison "reserved unto judgment" "knoweth he hath but a short time" Fate sealed, judgment coming

Key insight: Revelation 12 uses similar "cast down" language for angels who are clearly ACTIVE. This suggests "chains of darkness" describes their condemned spiritual state, not literal imprisonment.

docs.title: Peter's Argument in Context (2:1-9)
docs.text:
Peter's PURPOSE is to warn about false teachers (v.1-3). His argument:

If God judged THESE, He will judge false teachers: - v.4: Angels that sinned → judged - v.5: Ancient world → judged (but Noah delivered) - v.6-8: Sodom → judged (but Lot delivered) - v.9: CONCLUSION - God delivers the godly AND reserves the unjust for judgment

Peter's point is NOT to teach angel chronology. The three examples illustrate that God judges sin.

docs.title: The Question of Jude 6
docs.text:
Jude 6 provides parallel language:

"And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day."

docs.title: Jude Adds Detail About the Sin
docs.text:
• "kept not their first estate" = did not maintain their position
  • "left their own habitation" = departed from their dwelling

docs.title: Connection to Revelation 12
docs.text:
• "kept not their first estate" → "neither was their place found any more in heaven" (Rev 12:8)
  • "left their own habitation" → "cast out into the earth" (Rev 12:9)

This describes the angelic rebellion - following Satan in the war against God.

docs.title: 1. Greek Cultural Background of "Tartaroo"
docs.text: Context: Tartaroo appears only here in the entire NT. In Greek usage, Tartarus was where the Titans were imprisoned after rebelling against the divine order -- not for sexual sin. Peter chose a word his audience would associate with punishment for rebellion against divine authority. Important: Understanding why Peter chose this word is standard lexicography, not importing pagan theology. The cultural background actually supports the rebellion reading (aligning with Revelation 12) rather than the sexual-sin reading. Confirmation: Revelation 12 provides the biblical parallel that confirms this meaning.

docs.title: 2. Two Classes of Fallen Angels
docs.text: Assumption: 2 Peter 2:4 describes "imprisoned" angels, separate from active demons. Problem: Revelation 12 uses the same "cast down" language for active beings. Better approach: All fallen angels are in "chains of darkness" (condemned state) yet active.

docs.title: 3. Genesis 6 Connection
docs.text: Assumption: These angels sinned by taking human wives in Genesis 6. Problem: 2 Peter 2:4 doesn't mention Genesis 6; sequence doesn't prove connection. Better approach: Revelation 12 provides a clearer explanation without interpretive leaps.

docs.title: Questions This Study Will Address
docs.text:
1. What does "cast down" (tartaroo) mean biblically?
  2. What are "chains of darkness" - literal or metaphorical?
  3. Are these angels different from active demons?
  4. How does Revelation 12 inform our interpretation?
  5. What is the relationship to Jude 6?
  6. Is the Genesis 6 connection warranted?

docs.title: The Primary Passage: 2 Peter 2:4
docs.text: "For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;"

docs.title: 2 Peter 2:1-3 (The Warning)
docs.text: 2:1 But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction. 2:2 And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of. 2:3 And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise of you: whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their damnation slumbereth not.

docs.title: 2 Peter 2:4-8 (Three Examples)
docs.text: 2:4 For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment; 2:5 And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly; 2:6 And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha into ashes condemned them with an overthrow, making them an ensample unto those that after should live ungodly; 2:7 And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: 2:8 (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)

docs.title: 2 Peter 2:9 (The Conclusion)
docs.text: 2:9 The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:

docs.title: Jude 1:5-7
docs.text: 1:5 I will therefore put you in remembrance, though ye once knew this, how that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not. 1:6 And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day. 1:7 Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

docs.title: Revelation 12:7-12 (War in Heaven - Cast Down but Active)
docs.text:
12:7 And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, 12:8 And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven. 12:9 And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. 12:10 And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night. 12:12 Therefore rejoice, [ye] heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.

Critical observation: Satan and his angels are "cast out" and "cast down" - yet remain ACTIVE on earth with "great wrath." Being "cast down" does not mean inactive.

docs.title: Isaiah 14:12-15 (Often Applied to Satan's Fall)
docs.text:
14:12 How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! 14:13 For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God... 14:15 Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.

Note: This passage is addressed to the king of Babylon. Application to Satan is an interpretation.

docs.title: Matthew 25:41
docs.text: Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

docs.title: Previous Study: 1 Peter 3:19-20
docs.text:
From the 1-peter-3-spirits-in-prison study:

3:19 By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison; 3:20 Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.

Conclusion from that study: The preaching happened through Noah, by Christ's Spirit, to those who were alive during the 120 years before the flood. The "spirits" are those who rejected Noah's preaching and are now dead (in the "prison" of death).

Important: That study concluded these were HUMANS who rejected Noah's preaching, not necessarily angels.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: This analysis will: 1. State what the text clearly says 2. Use Scripture to interpret Scripture (especially Revelation 12) 3. Identify what is genuinely ambiguous 4. Note common assumptions that go beyond the text

docs.title: The Text
docs.text: "For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;"

docs.title: Five Direct Statements
docs.text: Statement Text 1. Angels sinned "the angels that sinned" 2. God didn't spare them "God spared not" 3. They were cast down "cast them down to hell" 4. They are in chains of darkness "chains of darkness" 5. They await judgment "reserved unto judgment"

docs.title: Peter's Purpose
docs.text:
Peter is NOT teaching about: - Angel chronology - The nature of angelic sin - The identity of specific angels

Peter IS teaching: - God judges sin - If God didn't spare angels, He won't spare false teachers - The three examples (angels, flood, Sodom) prove God judges

docs.title: Revelation 12: A Single Vision with an Internal Narrative Timeline
docs.text: Revelation 12 is a single vision spanning from before Christ's birth to after His ascension. Understanding its narrative timeline is critical for interpreting 2 Peter 2:4.

docs.title: Event 1: Primordial Rebellion (Rev 12:4a)
docs.text:
12:4a And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth

Key observations: - Occurs BEFORE Christ's birth in the narrative (v.4b-5 follow) - "Stars" = angels (Job 38:7 - Hebrew parallelism: "morning stars" = "sons of God") - After this, the dragon waits to devour the child (v.4b) - fulfilled through Herod on earth (Matt 2:16) - This parallels 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 - the original angelic rebellion

docs.title: Event 2: Final Expulsion at Christ's Victory (Rev 12:7-12)
docs.text:
12:7 And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, 12:8 And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven. 12:9 And the great dragon was cast out... he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. 12:10 ...for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night. 12:12 ...the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.

Key observations: - Occurs AFTER Christ's ascension (v.5: "caught up unto God, and to his throne") - "NOW is come... the power of his Christ" (v.10) - explicitly tied to Christ's work - "By the blood of the Lamb" (v.11) - achieved at the cross - Satan's role as "accuser" was revoked

docs.title: Between the Two Events: Satan's Accuser Access
docs.text:
Between the primordial rebellion and Christ's victory, Satan retained limited heavenly access: - Job 1:6, 2:1 - Satan "came among them" before the LORD (~2000 BC) - Zechariah 3:1 - Satan "standing before the angel of the LORD" (~520 BC) - Revelation 12:10 - "accused them before our God day and night"

This explains why Satan could appear before God in Job despite having already "sinned" (2 Pet 2:4).

docs.title: The Vocabulary Distinction
docs.text:
Passage Greek Verb Meaning Jude 6 apoleipo (G620) "left" - voluntary departure 2 Peter 2:4 tartaroo (G5020) "cast to Tartarus" - divine judgment Rev 12:4a ballo (G906) "cast" - threw (Satan's action) Rev 12:9 ekballo (G1544) "cast out" - forcible expulsion

2 Peter 2:4 describes the primordial rebellion - Jude 6's "apoleipo" (left) vocabulary. Revelation 12:7-12 describes the later expulsion - "ekballo" (forcibly cast out) at Christ's victory.

docs.title: What This Shows
docs.text:
Event Passage Result Primordial rebellion Rev 12:4a, Jude 6, 2 Pet 2:4 Condemned, but retained accuser access Christ's victory Rev 12:7-12 "Place found no more" - access revoked Post-expulsion Rev 12:12-17 Active on earth with "great wrath"

Critical observation: At BOTH events, cast-down angels remain active. This transforms how we understand "chains of darkness."

docs.title: The Common Assumption
docs.text: Most interpreters assume "chains of darkness" means: - Literal imprisonment - Physical inability to act - A separate group of angels from active demons

docs.title: The Problem with This Assumption
docs.text:
1. Revelation 12 uses similar "cast down" language for active beings
  2. Nothing in 2 Peter 2:4 explicitly says they cannot act
  3. This creates an unnecessary distinction between "imprisoned angels" and "active demons" not supported by the text

docs.title: Alternative Reading (Consistent with Rev 12)
docs.text:
"Chains of darkness" may describe their spiritual state, not physical location:

Term Metaphorical Meaning Chains Bound to judgment - their fate is sealed, they cannot escape Darkness Spiritual condition - separated from God's light Reserved unto judgment Awaiting destruction - same as "short time" in Rev 12:12

This reading: - Is consistent with Revelation 12 - Doesn't require inventing two classes of fallen angels - Uses Scripture to interpret Scripture - Explains why demons are active yet still "reserved unto judgment"

docs.title: 1. WHEN Did These Angels Sin?
docs.text:
The text does not say.

The sequence (angels → flood → Sodom) is not necessarily chronological. Peter is giving examples of judgment, not a timeline. He arranges them: - Perhaps by type of being (angels → humans → cities) - Perhaps by severity - Perhaps rhetorically

docs.title: 2. WHAT Was Their Sin?
docs.text:
The text does not say.

It simply says "the angels that sinned" - no description of the sin.

docs.title: 3. WHO Are These Angels?
docs.text:
The text does not identify them.

Given Revelation 12's parallel language, these could simply be Satan and all his angels - not a special subset. There is no textual reason to distinguish them from the active demons elsewhere in Scripture.

docs.title: The Text
docs.text: "And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day."

docs.title: Similarities
docs.text: 2 Peter 2:4 Jude 6 "angels that sinned" "angels which kept not their first estate" "chains of darkness" "everlasting chains under darkness" "reserved unto judgment" "unto the judgment of the great day"

docs.title: Jude Adds Detail
docs.text:
Jude describes the sin: "kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation"

This likely refers to the rebellion described in Revelation 12: - They did not keep their proper position/rank (first estate) - They left their heavenly dwelling (habitation) - They followed Satan in his war against God

docs.title: "In Like Manner" (Jude 7)
docs.text:
"Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication..."

This phrase is grammatically ambiguous. It could mean: - Sodom sinned like the angels (sexual sin interpretation) - The surrounding cities sinned like Sodom - All three examples illustrate judgment "in like manner"

We cannot build doctrine on this ambiguous phrase.

docs.title: Previous Study Conclusion
docs.text: The 1-peter-3-spirits-in-prison study concluded: - The "spirits in prison" are those who were disobedient in Noah's day - Christ preached through Noah while they were ALIVE - These are HUMANS who rejected the message, not angels

docs.title: Should These Be Equated?
docs.text:
No. The vocabulary differs:

1 Peter 3:19-20 2 Peter 2:4 "spirits" (pneuma) "angels" (aggelos) "disobedient" "sinned" "in the days of Noah" No time reference Human spirits who rejected Noah Angelic beings who rebelled

These are different subjects. 1 Peter 3 refers to humans; 2 Peter 2:4 refers to angels.

docs.title: The Common Connection
docs.text: Many assume 2 Peter 2:4 refers to Genesis 6 ("sons of God took wives").

docs.title: Problems with This Connection
docs.text:
1. 2 Peter 2:4 doesn't mention Genesis 6
  2. The sequence argument is weak - Peter's list isn't necessarily chronological
  3. "Sons of God" is disputed - Genesis 6 doesn't explicitly identify them as angels
  4. Revelation 12 provides a simpler explanation - angels rebelled with Satan

docs.title: A Simpler Reading
docs.text:
If Revelation 12:4a describes the same event as 2 Peter 2:4 (the primordial rebellion): - The sin was rebellion against God - Satan "drew" a third of the angels - The angels "kept not their first estate" (Jude 6) - They were condemned - "tartaroo" (cast to Tartarus) - They retained accuser access until Christ's victory (Rev 12:7-12) - They remain active but await final judgment

This requires fewer interpretive leaps than the Genesis 6 connection.

docs.title: With Confidence
docs.text:
1. Angels sinned (rebelled against God)
  2. God judged them - cast them down
  3. They are in "chains of darkness" - a condemned spiritual state
  4. They await final judgment
  5. This proves God judges sin (Peter's point)

docs.title: With Reasonable Inference (from Rev 12)
docs.text:
1. "Cast down" doesn't mean inactive - Rev 12 shows active, cast-down angels
  2. "Chains of darkness" likely describes their condemned state, not physical prison
  3. These may be the same as Satan and demons active today
  4. Their "short time" / "reserved unto judgment" means their fate is sealed

docs.title: What Remains Uncertain
docs.text:
1. Whether a special subset of angels is meant
  2. Whether Genesis 6 is connected
  3. The exact timing of their rebellion

docs.title: What We Should NOT Do
docs.text:
1. Import Greek mythology to interpret "tartaroo"
  2. Assume chronology from Peter's list order
  3. Force connections to Genesis 6 without textual support
  4. Invent two classes of fallen angels (imprisoned vs. active) without biblical warrant

docs.title: Honest Conclusion
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:4, read alongside Revelation 12, teaches:

  1. Angels rebelled against God
  2. They were "cast down" from their heavenly position
  3. They exist in "chains of darkness" - spiritually condemned, separated from God
  4. They are "reserved unto judgment" - their fate is sealed
  5. This does NOT necessarily mean they are inactive - Revelation 12 shows cast-down angels who are very active

The main application stands: God judges sin. If He judged angels, He will certainly judge false teachers. And He will deliver the godly (2 Peter 2:9).

docs.title: The Word
docs.text: Greek: ταρταρόω (tartaroo) Strong's: G5020 Occurrence: Only here in the entire New Testament Translation: KJV renders "cast down to hell"

docs.title: What "Tartaroo" Meant
docs.text:
Tartaroo appears nowhere else in the entire Bible -- this is its sole occurrence. Peter chose this word deliberately. Understanding its cultural meaning is standard lexicography: the same principle that leads us to Greek lexicons for any NT word applies here.

In Greek cultural usage, Tartarus was where the Titans were imprisoned after rebelling against the divine order. The Titans did not marry humans; they waged war against Zeus. Peter's Greek-speaking audience would have understood tartaroo as punishment for rebellion against divine authority -- not sexual transgression.

This cultural background actually reinforces the biblical evidence. Peter was not endorsing Greek theology; he was selecting a word his audience would recognize as describing the punishment of rebels against divine authority -- which aligns precisely with Revelation 12's description of angelic rebellion.

Key point: While Greek background illuminates why Peter chose this word, we should also confirm the meaning from biblical parallels:

docs.title: Biblical Parallel: Revelation 12
docs.text:
While tartaroo is unique, the concept of angels being "cast down" is clearly described in Revelation 12:

Revelation 12:9-10 2 Peter 2:4 "cast out" (ekballo, G1544) "cast down" (tartaroo, G5020) "cast down" (kataballo, G2598)

The critical observation: In Revelation 12, Satan and his angels are "cast out" and "cast down" - yet they remain fully active on earth: - v.12: "the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath" - v.13: "he persecuted the woman" - v.17: "went to make war with the remnant"

docs.title: What "Tartaroo" Means (from Scripture)
docs.text: Using Revelation 12 as the interpretive key: - Cast down from heaven - expelled from their original position - Change in status - "neither was their place found any more in heaven" (Rev 12:8) - NOT necessarily imprisonment - Rev 12 shows cast-down angels who are active

docs.title: The Words
docs.text:
• seira (G4577) = chain, bond
  • zophos (G2217) = darkness, gloom

docs.title: The Common Assumption
docs.text: Most interpret this as literal imprisonment - angels physically bound and unable to act.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
This assumption creates an unbiblical distinction: - "Imprisoned angels" in 2 Peter 2:4 - "Active demons" elsewhere in Scripture

But Scripture doesn't support this distinction. Revelation 12 shows: - Angels "cast down" → still active - "Reserved unto judgment" → same as "knoweth he hath but a short time"

docs.title: Metaphorical Reading (Consistent with Rev 12)
docs.text:
Term Meaning Chains Bound to judgment - fate sealed, cannot escape Darkness Spiritual state - separated from God's light

This is similar to how humans can be described as being in "darkness" while still physically active: - "the people which sat in darkness" (Matt 4:16) - "men loved darkness rather than light" (John 3:19) - "the power of darkness" (Luke 22:53, Col 1:13)

The angels are spiritually in darkness - condemned, separated from God - while still active.

docs.title: The Words
docs.text:
• tereo (G5083) = to keep, guard, reserve, watch over
  • krisis (G2920) = judgment, decision

docs.title: The Parallel in Revelation 12
docs.text:
"the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time" (Rev 12:12)

Both passages describe the same reality: - Their fate is determined - Judgment is coming - They cannot escape - But they remain active until that judgment

docs.title: Usage of "Reserved" Elsewhere
docs.text:
Peter uses the same word (tereo) in this context:

"The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished" (2 Peter 2:9)

The "unjust" (human false teachers) are "reserved unto judgment" - yet they are clearly still active and causing harm. Being "reserved" doesn't mean imprisoned; it means their fate is sealed.

docs.title: "First Estate" (arche, G746)
docs.text:
Meaning: beginning, origin, principality, rule, domain

Jude says they "kept not their first estate" - they did not maintain their proper position/domain.

Connection to Rev 12: "neither was their place found any more in heaven" (Rev 12:8)

They abandoned their proper heavenly position by rebelling with Satan.

docs.title: "Own Habitation" (oiketerion, G3613)
docs.text:
Meaning: dwelling place, habitation

Jude says they "left their own habitation" - they departed from their proper dwelling.

Connection to Rev 12: They were "cast out" of heaven to earth (Rev 12:9).

They left heaven - whether voluntarily (rebellion) or as consequence of judgment.

docs.title: What Word Studies Confirm
docs.text:
1. Tartaroo = "cast down" - parallel language to Revelation 12
  2. Chains of darkness = condemned spiritual state, not necessarily physical prison
  3. Reserved unto judgment = fate sealed, same as "short time" in Rev 12:12
  4. Kept not first estate / left habitation = rebelled, lost place in heaven

docs.title: What Word Studies Do NOT Support
docs.text:
1. A special class of "imprisoned" angels separate from active demons
  2. Literal physical chains preventing activity
  3. A sexual-sin reading of tartaroo -- the Greek cultural background points to rebellion, not sexual transgression

docs.title: The Consistent Picture
docs.text: Both 2 Peter 2:4 and Revelation 12 describe the same reality: - Angels rebelled with Satan - They were cast out of heaven - They exist in spiritual darkness (condemned, separated from God) - They remain active but their judgment is certain - They have "but a short time" / are "reserved unto judgment"

docs.title: Conclusion: 2 Peter 2:4 - The Angels That Sinned
The Key Insight: Revelation 12's Narrative Timeline
docs.text: Revelation 12 is a single vision with an internal narrative timeline spanning from before Christ's birth to after His ascension:

docs.title: Event 1: Primordial Rebellion (Rev 12:4a)
docs.text:
"And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth"

  • Occurs BEFORE Christ's birth in the narrative (v.4b-5 follow)
  • "Stars" = angels (Job 38:7 - Hebrew parallelism: "morning stars" = "sons of God")
  • After this, the dragon waits to devour the child (v.4b) - fulfilled through Herod on earth (Matt 2:16)
  • This parallels 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 - the original angelic rebellion

docs.title: Event 2: Final Expulsion at Christ's Victory (Rev 12:7-12)
docs.text:
"And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon"

  • Occurs AFTER Christ's ascension (v.5: "caught up unto God, and to his throne")
  • "NOW is come... the power of his Christ" (v.10) - connected to Christ's work
  • Achieved by "the blood of the Lamb" (v.11)
  • Satan's role as "accuser" (Job 1-2, Zech 3) is revoked

docs.title: The Vocabulary Distinction
docs.text:
Passage Greek Verb Meaning Jude 6 apoleipo (G620) "left" - voluntary departure 2 Peter 2:4 tartaroo (G5020) "cast to Tartarus" - divine judgment Rev 12:9 ekballo (G1544) "cast out" - forcible expulsion

2 Peter 2:4 describes the primordial rebellion - when angels "sinned" and were condemned. Revelation 12:7-12 describes the later expulsion at Christ's victory.

docs.title: What This Means
docs.text:
Between the primordial rebellion and Christ's victory, Satan retained limited heavenly access as "the accuser": - Job 1:6, 2:1 - Satan "came among them" before the LORD (~2000 BC) - Zechariah 3:1 - Satan accusing Joshua (~520 BC) - Revelation 12:10 - "accused them before our God day and night"

At Christ's victory, this accuser role was revoked: "their place found no more in heaven" (Rev 12:8).

Both events show that "cast down" angels remain active. This transforms how we understand "chains of darkness."

docs.title: 1. Angels Rebelled Against God
docs.text: At the primordial rebellion, Satan drew a third of the angels away from God (Rev 12:4a). They "kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation" (Jude 6). They sinned by rebelling against God.

docs.title: 2. God Judged Them
docs.text: God "cast them down to hell" (tartaroo - 2 Peter 2:4). They were condemned - "delivered into chains of darkness."

docs.title: 3. They Exist in "Chains of Darkness"
docs.text:
This describes their spiritual state, not physical imprisonment: - Chains = bound to judgment, fate sealed, cannot escape - Darkness = spiritual condition, separated from God's light

This is consistent with how Scripture describes humans in "darkness" who are still active (Matt 4:16; John 3:19; Col 1:13).

docs.title: 4. They Are "Reserved unto Judgment"
docs.text: Their fate is determined. They "know they have but a short time" (Rev 12:12). The lake of fire is "prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matt 25:41). But until that judgment, they remain active.

docs.title: 5. Peter's Main Point
docs.text: God judges sin. If He judged angels, He will certainly judge false teachers. This is Peter's argument - not a treatise on angelology.

docs.title: What This Means for Common Assumptions
The "Two Classes of Fallen Angels" Theory
docs.text:
Common view: 2 Peter 2:4 describes a special group of imprisoned angels, separate from Satan and active demons.

Problem: This creates an unbiblical distinction not found in Scripture. Revelation 12 uses the same "cast down" language for angels who are clearly active.

Simpler reading: All fallen angels are "in chains of darkness" (spiritually condemned) and "reserved unto judgment" - yet remain active until that judgment comes.

docs.title: The Genesis 6 Connection
docs.text:
Common view: These angels are specifically those who sinned in Genesis 6 by taking human wives.

Problems: 1. 2 Peter 2:4 doesn't mention Genesis 6 2. Peter's sequence isn't necessarily chronological 3. "Sons of God" in Genesis 6 isn't explicitly identified as angels 4. Revelation 12 provides a simpler explanation

Simpler reading: These are the angels who rebelled with Satan, as described in Revelation 12 and Jude 6.

docs.title: The Cultural Background of "Tartaroo"
docs.text:
Tartaroo appears only here in the entire NT. Peter chose this word deliberately. In Greek cultural usage, Tartarus was where the Titans were imprisoned after rebelling against the divine order. The Titans did not marry humans; they waged war against Zeus. Peter's audience would have understood tartaroo as punishment for rebellion against divine authority -- not sexual transgression.

Understanding why Peter chose this specific word is standard lexicography, not importing pagan theology. The cultural background actually reinforces the rebellion reading, which aligns with Revelation 12's biblical description of angels being "cast down" after warring against God.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Question Answer Did some angels sin? Yes - they rebelled with Satan Did God judge them? Yes - cast them out of heaven What are "chains of darkness"? Spiritual state - condemned, in darkness, fate sealed Are they inactive? No - Rev 12 shows cast-down angels active with "great wrath" Do they await judgment? Yes - "reserved" / "short time" Are they different from active demons? No evidence - same language describes both Is this Genesis 6? Uncertain - text doesn't say, Rev 12 provides simpler explanation Is this 1 Peter 3:19? No - different vocabulary (spirits vs. angels), different subjects

docs.title: Final Statement
docs.text:
2 Peter 2:4, read alongside the Revelation 12 timing study, teaches that:

  1. Angels rebelled against God at the primordial rebellion (Rev 12:4a, Jude 6)
  2. God condemned them - "tartaroo" (cast to Tartarus), "chains of darkness"
  3. They retained limited heavenly access as "the accuser" (Job 1-2, Zech 3)
  4. At Christ's victory, they were expelled - "their place found no more" (Rev 12:7-12)
  5. They remain active on earth - Rev 12:12-17 shows them with "great wrath," making war
  6. They await final judgment - lake of fire (Matt 25:41, Rev 20:10)

The phrase "chains of darkness" describes their condemned spiritual state, not physical imprisonment. There is no biblical warrant for distinguishing between "imprisoned angels" and "active demons" - the same language describes beings who are clearly active.

See also: /home/michael/bible/bible-studies/revelation-12-timing/ for the full analysis of the two events in Revelation 12.

Peter's application remains: If God judged angels, He will judge false teachers. And He will deliver the godly (2 Peter 2:9).

docs.title: State of the Dead
docs.text: This study is consistent with the state-of-the-dead conclusion. The final judgment (lake of fire) results in destruction, not eternal conscious torment. The angels are "reserved" for this destruction.

docs.title: Fate of the Wicked
docs.text: Satan and his angels face the same fate as the wicked: the lake of fire, which Ezekiel 28:18-19 describes as bringing Satan to "ashes" so he exists "no more."

docs.title: 1 Peter 3:19-20
docs.text: That study concluded the "spirits in prison" were HUMANS who rejected Noah's preaching. This is a different subject from the "angels that sinned" in 2 Peter 2:4. The vocabulary differs (pneuma vs. aggelos), and the contexts are distinct.

docs.title: Topics Research: "All Flesh Had Corrupted His Way" (Genesis 6:12)
Question
docs.text:
The angel view argues that "all flesh had corrupted his way" implies more than moral corruption - suggesting genetic/biological contamination through angel-human hybridization that required the flood to purify the corrupted gene pool.

Does this phrase support the genetic corruption interpretation?

docs.title: FLESH
docs.text:
• FIGURATIVE
  • Fruits of GAL 5:19-21
  • SYMBOLICAL
  • Body of Christ symbolized by the bread JHN 6:51-63

Never for genetics or biology.

docs.title: Verse Analysis: "All Flesh Had Corrupted His Way" (Genesis 6:12)
The Angel View Claim
docs.text: "'All flesh had corrupted his way' implies more than moral corruption. The phrase suggests genetic/biological contamination through angel-human hybridization. The flood was necessary to purify the corrupted gene pool."

docs.title: The Question
docs.text: Does the phrase "all flesh had corrupted his way" support a genetic/biological interpretation, or does it describe moral corruption?

docs.title: What Genesis 6 Actually Says
docs.text:
Verse Description Type 6:3 "he also [is] flesh" Human nature (mortal) 6:5 "wickedness of man was great" Moral 6:5 "every imagination of thoughts...only evil continually" Moral 6:6 "grieved him at his heart" Response to moral failure 6:11 "earth was corrupt before God" Moral (before God = spiritually) 6:11 "filled with violence" Moral (behavior) 6:12 "all flesh had corrupted his way" Moral (conduct) 6:13 "filled with violence through them" Moral (behavior)

The context is entirely moral. There is no mention of: - Genetics or DNA - Biological contamination - Hybrid offspring - Gene pool corruption

docs.title: The Flow of Thought
docs.text:
1. God observes that wickedness is great (v.5)
  2. Every thought is only evil (v.5) - MORAL condition
  3. God is grieved at heart (v.6) - emotional response to rebellion
  4. Earth is corrupt and violent (v.11) - MORAL state
  5. All flesh had corrupted his way (v.12) - MORAL conduct
  6. Earth filled with violence (v.13) - MORAL behavior
  7. Therefore God will destroy (v.13) - judgment for SIN

docs.title: Hebrew Analysis
docs.text:
שָׁחַת דַּרְכּוֹ (shachath darko) = "corrupt his way"

  • שָׁחַת (shachath) - to ruin, spoil, act corruptly
  • דֶּרֶךְ (derek) - way, road, path; figuratively: manner of life, conduct

The phrase means: "ruined/spoiled his manner of life" = corrupt CONDUCT.

docs.title: How Scripture Uses "Corrupt + Way"
docs.text:
Every parallel passage uses this phrase for MORAL corruption:

Passage Context Type of Corruption Deuteronomy 9:12 Golden calf idolatry Moral - idolatry Deuteronomy 31:29 Future apostasy Moral - turning from God Deuteronomy 32:5 "Perverse and crooked generation" Moral - character Judges 2:19 Following false gods Moral - religious apostasy Hosea 9:9 "As in the days of Gibeah" Moral - depravity Psalm 14:1; 53:1 "Abominable works" Moral - sinful actions Ezekiel 16:47 Jerusalem's sins Moral - abominations Malachi 2:8 Corrupt priests Moral - covenant violation

Zero instances of "corrupt way" meaning genetic corruption.

docs.title: The Burden of Proof
docs.text:
If "corrupt his way" means genetic corruption in Genesis 6:12, we would expect: 1. At least one other passage using the phrase genetically 2. Context indicating biological meaning 3. Some Hebrew indication of physical/genetic damage

None of these exist. The genetic interpretation is read INTO the text, not derived FROM it.

docs.title: Biblical Usage Categories
docs.text: Category Examples Meaning All creatures Gen 6:17, 19; 7:15, 21; 9:15-17 Every air-breathing animal All humanity Ps 65:2; Isa 40:5; Luke 3:6; Acts 2:17 All people everywhere Human frailty Gen 6:3; Isa 40:6; Job 34:15; 1 Pet 1:24 Mortal nature

docs.title: Genesis 6:3 - The Defining Statement
docs.text:
"My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also [is] flesh"

God identifies the problem: man is "flesh" - meaning: - Mortal, earthly nature - Weak, prone to sin - Contrasted with God's Spirit

This is NOT about genetics but about human nature prone to sin.

docs.title: The Scope in Genesis 6:12
docs.text:
"All flesh had corrupted his way" means: - All humanity (possibly including animals as collateral) - Had ruined their manner of life - Universal moral corruption

The word "all" emphasizes extent, not a special type of corruption.

docs.title: The Angel View's Reasoning
docs.text:
1. "All flesh" is mentioned
  2. Flood destroyed "all flesh"
  3. Therefore "all flesh" must have been genetically corrupted
  4. Therefore angels corrupted human genetics

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: This is circular reasoning: - It assumes genetic corruption to prove genetic corruption - It ignores the explicit moral descriptions in the text - It imports a meaning not found in any parallel passage

docs.title: What the Text Actually Says
docs.text:
What God SAW What God SAID Category Wickedness great (6:5) "I will destroy man" (6:7) Moral Every thought evil (6:5) "End of all flesh is come" (6:13) Moral Earth corrupt (6:11) "Filled with violence through them" (6:13) Moral Filled with violence (6:11) "I will destroy them" (6:13) Moral

God explains His own reasons - all are MORAL.

docs.title: Double Emphasis
docs.text: Verse Statement 6:11 "the earth was filled with violence" 6:13 "the earth is filled with violence through them"

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
If the concern were genetic corruption: - Why emphasize VIOLENCE twice? - Why not mention genetic damage? - Why focus on behavior rather than biology?

Violence is a MORAL problem - the result of "every imagination only evil continually" (6:5).

docs.title: The Causal Chain
docs.text:
1. Evil thoughts (6:5) →
  2. Corrupt ways (6:12) →
  3. Violence filling the earth (6:11, 13) →
  4. Divine judgment (6:7, 13)

This is a moral chain, not a genetic one.

docs.title: Genesis 6:11
docs.text:
"The earth also was corrupt before God"

Hebrew: לִפְנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (liphnei ha'elohim) = "before the face of God"

This phrase emphasizes: - Moral/spiritual offense - God as the standard being violated - Corruption in His sight

If the corruption were merely biological/genetic: - It would exist regardless of God - It wouldn't need the qualifier "before God" - The emphasis on God's perspective indicates MORAL offense

docs.title: flood-judgment-severity Study
docs.text: That study established: - Every stated reason for the flood is MORAL (wickedness, evil thoughts, violence) - Hebrew words (shachath, tamim, chamas) describe MORAL qualities - The severity matches the UNIVERSALITY of moral corruption, not a special type

docs.title: genesis-6-sons-of-god Study
docs.text: That study established: - "Sons of God" are more likely the Sethite line than angels - The context is an earthly scene of marriage - Moses uses different terminology for angels (malak) elsewhere - Genesis 6:3 calls them "flesh" - human, not angelic

docs.title: If "All Flesh Corrupted" = Genetic Damage
docs.text:
The angel view must explain:

  1. Why does every parallel use of "corrupt way" mean MORAL corruption?

  2. Why does the context emphasize violence (behavior) twice?

  3. Why does God say "filled with violence THROUGH THEM"?

  4. "Through them" indicates THEIR actions caused the violence

  5. Not that something was done TO them (genetic damage)

  6. Why does God focus on "every imagination of the thoughts"?

  7. Thoughts are MORAL, not genetic

  8. Imagination is about choices, not DNA

  9. Why is "corrupt before God" used?

  10. Moral offense before God
  11. Not biological damage

"all flesh [בָּשָׂר] had corrupted his way"

docs.title: Conclusion: "All Flesh Had Corrupted His Way" (Genesis 6:12)
Question
docs.text: The angel view argues that "all flesh had corrupted his way" implies genetic/biological contamination through angel-human hybridization. Does this phrase support the genetic corruption interpretation?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text:
The phrase "all flesh had corrupted his way" describes MORAL corruption, not genetic contamination. Every word in the phrase has established moral/behavioral meaning in Scripture:

  • "All flesh" = all humanity (never genetics)
  • "Corrupted" (shachath) = ruined morally (Deut 9:12; 32:5; Judges 2:19 - always moral)
  • "His way" (derek) = manner of life, conduct (never genetics)

The identical phrase pattern "corrupt + way" appears multiple times in Scripture and always describes moral corruption - idolatry, apostasy, covenant violation. The immediate context (Genesis 6:5-13) gives exclusively MORAL reasons for the flood: wickedness, evil thoughts, violence. The genetic interpretation has no textual support.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Genesis 6:5 And GOD saw that the wickedness of man [was] great in the earth, and [that] every imagination of the thoughts of his heart [was] only evil continually.

Genesis 6:11 The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.

Genesis 6:12 And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.

Genesis 6:13 And God said unto Noah, The end of all flesh is come before me; for the earth is filled with violence through them.

docs.title: Genesis 6 Exclusively Describes MORAL Corruption
docs.text:
Verse Description Category 6:5 "wickedness of man was great" Moral 6:5 "every imagination...only evil continually" Moral 6:11 "corrupt before God" Moral (spiritual offense) 6:11 "filled with violence" Moral (behavior) 6:12 "all flesh had corrupted his way" Moral (conduct) 6:13 "filled with violence through them" Moral (behavior)

docs.text: Hebrew Transliteration Meaning כָּל־בָּשָׂר kol-basar "all flesh" = all humanity שָׁחַת shachath "corrupt" = ruin morally (H7843) דֶּרֶךְ derek "way" = manner of life, conduct (H1870)

docs.title: שָׁחַת (shachath) - Key Observation
docs.text: When this word describes people corrupting themselves, it ALWAYS refers to MORAL corruption: - Exodus 32:7 - Golden calf - Deuteronomy 4:16 - Idolatry - Deuteronomy 9:12 - Golden calf - Deuteronomy 31:29 - Future apostasy - Judges 2:19 - Religious apostasy - Hosea 9:9 - Gibeah's depravity

docs.title: The Angel View's Argument
docs.text:
1. "All flesh" is mentioned
  2. The flood was severe
  3. Therefore the corruption must have been genetic
  4. Therefore angels corrupted human genetics

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
This is circular reasoning that ignores the text:

  1. The text explicitly says the corruption was moral (wickedness, evil thoughts, violence)
  2. Every parallel use of "corrupt way" is moral
  3. The phrase "before God" indicates spiritual/moral offense
  4. "Filled with violence through them" describes behavior, not biology

docs.title: The Counter-Questions
docs.text:
If "all flesh had corrupted his way" means genetic damage:

  1. Why does every parallel passage use this phrase for MORAL corruption?

  2. Why is violence emphasized twice (v.11, 13)?

  3. Violence is behavior, not genetics

  4. Why does God say "through them"?

  5. "Filled with violence through them" = THEY caused it

  6. Not something done TO them

  7. Why focus on "imagination of thoughts"?

  8. Thoughts are moral, not genetic

  9. Why "corrupt before God"?

  10. Moral offense in God's sight, not biological damage

docs.title: flood-judgment-severity Study
docs.text: That study established: - Every stated reason for the flood is MORAL - Hebrew words (shachath, tamim, chamas) describe moral qualities - Severity matches universality of moral corruption

docs.title: genesis-6-sons-of-god Study
docs.text: That study established: - "Sons of God" are more likely the Sethite line - Genesis 6:3 calls them "flesh" (human, not angelic) - Moses uses different terminology for angels (malak)

docs.title: Final Assessment
docs.text:
The phrase "all flesh had corrupted his way" describes universal moral corruption:

Element Meaning "All flesh" Every human being "Had corrupted" Ruined morally "His way" His manner of life/conduct

Full meaning: Every person had ruined their manner of life through sin.

The angel view's genetic interpretation: - Has no support from the Hebrew words - Has no parallel in Scripture - Contradicts the explicit moral descriptions in context - Ignores the emphasis on violence (behavior) - Ignores "before God" (spiritual offense)

The text explains itself. The flood came because of universal moral corruption - wickedness, evil thoughts, and violence - not genetic contamination.

Genesis 18:1 And the LORD appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre: and he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day;

docs.text:
Genesis 19:1 And there came two angels to Sodom at even; and Lot sat in the gate of Sodom: and Lot seeing [them] rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face toward the ground;

Genesis 19:2 And he said, Behold now, my lords, turn in, I pray you, into your servant's house, and tarry all night, and wash your feet, and ye shall rise up early, and go on your ways. And they said, Nay; but we will abide in the street all night.

Genesis 19:3 And he pressed upon them greatly; and they turned in unto him, and entered into his house; and he made them a feast, and did bake unleavened bread, and they did eat.

Genesis 19:6 And Lot went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him,

Genesis 19:7 And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.

docs.text:

docs.title: Part 2: The Logical Fallacy
docs.text:
The angel view's argument follows this pattern:

  1. Angels can appear in physical form ✓ (Scripture shows this)
  2. Angels can eat food in physical form ✓ (Scripture shows this)
  3. Therefore angels can reproduce ✗ (Non sequitur)

This is a logical fallacy. One capability does not prove another.

docs.title: Analogies Showing the Fallacy
docs.text:
Premise 1 Premise 2 Invalid Conclusion A man can walk A man can talk Therefore a man can fly Angels can appear Angels can eat Therefore angels can reproduce

The ability to temporarily appear in human form and eat food does not demonstrate the ability to reproduce biologically.

docs.title: Part 3: Temporary Manifestation vs. Biological Nature
Key Distinctions
docs.text: Temporary Manifestation Biological Nature Appearing in form for a specific mission Having reproductive DNA/genetics Eating as accommodation to hospitality Having a functioning digestive system Form disappears after mission Permanent biological existence No offspring ever mentioned Would produce offspring

docs.title: The Evidence from Genesis 18-19
docs.text:
The angels: - Appeared for a specific mission (announcing Isaac's birth, judging Sodom) - Ate as guests (accommodation to human hospitality customs) - Left/disappeared after the mission was complete - Produced no offspring despite appearing in physical form

Critical question: If angels could reproduce in physical form, where is the biblical evidence of it happening in Genesis 18-19?

The angels in Sodom: - Appeared as desirable men - Were pursued by the Sodomites - Produced no offspring

docs.text:
"Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?"

Analysis:

Angels are spirits (πνεύματα, pneumata) by nature. A spirit can appear in physical form; that doesn't change its essential nature into a biological being with reproductive capability.

What Angels ARE What Angels CAN DO Spirits by nature Appear in physical form Non-biological Eat food (accommodation) Non-reproductive Deliver messages Immortal Execute judgment

Appearing in a form does not equal becoming that form with all its biological capabilities.

docs.text: "This refers to angels 'in heaven,' not fallen angels. Fallen angels may have different capabilities."

docs.title: Problems with This Response
docs.text:
1. Jesus speaks of angelic NATURE, not just location

  • "Are as the angels" - describing what they are like
  • Resurrected humans will be "equal unto the angels" - same nature
  • The comparison is about essential nature, not geography

2. No biblical evidence fallen angels gain new abilities

  • Scripture never states that rebels gain reproductive powers
  • This is pure speculation with no textual support
  • Why would rebellion GRANT new capabilities?

3. The teaching is categorical

  • Jesus compares resurrected saints TO angels
  • The logic: angels don't marry → resurrected saints won't marry
  • This only works if angels categorically don't marry
  • If some angels (fallen) could marry, the comparison fails

docs.title: Part 7: The Angel in Judges 13 - A Counter-Example
The Angel Refused to Eat
docs.text:

docs.title: What the Angel View Must Prove
docs.text:
1. That temporary physical manifestation includes reproductive biology
  2. That eating food proves reproductive capability
  3. That fallen angels gain abilities faithful angels lack
  4. That this is what Genesis 6 describes

docs.text:
The argument from Genesis 18-19 proves only what everyone agrees on: angels can temporarily appear in physical form.

It does NOT prove: - Angels have biological reproductive capability - Angels can produce offspring with humans - Fallen angels have abilities faithful angels lack - Genesis 6 describes angel-human marriages

docs.text: Demonstrated NOT Demonstrated Angels can appear in human form Angels have reproductive biology Angels can eat food (accommodation) Eating proves reproductive capability Angels appeared as ordinary men Fallen angels can do what faithful cannot The Sodomites didn't recognize them as angels Genesis 6 describes angel-human unions

docs.title: The Key Distinction
docs.text:
Temporary manifestation for mission ≠ Permanent biological nature with reproduction

A spirit can appear in a form without becoming a biological being. The angels ate, appeared desirable, were pursued by the Sodomites - and produced no offspring. If physical form included reproductive capability, where is the evidence?

docs.title: Word Studies: Angels Appearing in Physical Form
מַלְאָךְ (mal'ak) - "Angel/Messenger"
docs.text:
Strong's H4397

  • Transliteration: mal'ak
  • Pronunciation: mal-awk'
  • Part of Speech: Masculine noun
  • Etymology: From an unused root meaning "to despatch as a deputy"

Definition: Messenger, representative. Used for both human messengers and divine messengers (angels).

KJV Translation Frequency: - "angel" - 111 occurrences - "messenger" - 98 occurrences - "ambassadors" - 4 occurrences - Total: 214 times

Genesis 19:1 Usage:

"And there came two angels [מַלְאָכִים, malakim] to Sodom..."

Significance: Moses explicitly calls these beings "angels" (malakim). He knew the Hebrew word for celestial messengers and used it here. In Genesis 6:2, Moses uses a different phrase entirely - "sons of God" (bene ha'elohim) - suggesting different referents.

docs.title: אֲנָשִׁים (anashim) - "Men"
docs.text:
Strong's H582 (plural of אֱנוֹשׁ enosh)

  • Transliteration: anashim
  • Pronunciation: an-aw-sheem'
  • Definition: Men, people, mankind

Genesis 18:2 Usage:

"lo, three men [אֲנָשִׁים, anashim] stood by him"

Genesis 19:5 Usage:

"Where are the men [אֲנָשִׁים, anashim] which came in to thee this night?"

Significance: - In Genesis 18:2, the beings are described as "men" - their appearance - In Genesis 19:5, the Sodomites call them "men" - they didn't know they were angels - Moses (the author) calls them "angels" in 19:1, but the Sodomites saw only "men"

docs.title: πνεῦμα (pneuma) - "Spirit"
docs.text:
Strong's G4151

  • Transliteration: pneuma
  • Pronunciation: pnyoo'-mah
  • Part of Speech: Neuter noun
  • Root Etymology: From G4154 (πνέω - to blow or breathe)

Definition: A current of air, breath; by extension, a spirit - the human soul, angels, demons, or God's Holy Spirit.

KJV Translation Frequency: - "Spirit" - 111 occurrences - "Holy Ghost" - 89 occurrences - "spirit" (human) - 49 occurrences - "spirit" (evil) - 47 occurrences

Hebrews 1:7 Usage:

"Who maketh his angels spirits [πνεύματα, pneumata]"

Hebrews 1:14 Usage:

"Are they not all ministering spirits [πνεύματα, pneumata]"

Significance: Angels are defined as "spirits" by essential nature. A spirit can appear in physical form without becoming a biological being. The form is temporary; the nature (spirit) is permanent.

docs.title: ἄγγελος (angelos) - "Angel/Messenger"
docs.text:
Strong's G32

  • Transliteration: angelos
  • Pronunciation: ang'-el-os
  • Part of Speech: Masculine noun

Definition: A messenger; specifically, an angel (divine messenger)

Matthew 22:30 Usage:

"but are as the angels [ἄγγελοι, angeloi] of God in heaven"

Luke 20:36 Usage:

"for they are equal unto the angels [ἀγγέλοις, angelois]"

Significance: Jesus uses "angels" (angeloi) as the comparison point for resurrected believers who will not marry. The comparison is categorical - describing angelic nature, not just location.

docs.title: γαμέω (gameo) - "Marry"
docs.text:
Strong's G1060

  • Transliteration: gameo
  • Pronunciation: gam-eh'-o
  • Part of Speech: Verb

Definition: To wed, marry (of either sex)

Matthew 22:30 Usage:

"they neither marry [γαμοῦσιν, gamousin], nor are given in marriage"

Mark 12:25 Usage:

"they neither marry [γαμοῦσιν, gamousin], nor are given in marriage"

Significance: Jesus states that in the resurrection, people will be "as the angels" - who do not marry. This statement about angelic nature is the basis for the teaching about resurrected humans.

docs.title: "As the Angels of God in Heaven" (Matthew 22:30)
docs.text:
Greek: ὡς ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν οὐρανῷ (hos angeloi tou theou en ourano)

Components: - ὡς (hos) - "as, like" - comparison - ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ - "angels of God" - ἐν οὐρανῷ - "in heaven"

Angel View Response: This refers only to "angels in heaven," not fallen angels.

Problems with This Interpretation:

  1. The comparison is about NATURE
  2. "Are as the angels" - what they are like
  3. Jesus is describing what resurrected humans will resemble

  4. The comparison requires angels to categorically not marry

  5. No distinction between faithful and fallen

  6. Scripture never says fallen angels can marry while faithful cannot
  7. Rebellion does not grant new capabilities

  8. This is speculation without textual support

  9. Luke 20:36 removes the location qualifier

  10. "Equal unto the angels" - no "in heaven" here
  11. The comparison is to angelic nature itself

docs.title: "Equal unto the Angels" (Luke 20:36)
docs.text:
Greek: ἰσάγγελοι (isangeloi)

  • Transliteration: isangeloi
  • Pronunciation: ee-sang'-el-oi
  • Definition: "Like angels" or "equal to angels"
  • Compound: ἴσος (isos, "equal") + ἄγγελος (angelos, "angel")

Significance: This unique word describes resurrected believers as having angelic-like nature. The specific quality in view is the non-marrying state. This confirms that the teaching is about essential angelic nature, not merely the behavior of angels currently in heaven.
