docs.title: Analysis: Jesus on Angels and Marriage -- The Hermeneutical Ceiling
The Sadducees' Challenge
docs.text: The Sadducees denied the resurrection (Matt 22:23; Mark 12:18; Luke 20:27). Their question about the woman married to seven brothers was designed as a reductio ad absurdum -- if resurrection is real, whose wife is she? They assumed the resurrection life would be identical to earthly life, making multiple marriages absurd.

docs.title: Jesus's Double Rebuke
docs.text: Jesus rebuked them for two failures (Matt 22:29; Mark 12:24): 1. Not knowing the Scriptures -- the OT teaches resurrection 2. Not knowing the power of God -- God can create a new order of existence

docs.title: The Nature of Jesus's Answer
docs.text: Jesus does not merely answer "she belongs to none of them." He makes a far more profound statement: the entire CATEGORY of marriage ceases in the resurrection, and He grounds this in angelic nature. This is not a passing comment -- it is a doctrinal declaration about both resurrection existence and angelic nature.

docs.title: Matthew 22:30
docs.text:
Greek: ἐν γὰρ τῇ ἀναστάσει οὔτε γαμοῦσιν οὔτε γαμίζονται, ἀλλ' ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ εἰσιν.

Structure: - Temporal frame: ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει -- "in the resurrection" (dative of time) - Double negation: οὔτε...οὔτε -- "neither...nor" (comprehensive denial) - γαμοῦσιν (gamousin) -- [V-PAI-3P] Present Active Indicative 3rd Plural -- "they marry" - γαμίζονται (gamizontai) -- [V-PPI-3P] Present Passive Indicative 3rd Plural -- "they are given in marriage" - Contrast: ἀλλ' -- "but" (strong adversative) - Comparison: ὡς ἄγγελοι -- "as angels" - Location/description: ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ εἰσιν -- "in heaven are/exist"

Unique to Matthew: "of God" (τοῦ Θεοῦ in some manuscripts) -- "angels of God in heaven." This adds divine association.

docs.title: Mark 12:25
docs.text:
Greek: ὅταν γὰρ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῶσιν, οὔτε γαμοῦσιν οὔτε γαμίζονται, ἀλλ' εἰσὶν ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς.

Structure: - Temporal frame: ὅταν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῶσιν -- "when from [the] dead they rise" (temporal clause with subjunctive ἀναστῶσιν [V-2AAS-3P]) - Double negation: οὔτε...οὔτε -- identical to Matthew - Same verbs: γαμοῦσιν, γαμίζονται - Contrast: ἀλλ' -- strong adversative - Being-state + comparison: εἰσὶν ὡς ἄγγελοι -- "they are as angels" - Location: ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς -- "in the heavens" (plural, different from Matthew's singular)

Note: Mark's word order places the verb "are" (εἰσιν) BEFORE the comparison, emphasizing the state of being: "they ARE as angels." Matthew places it after: "as angels in heaven they are."

docs.title: Luke 20:34-36
docs.text:
Greek (v.34): Οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου γαμοῦσιν καὶ γαμίσκονται, Greek (v.35): οἱ δὲ καταξιωθέντες τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐκείνου τυχεῖν καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῆς ἐκ νεκρῶν οὔτε γαμοῦσιν οὔτε γαμίζονται· Greek (v.36): οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀποθανεῖν ἔτι δύνανται, ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσιν, καὶ υἱοί εἰσιν Θεοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως υἱοὶ ὄντες.

Structure: - Two-age contrast (v.34-35): - "The sons of this age" (οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου) -- marry and are given in marriage - "Those counted worthy of that age" (οἱ καταξιωθέντες τοῦ αἰῶνος ἐκείνου) -- neither marry nor are given in marriage - Three explanatory clauses (v.36): 1. "Neither CAN they die any more" (οὐδὲ ἀποθανεῖν ἔτι δύνανται) 2. "For they are equal-to-angels" (ἰσάγγελοι γάρ εἰσιν) 3. "And they are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection" (καὶ υἱοί εἰσιν Θεοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως υἱοὶ ὄντες)

Unique to Luke: 1. The "this age / that age" contrast -- marriage belongs to THIS age, not the age to come 2. The explicit statement about inability to die (ἀποθανεῖν δύνανται -- with δύνανται indicating capability) 3. The hapax ἰσάγγελοι -- "angel-equal" without any "in heaven" qualifier 4. The title "children of God" linked to "children of the resurrection"

docs.title: 3. The "In Heaven" Qualifier -- Does It Limit the Statement?
The Angel View Argument
docs.text: Some who hold the angel view of Genesis 6 argue: "Jesus said 'the angels of God in heaven' -- this limits the statement to faithful angels who remain in heaven. Fallen angels, who are NOT in heaven, may be capable of marriage."

docs.title: A. Luke's Parallel Eliminates the Limitation
docs.text: Luke's account uses ἰσάγγελοι (isangeloi) -- "equal unto the angels" -- with NO "in heaven" qualifier. If "in heaven" were a theologically significant limitation (restricting the teaching to faithful angels only), Luke's omission would be a serious theological error. But all three accounts report the same teaching of Jesus. Luke's version shows that the "in heaven" phrase is descriptive (telling us where angels are), not restrictive (limiting which angels the statement covers).

docs.title: B. Grammatical Analysis
docs.text: In both Matthew and Mark, "in heaven" (ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ / ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς) is a standard locative phrase. It tells WHERE the angels are. Compare: - "the God of Abraham" -- does this mean God is ONLY the God of Abraham? No, it describes His relationship. - "the angels in heaven" -- does this mean ONLY angels in heaven? The phrase describes their location, not an exclusive category.

docs.title: C. The Logical Test
docs.text: If Jesus meant "ONLY the faithful angels in heaven don't marry, but fallen angels CAN marry," then: 1. His comparison fails. Saying "you'll be like the angels in heaven who don't marry" would be meaningless if other angels DO marry. 2. It would be like saying "in the resurrection you'll be like the birds in the sky that can fly" -- implying some birds cannot fly, which undermines the comparison. 3. The Sadducees would not have been answered -- they could reply: "So some angels DO marry? Then resurrection beings MIGHT marry too."

docs.title: D. The Textual Tradition
docs.text: The Textus Receptus of Matthew 22:30 includes "τοῦ Θεοῦ" (of God) -- "angels of God in heaven." But this is a further description ("God's angels"), not a restriction. All angels are God's angels by creation, whether faithful or fallen.

docs.title: Conclusion on "In Heaven"
docs.text: "In heaven" is a locative descriptor, not a categorical restrictor. It tells us where angels properly belong and exist. Luke's parallel (isangeloi, without qualifier) proves this is a statement about ANGELIC NATURE, not a statement limited to a subset of angels.

docs.title: 4. The Logical Structure of Jesus's Comparison
The Comparison Stated
docs.text: Jesus says: Resurrected saints will be like angels in that they do not marry.

docs.title: Formal Logic
docs.text: Let the comparison be expressed as: - P = "Resurrected saints will not marry" - Q = "Angels do not marry" - Jesus's statement: P is true BECAUSE they will be like beings for whom Q is true

docs.title: For the Comparison to Work
docs.text:
Q must be categorically true of angels -- ALL angels must not marry. If some angels (fallen ones) CAN and DO marry, then Q is not categorically true, and the comparison breaks.

Analogy 1: "In the new creation, humans will not lie, but will be like dogs in their loyalty." - This comparison works only if dogs are categorically loyal. - If some dogs are disloyal, the comparison fails -- you cannot predicate a quality of a class if that class does not universally possess it.

Analogy 2: "In heaven, the saints will not steal, but will be like the angels who do not steal." - If some angels DO steal, this comparison is meaningless. - The comparison assumes the quality is a categorical feature of the comparison class.

Analogy 3: "You will be like humans who don't murder." - This is absurd because some humans DO murder. - It fails as a comparison precisely because the quality is not universal to the class.

docs.title: The Angel View's Dilemma
docs.text: If fallen angels CAN marry (as the angel view of Genesis 6 requires), then: - "Angels" as a class do NOT categorically abstain from marriage - Jesus's comparison ("like angels who don't marry") would be comparing resurrected saints to a class that DOES contain members who marry - The comparison fails logically

docs.title: No Escape via "In Heaven"
docs.text: Even if one argues "in heaven" limits it to faithful angels, the comparison still has problems: 1. Why would Jesus compare resurrected saints to a SUBSET of angels? 2. If the quality (not marrying) is only true of SOME angels, it is not a defining characteristic of angelic nature 3. The Sadducees would have no reason to accept the answer -- the exception would undermine the rule

docs.title: 5. What Does "Equal Unto the Angels" (isangeloi) Actually Predicate?
Luke's Three-Part Statement (20:36)
docs.text:
1. "Neither can they die any more" -- IMMORTALITY
  2. "For they are equal unto the angels" -- ANGELIC NATURE
  3. "And are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection" -- DIVINE SONSHIP

docs.title: The Connecting Logic
docs.text:
The word γάρ (gar, "for") connects these clauses causally: - They cannot die because (gar) they are isangeloi - They are isangeloi and (kai) they are sons of God

The inability to die is GROUNDED IN being angel-equal. This means isangeloi refers to a NATURE or CONDITION, not merely a behavioral comparison. Angels by nature do not die. Resurrected saints, being isangeloi, will by nature not die. The same logic applies to marriage: angels by nature do not marry (v.35), and resurrected saints, being isangeloi, will by nature not marry.

docs.title: What Quality Is Being Predicated?
docs.text:
Some argue isangeloi refers ONLY to immortality. But the context is broader: - v.34: This age -- they marry - v.35: That age -- they do NOT marry - v.36: They cannot die; they are isangeloi; they are children of God

The structure shows that BOTH non-marriage (v.35) AND immortality (v.36a) are characteristics of being isangeloi. The angel-equality encompasses the full range of qualities Jesus has just described.

docs.title: gameo (G1060) + gamizo/gamisko (G1061)
docs.text: These are the standard Greek words for the marriage institution: - gameo = to marry (active, typically the groom's action) - gamizo/gamisko = to give in marriage (passive, typically the father giving the bride)

docs.title: Usage Throughout the NT
docs.text:
gameo appears 29 times in the NT, always meaning literal marriage: - Matt 5:32; 19:9, 10 -- divorce and remarriage teaching - 1 Cor 7:9, 28, 33, 36, 38, 39 -- Paul's marriage counsel - 1 Tim 4:3; 5:11, 14 -- pastoral instructions about marriage

There is NO instance in the NT where gameo is used euphemistically for sexual relations outside marriage. It always refers to the institution of marriage itself.

docs.title: Significance for Genesis 6
docs.text: The angel view of Genesis 6 argues that angels "took wives" (laqach ishshah, Gen 6:2). Jesus uses the specific Greek marriage vocabulary (gameo/gamizo) to say angels do NOT do this. The angel view must argue that some angels DID what Jesus says angels categorically do NOT do.

docs.title: The Principle
docs.text: A hermeneutical ceiling is an interpretive constraint established by a clear, authoritative text that limits how other, less clear texts may be interpreted. It is a boundary that no interpretation may exceed without contradicting established teaching.

docs.title: Jesus's Authority
docs.text:
Jesus is not merely one interpreter among many. He is: - The Son of God (Matt 16:16; John 1:1, 14) - The Truth (John 14:6) - The ultimate authority on Scripture (Matt 5:17-18; Luke 24:27, 44-45) - The Creator of angels (Col 1:16; Heb 1:2)

When Jesus makes a statement about angelic nature, He speaks with absolute authority. He made the angels. He knows their nature.

docs.title: The Ceiling Applied
docs.text:
Clear text (ceiling): Matthew 22:30 / Mark 12:25 / Luke 20:35-36 -- Angels do not marry.

Ambiguous text (below the ceiling): Genesis 6:1-4 -- "Sons of God" took "daughters of men" as wives.

The hermeneutical principle is: Clear NT teaching interprets ambiguous OT passages, not vice versa.

If Jesus teaches that angels do not marry, then no interpretation of Genesis 6 that requires angel marriages can be correct. The ceiling constrains the interpretation.

docs.title: This Is Not an Argument from Silence
docs.text:
An argument from silence would be: "The Bible never says angels CAN marry, therefore they cannot." That would be weak.

This is different. This is a direct, positive teaching from Christ: angels do NOT marry. This is not silence -- it is declaration. It is not inference -- it is assertion. Jesus did not merely fail to mention angel marriages; He explicitly stated that angels do not marry, and used this as the basis for a theological comparison.

docs.title: The Counter-Argument Examined
docs.text:
The angel view responds: "Jesus was only describing the normal state of faithful angels. He wasn't ruling out what fallen angels might do."

Problems with this response: 1. Luke's isangeloi has no qualifier -- it is a statement about angelic nature, not a specific subset 2. The comparison requires categorical truth -- a comparison to a class fails if the class has exceptions 3. No Scripture says fallen angels gain new abilities -- rebellion does not grant reproductive powers 4. It contradicts Jesus's purpose -- He was answering a question about resurrection with certainty; an answer that allows exceptions would not silence the Sadducees (yet Luke 20:39-40 shows they were silenced) 5. It makes Jesus's teaching misleading -- If some angels DO marry, Jesus would be giving a misleading comparison. This impugns His integrity as a teacher.

docs.title: genesis-6-sons-of-god Study
docs.text: That study concluded the Sethite view is better supported, listing "Jesus teaches angels do not marry (Matt 22:30)" as one of six key reasons. This current study provides the detailed exegetical support for that point.

docs.title: angels-physical-form Study
docs.text: That study concluded the argument "angels can eat, therefore they can reproduce" is a non sequitur. This current study establishes the positive teaching: Jesus says they do not marry, grounding the negative conclusion from the previous study in a positive text.

docs.title: jude-6-7-angels-sin Study
docs.text: That study concluded Jude 6-7 does not require a Genesis 6 connection. This current study provides the hermeneutical principle that CONSTRAINS the interpretation: even if someone reads Jude 6 as possibly related to Genesis 6, Jesus's teaching that angels do not marry creates a ceiling that interpretation cannot breach.

docs.title: matthew-24-days-of-noah Study
docs.text: That study showed Jesus did NOT reference the "sons of God" or any supernatural element when discussing Noah's days. Combined with this study, we see two facts: (1) Jesus explicitly teaches angels don't marry, and (2) Jesus does not reference angel marriages when discussing Noah. Both point in the same direction.

docs.title: 9. Summary of Findings
docs.text:
Finding Evidence Jesus teaches angels do not marry Matt 22:30; Mark 12:25; Luke 20:35 This is about nature, not just location Luke 20:36 (isangeloi -- no "in heaven" qualifier) The comparison requires categorical truth Logical structure of the analogy "In heaven" is locative, not restrictive Luke's parallel proves this Marriage vocabulary is literal, not euphemistic gameo/gamizo are standard marriage terms Non-marriage is connected to angelic nature Luke 20:36 links it to immortality and isangeloi Jesus's teaching creates a hermeneutical ceiling Clear NT constrains ambiguous OT Previous studies confirm the pattern Genesis 6, angels-physical-form, Jude 6-7, Matt 24

docs.title: Word Studies: Jesus on Angels and Marriage
Lexicon Data
docs.text:
• Greek: ἰσάγγελος (isangelos)
  • Strong's: G2465
  • Transliteration: isangelos
  • Part of Speech: Adjective (adj)
  • Pronunciation: ee-sang-el-los
  • Definition: Like an angel, i.e. angelic; equal unto the angels
  • Compound: From isos (G2470, "equal") + angelos (G32, "angel/messenger")
  • BLB Count: 1 occurrence

docs.title: Occurrences
docs.text:
• Luke 20:36 -- "Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels (isangeloi); and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection."

This is a hapax legomenon -- it appears only once in the entire New Testament. This makes it significant: Luke (or Luke's source) coined or selected this specific compound adjective to express what Matthew and Mark describe with the phrase "as the angels."

docs.title: Greek Grammar (from parser analysis)
docs.text:
ἰσάγγελοι  [A-NPM] Nominative Plural Masculine
- Nominative: Subject complement (predicate adjective) -- describing what the resurrected saints ARE - Plural: Matches the plural subjects (those accounted worthy) - Masculine: Grammatical agreement

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
The compound is critically important:

  1. isos (G2470) means "equal in quantity or quality." It is not a weaker word like "similar" or "comparable." It denotes genuine equality in the quality being compared.

  2. The compound form (isos + angelos) creates a single-concept adjective: "angel-equal." This is stronger than "like angels" (hos angeloi) used in Matthew/Mark. Luke's isangeloi predicates a quality of BEING, not merely a point of comparison.

  3. No qualifier appears with isangeloi. Matthew has "angels of God in heaven." Mark has "angels which are in heaven." But Luke's isangeloi stands unqualified -- "equal unto THE ANGELS." This is a categorical statement about angelic nature, not limited to a subset of angels.

  4. Context links it to nature, not behavior: Luke 20:36 connects isangeloi to "neither can they die any more" -- the comparison is about the NATURE of resurrected beings (immortality, non-marriage) being equal to angelic nature.

docs.title: Lexicon Data
docs.text:
• Greek: γαμέω (gameo)
  • Strong's: G1060
  • Transliteration: gameo
  • Part of Speech: Verb (v)
  • Definition: To wed (of either sex); to marry (a wife)
  • BLB Count: 29 occurrences

docs.title: Key Translations (29 total)
docs.text: Count Translation 8 (27.6%) marry 3 (10.3%) to marry 2 (6.9%) shall marry 2 (6.9%) marrieth 2 (6.9%) let them marry 2 (6.9%) is married

docs.title: Usage in Our Passages
docs.text:
Matthew 22:30: γαμοῦσιν (gamousin) -- Present Active Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "they [do not] marry"

Mark 12:25: γαμοῦσιν (gamousin) -- Present Active Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "they [do not] marry"

Luke 20:34: γαμοῦσιν (gamousin) -- Present Active Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "The children of this world marry"

Luke 20:35: γαμοῦσιν (gamousin) -- Present Active Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "[they do not] marry"

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
gameo is the standard, ordinary Greek word for marriage. It is used throughout the NT for normal human marriage (Matt 5:32; 19:9-10; 1 Cor 7:9, 28, 33, 36, 38, 39; 1 Tim 4:3; 5:11, 14). There is nothing euphemistic or unusual about this word. Jesus is speaking about literal marriage.

The active voice (gamousin) traditionally refers to the male action of taking a wife.

docs.title: Lexicon Data
docs.text:
• Greek: γαμίσκω/γαμίζω (gamisko/gamizo)
  • Strong's: G1061
  • Transliteration: gamisko
  • Part of Speech: Verb (v)
  • Definition: To espouse (a daughter to a husband); to give in marriage
  • Derived from: G1062 (gamos, "a wedding")
  • BLB Count: 1 occurrence (some MSS use gamizo G1061 in multiple passages)

docs.title: Key Translation
docs.text: Count Translation 1 (100%) are given in marriage

docs.title: Usage in Our Passages
docs.text:
Matthew 22:30: γαμίζονται (gamizontai) -- Present Passive Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "they are [not] given in marriage"

Mark 12:25: γαμίζονται (gamizontai) -- Present Passive Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "they are [not] given in marriage"

Luke 20:34: γαμίσκονται (gamiskontai) -- Present Passive Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "are given in marriage"

Luke 20:35: γαμίζονται (gamizontai) -- Present Passive Indicative, 3rd Person Plural - "[are not] given in marriage"

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
gamisko/gamizo is the passive counterpart to gameo. While gameo describes the act of marrying (typically the groom), gamizo/gamisko describes being given in marriage (typically the bride, given by the father). Together, the pair gameo + gamizo covers the ENTIRETY of the marriage institution -- both the active marrying and the passive being given in marriage. Jesus uses both words to leave no aspect of marriage unaddressed.

The passive voice (gamizontai/gamiskontai) is significant. In the Sadducees' question, the woman was "given" to seven brothers. Jesus addresses both sides of the marriage transaction.

Luke's variant: Luke 20:34 uses gamiskontai (from gamisko), while Luke 20:35 and the Matthew/Mark parallels use gamizontai (from gamizo). These are variant forms of the same concept.

docs.title: Lexicon Data
docs.text:
• Greek: ἄγγελος (angelos)
  • Strong's: G32
  • Transliteration: angelos
  • Part of Speech: Masculine Noun (n-m)
  • Definition: A messenger; especially an angel; by implication, a pastor
  • BLB Count: 186 occurrences (181 in KJV translation data)

docs.title: Key Translations
docs.text: Count Translation 71 (39.2%) angel 59 (32.6%) angels 10 (5.5%) the angel 10 (5.5%) an angel 7 (3.9%) of angels 3 (1.7%) messenger

docs.title: Usage in Our Passages
docs.text:
Matthew 22:30: ἄγγελοι (angeloi) -- Nominative Plural Masculine - "as the angels of God in heaven" - Greek: ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ (hos angeloi en to ourano)

Mark 12:25: ἄγγελοι (angeloi) -- Nominative Plural Masculine - "as the angels which are in heaven" - Greek: ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς (hos angeloi en tois ouranois)

Luke 20:36: [embedded in compound ἰσάγγελοι] - "equal unto the angels"

docs.title: The "In Heaven" Phrase -- Scope Analysis
docs.text:
Gospel Greek English Qualifier Matthew ὡς ἄγγελοι [τοῦ Θεοῦ] ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ as [the] angels [of God] in heaven "of God in heaven" Mark ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς as [the] angels in the heavens "in the heavens" Luke ἰσάγγελοι equal-to-angels NONE

Critical grammatical observation: In both Matthew and Mark, the phrase "in heaven" (en to ourano / en tois ouranois) is a locative prepositional phrase that could modify either: 1. The noun "angels" -- describing WHERE the angels are (locative) 2. The verb "are" (eisin) -- describing WHERE the comparison applies

The word order in Greek places "in heaven" after "angels" and before "are" (eisin): - Matthew: ἀλλ' ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ εἰσιν - Mark: ἀλλ' εἰσὶν ὡς ἄγγελοι ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς

The decisive evidence is Luke's parallel. Luke omits "in heaven" entirely and replaces the phrase-comparison (hos angeloi) with the compound adjective (isangeloi). If "in heaven" were a theologically limiting qualifier (restricting the statement to faithful angels only), Luke could not omit it without changing the meaning. The fact that Luke considers isangeloi (angel-equal) a faithful representation of Jesus's teaching demonstrates that "in heaven" describes WHERE angels ARE, not which angels are meant.

docs.title: G5613 -- hos (as, like)
docs.text: Used in Matthew 22:30 and Mark 12:25 as the comparative particle. hos introduces a comparison of similarity: resurrected saints will be "like" or "as" angels. This is a comparison of KIND, not of degree.

docs.title: G386 -- anastasis (resurrection)
docs.text:
• Matthew 22:30: ἐν τῇ ἀναστάσει (en te anastasei) -- "in the resurrection" (locative dative)
  • Luke 20:35: τῆς ἀναστάσεως (tes anastaseos) -- "the resurrection" (genitive, objective)
  • Luke 20:36: τῆς ἀναστάσεως (tes anastaseos) -- "the resurrection" (genitive, descriptive -- "children of the resurrection")

docs.title: G2661 -- kataxioo (to count worthy)
docs.text:
• Luke 20:35: καταξιωθέντες (kataxiothentes) -- Aorist Passive Participle, Nominative Plural Masculine
  • Unique to Luke's account. Those who "attain" (tuchein) that age are those who have been "counted worthy." This adds a soteriological dimension: the resurrection state (including being isangeloi) is for the redeemed.

docs.title: G1410 -- dunamai (to be able)
docs.text:
• Luke 20:36: δύνανται (dunantai) -- Present Middle/Passive Indicative, 3rd Plural
  • "Neither can they die any more" -- the inability to die is stated as a power/capability issue. They CANNOT die. This is not a choice but a condition of nature. Similarly, the connection to isangeloi suggests the non-marriage is also a matter of nature, not mere prohibition.

docs.title: Conclusion: Jesus on Angels and Marriage -- The Hermeneutical Ceiling
Question
docs.text: What does Jesus teach about angels and marriage in Matthew 22:30, Mark 12:25, and Luke 20:35-36? Does this teaching create a hermeneutical ceiling -- a constraint that no interpretation of Genesis 6 can violate?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text:
Yes. Jesus's teaching that angels do not marry constitutes a hermeneutical ceiling that constrains all interpretation of Genesis 6. Analysis of all three Synoptic accounts demonstrates that:

  1. Jesus makes a categorical statement about angelic nature -- angels do not marry (Matt 22:30; Mark 12:25; Luke 20:35)
  2. Luke's isangeloi (G2465) removes any "in heaven" limitation -- the statement is about what angels ARE, not where they are
  3. The logical structure of Jesus's comparison requires the quality to be universal -- if any angels could marry, the comparison breaks
  4. The marriage vocabulary (gameo/gamizo) is literal -- Jesus is speaking about actual marriage, not a euphemism
  5. This teaching, as a direct statement from Christ, takes interpretive priority over the ambiguous "sons of God" passage in Genesis 6

docs.title: What Each Account Contributes
docs.text: Gospel Unique Contribution Matthew 22:30 "Angels of God in heaven" -- links angels to divine identity Mark 12:25 "When they shall rise from the dead" -- temporal precision about when this applies Luke 20:34-36 Three unique elements: (1) "this age / that age" contrast, (2) isangeloi without qualifier, (3) explicit connection to immortality and inability to die

docs.title: The Combined Teaching
docs.text:
Taking all three accounts together, Jesus teaches:

  1. The children of this age marry (Luke 20:34)
  2. Those counted worthy of that age and the resurrection neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matt 22:30; Mark 12:25; Luke 20:35)
  3. They cannot die any more (Luke 20:36a)
  4. They are equal unto the angels -- isangeloi (Luke 20:36b)
  5. They are children of God, being children of the resurrection (Luke 20:36c)

Marriage belongs to this age. Non-marriage is a characteristic of the age to come, grounded in angelic nature. Immortality and non-marriage are both features of being isangeloi.

docs.title: The Argument
docs.text: The angel view claims: "Angels of God in heaven limits the statement to faithful angels. Fallen angels are not in heaven and could marry."

docs.title: The Refutation
docs.text:
1. Luke's parallel eliminates this reading. Luke uses isangeloi ("equal unto THE angels") with no "in heaven" qualifier. If "in heaven" were theologically restrictive, Luke's omission would be a doctrinal error. Since all three Synoptics report the same teaching, Luke proves "in heaven" is a locative descriptor (telling where angels are), not a categorical restrictor (limiting which angels are meant).

  2. Grammatically, "in heaven" is locative. The prepositional phrases ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ (Matthew) and ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς (Mark) describe location. Compare: "the God of Abraham" does not mean God is ONLY Abraham's God.

  3. The comparison demands universality. Jesus compares resurrected saints to angels. The comparison only works if the quality (non-marriage) is categorical for the entire class. If some angels marry, the comparison would be: "You'll be like the class of beings that mostly don't marry" -- which is not a comparison at all.

docs.title: The Logical Structure of the Comparison
How Comparisons Work
docs.text:
When Jesus says "they will be as the angels" regarding marriage, He uses angels as the standard of comparison. For any comparison to A to work, the quality compared must be categorically true of A:

  • "White as snow" works because snow IS white.
  • "Strong as a lion" works because lions ARE strong.
  • "They will not marry, like angels" works because angels do NOT marry.

If the quality has exceptions within the comparison class, the comparison fails:

  • "Honest as politicians" fails because politicians are not categorically honest.
  • "They will not marry, like angels" would fail if some angels DO marry.

docs.title: The Angel View's Logical Problem
docs.text:
The angel view of Genesis 6 requires that some angels (the "sons of God") DID marry human women. But if this is true: - Angels as a class are NOT categorically non-marrying - Jesus's comparison is flawed or misleading - The Sadducees' question is not actually answered (if exceptions exist, the resurrected woman COULD be married)

This is not a peripheral problem. It strikes at the integrity of Jesus's teaching.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• Hapax legomenon -- appears only in Luke 20:36 in all of Scripture
  • Compound: isos (equal) + angelos (angel) = "angel-equal"
  • Grammar: Predicate adjective (Nominative Plural Masculine) -- describes what the resurrected saints ARE
  • No qualifier: Unlike Matthew/Mark's "in heaven," isangeloi stands alone

docs.title: What It Predicates
docs.text:
Luke 20:36 uses a causal chain with gar (for/because): - They cannot die any more because (gar) they are isangeloi - Isangeloi is the reason for both their immortality and their non-marriage (from v.35)

This means non-marriage and immortality are BOTH grounded in angelic nature. Just as angels do not die, angels do not marry. The resurrected saints, being angel-equal, share both characteristics.

docs.title: gameo (G1060) -- "to marry"
docs.text:
• 29 NT occurrences, always referring to literal marriage
  • Active voice, typically the groom's action
  • Standard Greek marriage vocabulary

docs.title: gamizo/gamisko (G1061) -- "to give in marriage"
docs.text:
• Passive counterpart to gameo
  • The father's act of giving the bride
  • Together with gameo, covers the ENTIRE marriage institution

Jesus uses BOTH terms, leaving no aspect of marriage unaddressed. The double formulation (oute gamousin oute gamizontai -- "neither marry nor are given in marriage") is comprehensive. This is not about one aspect of marriage; it is about the institution itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A hermeneutical ceiling is an interpretive constraint established by a clear, authoritative teaching that limits how other, less clear texts may be interpreted.

docs.title: Why Jesus's Teaching Creates a Ceiling
docs.text: Factor Explanation Authority Jesus is the Son of God, Creator of angels, the Truth (John 14:6; Col 1:16) Clarity Three Synoptic accounts, consistent teaching, explicit statement Directness Not an inference or argument from silence -- a positive declaration Scope Luke's isangeloi makes it a statement about angelic NATURE Logic The comparison structure requires categorical truth

docs.title: How the Ceiling Constrains Genesis 6
docs.text:
Genesis 6:1-4 is an ambiguous text. "Sons of God" could mean: - Angels (Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7 usage) - Godly Sethite line (Gen 4:26; 5 context; Deut 14:1 parallel)

The ceiling rules: No interpretation of Genesis 6 may require that angels marry human women, because Jesus teaches angels do not marry. This eliminates the angel view of Genesis 6, not by proving the Sethite view directly, but by making the angel view incompatible with Christ's teaching.

docs.title: This Is Not Circular Reasoning
docs.text:
The argument is not: 1. Genesis 6 is about humans 2. Therefore angels don't marry 3. Therefore Genesis 6 is about humans

The argument is: 1. Jesus teaches angels don't marry (independent of Genesis 6) 2. This teaching constrains Genesis 6 interpretation 3. Therefore Genesis 6 cannot describe angel marriages

Jesus's teaching stands on its own. He was not interpreting Genesis 6; He was answering a question about resurrection. His statement about angelic nature is independent of and prior to any Genesis 6 interpretation.

docs.title: 1. "In heaven limits it to faithful angels"
docs.text: Refuted by: Luke's isangeloi (no qualifier). See analysis above.

docs.title: 2. "Jesus was only describing the current state, not what fallen angels once did"
docs.text: Problem: Jesus uses the present tense (gamousin, gamizontai) to describe a timeless characteristic, not a temporary state. "Angels do not marry" is like "fish do not fly" -- a statement about nature, not about current behavior.

docs.title: 3. "Fallen angels could have gained abilities faithful angels lack"
docs.text: Problem: No Scripture supports this claim. Rebellion does not grant new abilities. This is pure speculation with zero biblical basis. (See angels-physical-form study.)

docs.title: 4. "This just means angels don't marry each other, not that they can't marry humans"
docs.text: Problem: The text does not say "angels do not marry each other." It says they do not marry (gamousin) and are not given in marriage (gamizontai). These are comprehensive terms covering all marriage -- not species-specific.

docs.title: 5. "Jesus was just accommodating popular belief"
docs.text: Problem: This impugns Jesus's integrity as a teacher. He explicitly said the Sadducees erred because they did not know the Scriptures or God's power. Jesus then made a doctrinal claim. If that claim was merely accommodation to popular belief, Jesus would be guilty of the very error He rebuked.

docs.title: Connection to Previous Studies
docs.text: Study How It Relates genesis-6-sons-of-god Listed "Jesus teaches angels don't marry" as key evidence. This study provides the full exegetical support. angels-physical-form Concluded eating does not prove reproductive capability. This study provides the positive teaching grounding that negative conclusion. jude-6-7-angels-sin Concluded Jude 6-7 does not establish a Genesis 6 connection. This study provides the hermeneutical constraint that makes the angel interpretation of Jude 6 + Genesis 6 untenable. matthew-24-days-of-noah Showed Jesus did NOT reference "sons of God" when discussing Noah. Combined with this study: Jesus never acknowledges angel marriages and positively denies them. 2-peter-2-4-angels-that-sinned Concluded 2 Peter 2:4 describes the angelic rebellion (Rev 12), not Genesis 6. This study confirms: even if one connects 2 Peter 2:4 to Genesis 6, the hermeneutical ceiling from Jesus's teaching prevents the angel-marriage interpretation.

docs.title: What Jesus Teaches
docs.text:
• Angels do not marry -- this is a categorical statement about angelic nature
  • Resurrected saints will be like angels in this respect
  • This likeness is grounded in their nature (isangeloi), not merely a behavioral choice
  • Non-marriage and immortality are both features of angelic existence

docs.title: What This Means for Genesis 6
docs.text:
• The angel view of Genesis 6 requires that some angels married human women
  • Jesus's teaching categorically denies that angels marry
  • Therefore, the angel view of Genesis 6 contradicts Jesus's teaching
  • The hermeneutical ceiling holds: no OT interpretation may violate clear NT teaching from Christ

docs.title: What This Study Does NOT Prove
docs.text:
• This study does not definitively identify who the "sons of God" in Genesis 6 ARE (though it eliminates angels as an option)
  • This study does not address every argument for the angel view (other studies cover 2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6-7, the meaning of Nephilim, etc.)
  • This study does not claim the angel view has no scholarly support -- it does; but scholarly opinion cannot override Jesus's direct teaching

docs.title: The Interpretive Question
docs.text: In Jude 1:7, the phrase τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις ("in like manner to these") appears. The question is: What does τούτοις ("these") refer to?

docs.title: Two Possible Antecedents
docs.text: Option τούτοις refers to Meaning A The angels (v6) Sodom sinned "in like manner to the angels" B The inhabitants of the cities (v7) The surrounding cities sinned "like the people of Sodom"

docs.title: The Gender Problem
docs.text:
τούτοις is Dative Plural MASCULINE

But the nouns in verse 7 are all FEMININE (or neuter): - Σόδομα (Sodom) - N-NSF - Γόμορρα (Gomorrah) - N-NSF - πόλεις (cities) - N-NPF

Note on Σόδομα/Γόμορρα gender: The N1904 Text-Fabric database parses these as feminine. However, Strong's classifies Σόδομα as neuter* (G4670) and Γόμορρα as neuter or feminine (G1116). Hebrew place names transliterated into Greek can have variable gender. This discrepancy does not affect the argument: whether feminine or neuter, these nouns are not masculine, so the grammatical tension with τούτοις (masculine) remains.

The only MASCULINE plural noun in the immediate context is: - ἀγγέλους (angels) - N-APM (v6)

docs.title: Initial Conclusion
docs.text: Strict grammatical agreement suggests τούτοις refers to the angels.

docs.title: Counter-Evidence: Constructio ad Sensum
docs.text: Greek authors sometimes use constructio ad sensum (construction according to sense) - where grammatical gender follows the meaning rather than strict agreement.

docs.title: Example 1: Luke 10:13
docs.text:
Greek: καθήμενοι (sitting) - V-PNP-NPM (Nominative Plural MASCULINE)

Context: Describes Tyre and Sidon (both FEMININE cities) "sitting in sackcloth"

Word Gender Meaning Τύρῳ Feminine Tyre Σιδῶνι Feminine Sidon καθήμενοι Masculine sitting

Pattern: Feminine cities → Masculine participle (referring to the inhabitants)

docs.title: Example 2: Matthew 23:37
docs.text: Greek: Jerusalem is addressed with feminine participle (ἀποκτείνουσα - "killing"), but then the verb switches to 2nd person plural (ἠθελήσατε - "you [plural] were not willing") addressing the people.

docs.title: Example 3: Galatians 3:16
docs.text:
Word Gender Meaning σπέρματι Neuter seed ὅς Masculine who

Paul uses a masculine pronoun for a neuter noun because he's referring to Christ (a person).

docs.title: Example 4: Revelation 4:8
docs.text:
Word Gender Meaning τὰ τέσσερα ζῷα Neuter plural the four living creatures λέγοντες Masculine plural saying

Neuter noun takes masculine participle (treating creatures as persons).

docs.title: Example 5: Acts 8:5 (Most Directly Parallel)
docs.text:
Greek: Φίλιππος δὲ κατελθὼν εἰς τὴν πόλιν τῆς Σαμαρίας ἐκήρυσσεν αὐτοῖς τὸν Χριστόν.

Word Parsing Gender Meaning τὴν πόλιν N-ASF Feminine the city τῆς Σαμαρίας N-GSF Feminine of Samaria αὐτοῖς P-DPM Masculine Plural to them

Philip preached to "the city" (feminine) but used αὐτοῖς (masculine dative plural) - referring to the inhabitants. This is the most directly parallel construction to Jude 1:7's τούτοις.

docs.title: Example 6: Acts 8:14
docs.text:
Greek: ...ὅτι δέδεκται ἡ Σαμάρια τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἀπέστειλαν πρὸς αὐτοὺς Πέτρον καὶ Ἰωάνην

Word Parsing Gender Meaning ἡ Σαμάρια N-NSF Feminine Samaria αὐτοὺς P-APM Masculine Plural them

"Samaria received the word" (feminine subject), but apostles sent πρὸς αὐτοὺς ("to them" - masculine plural) - again referring to the inhabitants.

docs.title: Application to Jude 1:7
docs.text:
Could τούτοις (masculine) refer to the inhabitants of Sodom/Gomorrah/cities rather than the cities themselves?

Passage City/Cities Gender Pronoun/Participle Refers to Luke 10:13 Tyre, Sidon Fem καθήμενοι (Masc Pl) Inhabitants sitting Matt 23:37 Jerusalem Fem ἠθελήσατε (2pl) Inhabitants not willing Acts 8:5 City of Samaria Fem αὐτοῖς (Masc Pl) Inhabitants preached to Acts 8:14 Samaria Fem αὐτοὺς (Masc Pl) Inhabitants sent to Jude 1:7 Sodom, cities Fem τούτοις (Masc Pl) ?

Conclusion: The pattern exists in the NT with multiple clear examples. Constructio ad sensum is a grammatically valid and well-attested option. The Acts 8:5 example is particularly strong because it uses the same dative case (αὐτοῖς) as Jude 1:7 (τούτοις).

docs.title: More Feminine → Masculine Examples
docs.text: Passage City/Town (Gender) Referring Word Gender Pattern Matt 8:34 πᾶσα ἡ πόλις (F sg) ἰδόντες "seeing" M pl participle F → M John 4:39 τῆς πόλεως ἐκείνης (F) πολλοί "many" M pl adj F → M Acts 21:30 ἡ πόλις ὅλη (F) ἐπιλαβόμενοι "seizing" M pl participle F → M

docs.title: Feminine → Feminine Examples (Strict Agreement)
docs.text: Passage City/Town (Gender) Referring Word Gender Pattern Matt 23:37 Ἰερουσαλήμ (F voc) ἀποκτείνουσα "killing" F sg participle F → F Matt 23:37 Ἰερουσαλήμ (F voc) λιθοβολοῦσα "stoning" F sg participle F → F Matt 23:37 Ἰερουσαλήμ (F voc) αὐτήν "to her" F sg pronoun F → F Mark 1:33 ὅλη ἡ πόλις (F) ἐπισυνηγμένη "gathered" F sg participle F → F Rev 11:8 τῆς πόλεως τῆς μεγάλης (F) ἥτις "which" F sg relative F → F

docs.title: What Determines the Pattern?
docs.text: The key question is: Can the action be predicated of a collective entity, or does it require individual agents?

docs.title: When F → F (Strict Agreement) is Used
docs.text:
Used when the city is personified as a unified entity:

Passage Text Why Feminine? Matt 23:37 Jerusalem... ἡ ἀποκτείνουσα (she who kills) Deliberate personification - Jerusalem as a mother figure (hen/chicks metaphor follows) Mark 1:33 the whole city was ἐπισυνηγμένη (gathered) Collective action - a crowd "gathers" as a unit Rev 11:8 the great city ἥτις (which) is called... City as a symbolic entity with a name

Pattern: Feminine is maintained when the author conceptualizes the city as a whole - a collective personality, a symbolic entity, or when the predicate can naturally apply to a collective noun.

docs.title: When F → M (Constructio ad Sensum) is Used
docs.text:
Used when the focus shifts to individual human actions:

Passage Text Why Masculine? Luke 10:13 Tyre and Sidon would have repented καθήμενοι (sitting) in sackcloth Physical posture - people sit, cities don't Matt 8:34 the whole city went out... ἰδόντες (seeing) him, they begged Sensory perception - people see, cities don't Acts 8:5 preached αὐτοῖς (to them) Receiving a message - people hear, not geography Acts 21:30 the city was stirred... ἐπιλαβόμενοι (seizing) Paul Physical action - people grab, cities don't

Pattern: Masculine appears when the predicate requires individual human agents - seeing, sitting, hearing, seizing, repenting. These actions cannot be predicated of a collective abstraction.

docs.title: Summary: The Decisive Factor
docs.text: Action Type Agreement Example "The city gathered" F → F Collective entity can "gather" "The city saw him" F → M Individuals see, not collectives "The city kills prophets" F → F Personification - city as agent "The city sat in sackcloth" F → M Physical posture requires bodies

docs.title: Application to Jude 1:7
docs.text:
The question for τούτοις is: What kind of action is "going after strange flesh"?

  • If Jude is thinking of individual human actors committing sexual sin → masculine for inhabitants makes sense (F → M)
  • If τούτοις refers back to angels (v6) → masculine is strict agreement (M → M)

The action "going after flesh" (ἀπελθοῦσαι... ὀπίσω σαρκός) describes individual pursuit of sexual gratification - an action requiring individual agents, not a collective abstraction. This would support the F → M reading for inhabitants.

However, this does not rule out the angelic referent - both remain grammatically viable.

docs.title: OT Pattern: Cities and Inhabitants
docs.text: The OT frequently refers to cities by their inhabitants:

docs.title: Explicit "Men of [City]" Phrases
docs.text:
• Genesis 13:13 - "the men of Sodom were wicked" - explicit masculine
  • Genesis 19:4 - "the men of the city, even the men of Sodom" - explicit masculine
  • Isaiah 1:10 - "ye rulers of Sodom... ye people of Gomorrah" - explicit reference to inhabitants

docs.title: Ezekiel 16:49-50 - Grammatical Analysis
docs.text:
In Ezekiel 16, Sodom is personified as Jerusalem's "sister" (feminine). The Hebrew maintains feminine agreement:

  • Ezekiel 16:50 - וַֽתִּגְבְּהֶ֔ינָה (wattigbəhenāh) = "and they were haughty"
  • Parsing: Qal Consecutive Imperfect - 3rd person FEMININE plural

This shows the Hebrew OT maintains strict grammatical agreement with feminine cities, unlike the more flexible Koine Greek of the NT.

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: The NT shows more grammatical flexibility (constructio ad sensum) than the Hebrew OT when referring to cities by their inhabitants. This reflects Koine Greek usage patterns and strengthens the case that such constructions were acceptable in NT Greek.

docs.title: Jude's Three Examples of Judgment (vv. 5-7)
docs.text:
Jude provides three historical examples of divine judgment:

  1. Israel in the wilderness (v5) - destroyed for unbelief
  2. Angels who sinned (v6) - reserved in chains for judgment
  3. Sodom and Gomorrah (v7) - destroyed by fire as an example

docs.title: Structure Question
docs.text:
How does v7 relate to v6?

Option A (angels reading): - v6 and v7 are connected - Sodom sinned "in like manner to" the angels - Both involved sexual transgression across categories ("strange flesh") - The sin of v7 parallels the sin of v6

Option B (inhabitants reading): - v7 is self-contained - the surrounding cities sinned like the people of Sodom - The three examples are separate illustrations of judgment - v7 explains how the surrounding cities shared Sodom's sin

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Element Jude 2 Peter Angels v6: "kept not their first estate... left their own habitation" v4: "angels that sinned" Connection "in like manner" (τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις) No connecting phrase Sodom v7: "giving themselves over to fornication, going after strange flesh" v6: "condemned with an overthrow, making them an ensample"

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
2 Peter does NOT connect the angels and Sodom with a comparative phrase.

2 Peter treats the three examples (angels, flood, Sodom) as parallel but separate illustrations.

If Peter and Jude drew from a common tradition, Jude's "in like manner" phrase is unique to Jude and represents his interpretive addition.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text:
1. If Jude meant to parallel the sins of angels and Sodom, his phrasing is intentional and significant
  2. If Jude meant the surrounding cities sinned like Sodom's inhabitants, the phrase is clarifying the scope of the example

docs.title: The Word ἕτερος (heteros)
docs.text: ἕτερος means "other of a different kind" - distinct from ἄλλος which means "another of the same kind."

docs.title: What is "Different" Flesh?
docs.text: Interpretation "Strange flesh" means Parallel to angels? Homosexuality Flesh of same sex (different from natural) No direct parallel Angelic beings Non-human flesh (Genesis 6 connection) Yes - both crossed categories Foreigners Non-Israelite flesh No parallel

docs.title: If Reading A (angels):
docs.text: The "strange flesh" Sodom pursued was angelic flesh (Gen 19 - the angels who visited Lot), paralleling the angels of v6 who pursued human flesh (Gen 6 connection).

docs.title: If Reading B (inhabitants):
docs.text: The "strange flesh" refers to homosexual relations - flesh "different" from what is natural.

docs.title: Reading A: τούτοις = Angels
docs.text:
Strengths: - Strict grammatical agreement (masculine → masculine) - Creates theological parallel: both angels and Sodomites crossed flesh-categories - Explains why Jude connects these two examples with "in like manner" - Fits with Genesis 6 / 1 Enoch tradition that Jude likely knew

Weaknesses: - Requires reading Gen 19 as Sodomites pursuing angelic flesh specifically - Less intuitive reading of the sentence flow - 2 Peter parallel doesn't make this connection

docs.title: Reading B: τούτοις = Inhabitants of Cities
docs.text:
Strengths: - Follows documented NT pattern (constructio ad sensum) - More natural sentence flow: "Sodom... and the cities around them in like manner [to Sodom's people]" - Explains scope: not just Sodom, but all the cities sinned similarly - Doesn't require specific view on Gen 6

Weaknesses: - Requires grammatical gender to shift from feminine to masculine - Why would Jude specify that surrounding cities sinned like Sodom? (Seems obvious) - Leaves the connection to v6 unexplained

docs.title: Summary of Grammatical Evidence
docs.text:
Factor Favors Reading A Favors Reading B Strict gender agreement ✓ Constructio ad sensum precedent ✓ Sentence flow ✓ Theological coherence ✓ 2 Peter parallel Neither - 2 Peter is silent

Conclusion: Grammar alone does not definitively resolve the question. Both readings are grammatically defensible.

docs.title: The Key Phrase
docs.text: Greek: τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις Transliteration: ton homoion tropon toutois Literal: "the similar manner to-these" KJV: "in like manner"

docs.title: Word Study 1: ὅμοιος (homoios) - G3664
docs.text: Parsing in Jude 1:7: A-ASM (Adjective, Accusative Singular Masculine)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• Strong's: "Similar (in appearance or character)" - rendered as "like" or "+ manner"
  • Thayer's: "Like, similar, resembling"
  • Resembling in form, appearance, nature, or condition
  • Corresponding or equivalent to; the same as

docs.title: Etymology
docs.text: From the base of G3674 (ὁμοῦ - "together")

docs.title: NT Usage (47 occurrences)
docs.text:
• Frequently used in parables: "The kingdom of heaven is like..." (Matt 13:31, 33, 44-45, 47)
  • Used for comparison: "like unto" (Luke 6:47-49; 7:31-32)
  • In Revelation: describing appearances (Rev 1:13, 15; 4:3, 6-7)

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: ὅμοιος establishes a comparison of similarity - the things compared share characteristics.

docs.title: Word Study 2: τρόπος (tropos) - G5158
docs.text: Parsing in Jude 1:7: N-ASM (Noun, Accusative Singular Masculine)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• Strong's: "A turn, i.e. (by implication) mode or style; figuratively, deportment or character"
  • Thayer's: "A manner, way, or fashion; manner of life, character, and deportment"

docs.title: NT Usage (13 occurrences)
docs.text: Reference KJV Translation Greek Construction Matt 23:37 "even as" ὃν τρόπον Luke 13:34 "as" ὃν τρόπον Acts 1:11 "in like manner as" ὃν τρόπον Acts 7:28 "as" ὃν τρόπον Acts 15:11 "even as" καθ' ὃν τρόπον Acts 27:25 "even as" καθ' ὃν τρόπον 2 Tim 3:8 "as" ὃν τρόπον Jude 1:7 "in like manner" τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: τρόπος with ὅμοιον creates an adverbial accusative phrase meaning "in the similar manner" - describing HOW the action was performed, not just that it was similar.

docs.title: Word Study 3: τούτοις (toutois) - from οὗτος (houtos) G3778
docs.text: Parsing in Jude 1:7: D-DPM (Demonstrative Pronoun, Dative Plural Masculine)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: • Strong's: "The he (she or it), i.e. this or that" - referring to someone or something present or previously mentioned

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: • "this" (157x), "these" (59x), "he" (31x), "the same" (28x)

docs.title: Critical Grammatical Point
docs.text:
τούτοις is Dative Plural MASCULINE

The dative case indicates the object of comparison: "in like manner to these"

The masculine gender is significant because: - Greek nouns must agree in gender with their referents - Sodom (Σόδομα) = Feminine - Gomorrah (Γόμορρα) = Feminine - Cities (πόλεις) = Feminine - Angels (ἀγγέλους) in v6 = Masculine

docs.title: Verse 6 Key Words
docs.text: Greek Parsing Meaning ἀγγέλους N-APM angels (Acc Pl Masc) τηρήσαντας V-AAP-APM having kept (Acc Pl Masc) ἀπολιπόντας V-2AAP-APM having left (Acc Pl Masc) δεσμοῖς N-DPM chains (Dat Pl Masc) ἀϊδίοις A-DPM everlasting (Dat Pl Masc)

docs.title: Verse 7 Key Words
docs.text:
Greek Parsing Meaning Σόδομα N-NSF* Sodom (Nom Sg Fem/Neut) Γόμορρα N-NSF* Gomorrah (Nom Sg Fem/Neut) πόλεις N-NPF cities (Nom Pl Fem) τὸν T-ASM the (Acc Sg Masc) ὅμοιον A-ASM similar (Acc Sg Masc) τρόπον N-ASM manner (Acc Sg Masc) τούτοις D-DPM to these (Dat Pl Masc) ἐκπορνεύσασαι V-AAP-NPF having fornicated (Nom Pl Fem) ἀπελθοῦσαι V-2AAP-NPF having gone after (Nom Pl Fem) σαρκὸς N-GSF flesh (Gen Sg Fem) ἑτέρας A-GSF strange/other (Gen Sg Fem)

*Note: N1904 parses Σόδομα/Γόμορρα as feminine. Strong's (G4670, G1116) classifies Σόδομα as neuter and Γόμορρα as neuter or feminine. Either way, they are not masculine.

docs.title: Grammatical Tension
docs.text:
• The subject of v7 (Sodom, Gomorrah, cities) is feminine
  • The participles describing their actions (ἐκπορνεύσασαι, ἀπελθοῦσαι) are feminine
  • But τούτοις is masculine

docs.title: Word Study 4: σαρκὸς ἑτέρας - "Strange Flesh"
docs.text: Greek: σαρκὸς ἑτέρας (sarkos heteras)

docs.title: σάρξ (sarx) G4561
docs.text:
• Meaning: flesh, body, human nature
  • Parsing: N-GSF (Genitive Singular Feminine)

docs.title: ἕτερος (heteros) G2087
docs.text:
• Meaning: other, another, different (of a different kind)
  • Parsing: A-GSF (Adjective, Genitive Singular Feminine)
  • Note: Distinct from ἄλλος (allos) which means "another of the same kind"

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
ἕτερος implies qualitative difference - not just "other flesh" but "flesh of a different kind/nature"

This could mean: 1. Different from their own (homosexuality - human with human of same sex) 2. Different category entirely (human with non-human)

The interpretation affects how we understand the "in like manner" comparison.

docs.title: Textual Note
docs.text:
Both Nestle 1904 and Textus Receptus contain τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις with only minor word order variation: - N1904: τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις - TR: τὸν ὅμοιον τούτοις τρόπον

The grammatical question is consistent across textual traditions.

docs.title: Conclusion: What Does "In Like Manner" Refer to in Jude 1:7?
The Question
docs.text: In Jude 1:6-7, the phrase τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις ("in like manner to these") connects verse 7 to something. What does τούτοις ("these") refer to?

docs.title: The Passages
docs.text:
Jude 1:6 And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

Jude 1:7 Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

docs.title: Reading A: τούτοις = The Angels (v6)
docs.text:
Translation: "Even as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities about them, in like manner to these [angels], giving themselves over to fornication and going after strange flesh..."

Meaning: Sodom's sin paralleled the angels' sin - both involved crossing categories of flesh (angels with humans; humans pursuing angelic/non-human flesh).

docs.title: Reading B: τούτοις = The Inhabitants of the Cities (v7)
docs.text:
Translation: "Even as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities about them in like manner [to the people of Sodom], giving themselves over to fornication and going after strange flesh..."

Meaning: The surrounding cities committed the same sins as the people of Sodom did.

docs.title: Supporting Reading A (Angels)
docs.text:
1. Gender agreement: τούτοις is masculine plural; the only masculine plural antecedent is ἀγγέλους (angels) in v6
  2. The cities are feminine: Σόδομα, Γόμορρα, and πόλεις are all feminine - τούτοις does not grammatically agree with them

docs.title: Supporting Reading B (Inhabitants)
docs.text:
1. Constructio ad sensum: NT authors use masculine pronouns/participles for feminine cities when referring to inhabitants:
  2. Acts 8:5: τὴν πόλιν τῆς Σαμαρίας (fem) + αὐτοῖς (masc dative pl) = preached to inhabitants
  3. Acts 8:14: ἡ Σαμάρια (fem) + αὐτοὺς (masc acc pl) = sent to inhabitants
  4. Luke 10:13: Tyre/Sidon (fem) + καθήμενοι (masc) = inhabitants sitting
  5. Matt 23:37: Jerusalem (fem) + ἠθελήσατε (2pl) = people not willing
  6. Gal 3:16: σπέρματι (neut) + ὅς (masc) = referring to Christ

  7. Rev 4:8: ζῷα (neut) + λέγοντες (masc) = creatures as persons

  8. The Acts 8:5 parallel is particularly strong: It uses αὐτοῖς (dative plural masculine) for a feminine city - the exact same case as τούτοις in Jude 1:7.

  9. The pattern is well-documented: Greek allows gender to follow sense rather than strict agreement, with multiple clear NT examples.

docs.title: Jude's Structure
docs.text:
Jude gives three examples of divine judgment: 1. Unbelieving Israel (v5) 2. Angels who sinned (v6) 3. Sodom and surrounding cities (v7)

Question: Are v6 and v7 linked by parallel sin, or are they separate examples?

docs.title: 2 Peter 2:4-6 Parallel
docs.text:
2 Peter gives the same three examples but does not include "in like manner." Peter treats them as separate illustrations of judgment, not as theologically connected by the nature of their sin.

This suggests: - If the connection is significant, it is unique to Jude's emphasis - If the connection is merely structural, the parallel to 2 Peter supports Reading B

docs.title: "Strange Flesh" (σαρκὸς ἑτέρας)
docs.text:
The word ἕτερος means "different in kind" (not just "another"). What was "different" about the flesh?

If Reading A If Reading B Angelic flesh (non-human) Same-sex flesh (unnatural) Parallels angels pursuing human flesh Common understanding of Sodom's sin

docs.title: What the Grammar Proves
docs.text:
The grammar does NOT definitively determine the antecedent.

Evidence Weight τούτοις is masculine High - but not decisive Cities are feminine High - creates tension if τούτοις refers to cities Constructio ad sensum exists High - provides legitimate alternative NT examples of city → inhabitants Very High - 6 documented examples Acts 8:5 uses same case (dative) Very High - direct grammatical parallel

docs.title: NT Examples Summary Table
docs.text: Passage City (Gender) Pronoun (Gender) Case Refers to Acts 8:5 City of Samaria (Fem) αὐτοῖς (Masc) Dative Inhabitants Acts 8:14 Samaria (Fem) αὐτοὺς (Masc) Accusative Inhabitants Luke 10:13 Tyre, Sidon (Fem) καθήμενοι (Masc) Nominative Inhabitants Matt 23:37 Jerusalem (Fem) ἠθελήσατε (2pl) - Inhabitants Jude 1:7 Sodom, cities (Fem) τούτοις (Masc) Dative ?

docs.title: What Determines When Authors Use F → M vs F → F?
docs.text: NT authors use both patterns, and the choice appears to depend on the type of action being described:

docs.title: F → F (Strict Agreement) - When City is Personified
docs.text:
Passage Construction Why Feminine? Matt 23:37 Jerusalem... ἡ ἀποκτείνουσα (she who kills) Deliberate personification - city as mother figure Mark 1:33 the whole city was ἐπισυνηγμένη (gathered) Collective action - a crowd can "gather" as a unit Rev 11:8 the great city ἥτις (which) is called... City as a symbolic entity with a name

Pattern: Feminine is maintained when the city is conceived as a unified collective entity or when the action can be predicated of an abstraction.

docs.title: F → M (Constructio ad Sensum) - When Inhabitants Act
docs.text:
Passage Construction Why Masculine? Luke 10:13 Tyre/Sidon... καθήμενοι (sitting) in sackcloth Physical posture - people sit, cities don't Matt 8:34 the whole city... ἰδόντες (seeing) him Sensory perception - people see, cities don't Acts 8:5 preached αὐτοῖς (to them) Receiving a message - people hear, not geography Acts 21:30 the city was stirred... ἐπιλαβόμενοι (seizing) Paul Physical action - people grab, cities don't

Pattern: Masculine appears when the predicate requires individual human agents - seeing, sitting, hearing, seizing, repenting.

docs.title: Application to Jude 1:7
docs.text:
The action in Jude 1:7 is "going after strange flesh" (ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας) - describing individual pursuit of sexual gratification.

  • This action requires individual agents (people pursuing flesh), not a collective abstraction
  • This supports the F → M pattern (masculine τούτοις for feminine cities' inhabitants)
  • However, it does not rule out the angelic referent (M → M strict agreement)

docs.title: OT Comparison
docs.text:
The Hebrew OT typically uses: - Explicit phrases like "men of Sodom" (Gen 13:13; 19:4) - Strict grammatical agreement (Ezek 16:50 uses 3rd fem plural verb for Sodom)

The NT shows more grammatical flexibility (constructio ad sensum), reflecting Koine Greek usage patterns.

docs.title: What Must Be Decided on Other Grounds
docs.text:
Since grammar permits both readings, the interpreter must decide based on:

  1. What makes better sense of Jude's argument?
  2. Is Jude connecting the sins of angels and Sodom theologically?

  3. Or is he clarifying that all the cities (not just Sodom) sinned?

  4. What does "strange flesh" mean?

  5. If angelic flesh: Reading A is strengthened

  6. If homosexual relations: Reading B is more natural

  7. What is the relationship to Genesis 6?

  8. If Jude assumes Gen 6:1-4 describes angel-human unions: Reading A fits

  9. If Jude is not making this connection: Reading B is simpler

  10. How much weight to give 2 Peter?

  11. If Peter and Jude share a tradition: Peter's silence on the parallel is notable
  12. If Jude is independent: his "in like manner" phrase may be significant

docs.title: What We Can Say with Confidence
docs.text:
1. τούτοις is grammatically masculine - this is unambiguous
  2. The cities in v7 are grammatically feminine - this is unambiguous
  3. Constructio ad sensum is a documented NT phenomenon - cities can take masculine when inhabitants are meant
  4. Both readings are grammatically defensible - neither can be ruled out on grammar alone
  5. The question must be resolved on contextual/theological grounds

docs.title: What Remains Disputed
docs.text:
The question cannot be definitively settled by grammar alone:

  • Reading A: Jude connects v6 and v7 theologically - Sodom sinned "in like manner to the angels" (both crossed flesh categories)
  • Reading B: Jude clarifies scope within v7 - the surrounding cities sinned "in like manner to the people of Sodom" (v6 and v7 remain separate examples)

Reading B does not create a connection between the angels' sin and Sodom's sin. It simply explains that all the cities of the plain committed the same sins as Sodom's inhabitants.

Interpreters should: - Acknowledge the grammatical ambiguity - Evaluate the contextual and theological arguments for each reading - Avoid claiming grammatical certainty for either position
