docs.text: Strong's Concordance References: - H430 (elohim) - H5945 (elyon) - H120 (adam) - H8199 (shaphat) - G2316 (theos)

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does Psalm 82:6 ("I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High. But ye shall die like men") describe divine beings who sinned and will be punished by mortality? Does "die like men" imply they weren't originally men?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text:
Psalm 82 describes human judges, not divine beings. This is established by:

  1. Jesus's interpretation (John 10:34-35) - He identifies the "gods" as those "unto whom the word of God came" (humans receiving the Law)
  2. The Hebrew word "elohim" is translated "judges" in Exodus 21:6; 22:8, 9, 28 - referring to human authorities
  3. The context is entirely judicial - judging unjustly, defending the poor, delivering the needy
  4. Psalm 58 (parallel psalm on corrupt judges) explicitly calls them "sons of men"
  5. "Die like men" is used in Hosea 6:7 of Israel - who WERE men

The phrase "die like men" emphasizes that despite their exalted title ("gods"), they will die like any ordinary mortal. It does not imply transformation from divine to human nature.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Psalm 82:6-7 I have said, Ye [are] gods; and all of you [are] children of the most High. But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.

John 10:34-35 Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods? If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken...

Exodus 22:28 Thou shalt not revile the gods [elohim = judges], nor curse the ruler of thy people.

Psalm 58:1 Do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?

docs.title: What Jesus Says (John 10:34-36)
docs.text:
1. The "gods" of Psalm 82 were those "unto whom the word of God came"
  2. This refers to Israel receiving the Law at Sinai
  3. Jesus uses this for an argument from lesser to greater

docs.title: Why Jesus's Interpretation is Decisive
docs.text:
Jesus's argument: - If Scripture calls mere humans "gods" (because they received God's word) - Then the Son of God cannot be accused of blasphemy for claiming deity

This argument ONLY WORKS if the "gods" in Psalm 82 are HUMANS.

If they were divine beings, Jesus's logic collapses.

docs.title: The Hebrew Evidence
docs.text:
The word אֱלֹהִים (elohim) is translated by the KJV as:

Translation Occurrences Referent God 2,346 The true God gods 244 False deities judges 5 Human authorities

docs.title: Passages Where Elohim = Human Judges
docs.text:
Passage Context Exodus 21:6 Servant brought before "the judges" Exodus 22:8 Theft case before "the judges" Exodus 22:9 Property dispute before "the judges" Exodus 22:28 "Revile not the gods" (margin: judges)

The same Hebrew word (elohim) used in Psalm 82 refers to HUMAN judges elsewhere.

docs.title: What the Psalm Describes
docs.text:
Verse Activity Type v.2 "Judge unjustly" Judicial v.2 "Accept persons of the wicked" Partiality v.3 "Defend the poor and fatherless" Judicial duty v.3 "Do justice to the afflicted" Judicial duty v.4 "Deliver the poor and needy" Judicial duty v.5 "They know not, neither understand" Human ignorance

Every element describes the work of human judges - not a heavenly council of divine beings.

docs.title: "Die Like Men" - What It Actually Means
The Argument
docs.text: The angel view claims: "'Die like men' implies they weren't originally men."

docs.title: The Refutation
docs.text:
1. Parallel in Hosea 6:7

"But they like men [כְּאָדָם, ke'adam] have transgressed the covenant"

Israel transgressed "like men" - but they WERE men. The phrase doesn't require non-human origin.

2. The Parallel in Psalm 82:7b

"and fall like one of the princes"

"Fall like princes" doesn't mean they weren't princes. It compares them to princes who have fallen. Similarly, "die like men" compares them to ordinary mortals.

3. The Rhetorical Point

The contrast is between their exalted title ("gods") and their mortal reality (dying like common men). Despite being called "gods," they will die like anyone else.

docs.title: Same Theme, Explicit Identification
docs.text:
Psalm 58:1 - "Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?"

Same elements: - Corrupt judges - Failure to judge righteously - Explicitly called "sons of men" (בְּנֵי אָדָם) - HUMANS

If Psalm 58 and Psalm 82 address the same issue (corrupt judges), and Psalm 58 explicitly calls them "sons of men," then Psalm 82 also addresses humans.

docs.title: Word Studies Summary
docs.text: Hebrew Meaning in Psalm 82 אֱלֹהִים (elohim) Judges - honorific title for human authorities בְּנֵי עֶלְיוֹן (bene elyon) Children of the Most High - relational title כְּאָדָם (ke'adam) Like men - ordinary mortal death שָׁפַט (shaphat) Judge - used 3x, judicial context הַשָּׂרִים (hasarim) Princes - human rulers

docs.title: The Angel View's Claim
docs.text: Psalm 82 is used to argue: 1. "Gods" and "children of the Most High" = divine beings 2. "Die like men" = divine beings punished with mortality 3. This parallels Genesis 6 where divine "sons of God" interacted with humans

docs.title: Why This Fails
docs.text:
Claim Evidence Against "Gods" = divine beings Jesus says they were those who received God's word (humans) "Children of Most High" = ontologically divine This title used for human believers (Matt 5:9; Rom 8:14) "Die like men" = transformation Hosea 6:7 uses same phrase of those who WERE men Context is celestial Context is judicial - human judges failing duties

Psalm 82 provides NO support for the angel view of Genesis 6.

docs.title: Final Assessment
docs.text:
Psalm 82 describes corrupt human judges who:

  1. Bear the honorific title "elohim" (gods) because they represent divine authority
  2. Are called "children of the Most High" because of their special relationship to God
  3. Failed in their judicial duties (judging unjustly, failing the poor)
  4. Will die like ordinary mortals despite their exalted position

Jesus himself interprets this psalm as referring to humans who received God's word.

The phrase "die like men" does not imply prior non-human status. It emphasizes that despite their titles, they are mortal and will face judgment like any other person.

This psalm cannot be used to support the angel view of Genesis 6.

docs.title: Nave's Topical Research: Second Temple Literature and Genesis 6
ENOCH
docs.text:
Nave's Entry: - 1. Oldest son of Cain (Gen 4:17,18) - 2. A city built by Cain (Gen 4:17) - 3. Father of Methuselah. Transporting of (Gen 5:18-24; Luk 3:37; Heb 11:5; Jude 1:14). Called HENOCH (1Ch 1:3)

Key Observations: - Nave's lists Jude 1:14 as a reference for Enoch the person, not for 1 Enoch the book - The entry connects Enoch to translation/walking with God, not to angelic narratives - Scripture's portrait of Enoch: walked with God, was translated, prophesied judgment

docs.title: ANTEDILUVIANS
docs.text:
Nave's Entry: - Worship God (Gen 4:3,4,26) - Occupations of (Gen 4:2,3,20-22) - Arts of (Gen 4:2,3,20-22; 6:14-22) - Enoch prophesies to (Jude 1:14,15) - Noah preaches to (Heb 11:7; 1Pe 3:18-20; 2Pe 2:5) - Wickedness of (Gen 6:5-7) - Destruction of (Gen 7:1,21-23; Job 22:15-17; Mat 24:37-39; Luk 17:26,27; 2Pe 2:5) - Giants among -- See GIANTS - Longevity of -- See LONGEVITY

Key Observations: - Nave's attributes Jude 1:14-15 to the person Enoch prophesying to antediluvians - The entry treats the antediluvian period as a time of human wickedness, arts, and occupations - No mention of angelic invasion or supernatural hybridization - Giants are listed separately, not as angelic offspring

docs.title: GIANTS
docs.text:
Nave's Entry: - General scriptures concerning (Gen 6:4) - See ANAKIM, EMIMS, GOLIATH, ISHBI-BENOB, OG, REPHAIM, ZAMZUMMIM

Key Observations: - The only "general scripture" for giants is Gen 6:4 - All specific giant references are to known human ethnic groups (Anakim, Rephaim, Emims, Zamzummims) - No mention of angelic parentage or supernatural origin - Giants are catalogued as races and individuals, not as angel-human hybrids

docs.title: ANGELS
docs.text:
Nave's Entry (relevant sections): - Legion of angels (Mat 26:53) - Entertains three angels (Gen 18:1-15) -- Abraham at Mamre - Election of good angels (1Ti 5:21) - Jacob's vision of angels (Gen 28:12; Gen 32:2) - Angels announced births, delivered messages, executed judgment

Key Observations: - Nave's extensive angel entry does NOT list Genesis 6 under angel references - Angels in Scripture function as messengers, executors of judgment, worshippers - No entry links angels to marriage, reproduction, or hybrid offspring

docs.title: PROPHECY
docs.text:
Nave's Entry (relevant selections): - A mode of divine communication - Prophets spoke under inspiration - Tests of prophets: fulfillment of predictions, alignment with Torah - Enoch's prophecy (Jude 1:14-15) listed under ANTEDILUVIANS

Key Observations: - Prophecy in Scripture is about divine communication through human vessels - Paul calls Epimenides "a prophet of their own" (Titus 1:12) -- using prophetes for a pagan poet - The term "prophesied" (propheteuo) can denote speaking truth, not necessarily canonical endorsement

docs.title: Summary of Topical Findings
docs.text:
1. Nave's does not connect Genesis 6 to angels -- The GIANTS topic references Gen 6:4 but lists only human giant races
  2. Enoch is treated as a historical person who prophesied -- Not as the author of 1 Enoch the book
  3. The antediluvian narrative focuses on human wickedness -- Arts, occupations, worship, moral corruption
  4. Angels in Nave's are messengers and ministers -- No references to reproduction or intermarriage
  5. Prophecy involves human vessels speaking divine truth -- The term can be applied broadly (Titus 1:12)

Research date: 2026-02-10

docs.title: Verse Texts: Second Temple Literature and Genesis 6
Genesis 6:1-4 (The Source Text)
docs.text:
Genesis 6:1 And it came to pass, when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them,

Genesis 6:2 That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they [were] fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.

Genesis 6:3 And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also [is] flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

Genesis 6:4 There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare [children] to them, the same [became] mighty men which [were] of old, men of renown.

Note: These four verses are the ENTIRE biblical text that 1 Enoch 6-16 (eleven chapters) expands upon.

docs.title: Jude 14-15 (Quoting 1 Enoch 1:9)
docs.text:
Jude 1:14 And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints,

Jude 1:15 To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard [speeches] which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.

docs.title: Paul Quoting Pagan Sources
docs.text:
Acts 17:28 For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

Paul quotes Epimenides of Crete ("in him we live and move and have our being") and Aratus of Soli ("for we are also his offspring") -- pagan Greek poets.

Titus 1:12 One of themselves, [even] a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians [are] alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.

Paul calls Epimenides "a prophet of their own" (prophetes, G4396) -- using the same Greek word used for biblical prophets.

1 Corinthians 15:33 Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.

Paul quotes Menander's comedy Thais -- a pagan theatrical work.

docs.title: Supporting Texts -- Moses Strips Pagan Mythology
Genesis 1:14-18 (Luminaries Stripped of Deity Status)
docs.text:
Genesis 1:14 And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years:

Genesis 1:15 And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so.

Genesis 1:16 And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: [he made] the stars also.

Genesis 1:17 And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth,

Genesis 1:18 And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that [it was] good.

Note: Moses calls the sun and moon "lights" (maor, H3974) -- functional terms. In pagan mythology, the sun was Shamash (a deity), the moon was Sin (a deity). Moses strips them of divine identity.

docs.title: Genesis 1:21 (Sea Creatures Stripped of Deity Status)
docs.text:
Genesis 1:21 And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that [it was] good.

Note: The Hebrew word translated "whales" is tanninim (H8577), which in pagan mythology were divine sea monsters (cf. Tiamat in Enuma Elish). Moses presents them as created beings, not divine rivals.

docs.title: Genesis 2:7 (Human Origin Stripped of Pagan Myth)
docs.text:
Genesis 2:7 And the LORD God formed man [of] the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

Note: In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, man is made from the blood of a slain god (Kingu). Moses says man is from dust -- radically de-divinizing human origin.

docs.title: Deuteronomy 4:19 (Celestial Worship Forbidden)
docs.text:
Deuteronomy 4:19 And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, [even] all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven.

Note: Moses explicitly warns against celestial worship -- treating heavenly bodies as deities is prohibited precisely because other nations had divinized them.

docs.title: Genesis 4:26 (Seth's Godly Line Marked)
docs.text: Genesis 4:26 And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.

docs.title: Genesis 5:21-24 (Enoch the Person)
docs.text:
Genesis 5:21 And Enoch lived sixty and five years, and begat Methuselah:

Genesis 5:22 And Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah three hundred years, and begat sons and daughters:

Genesis 5:23 And all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years:

Genesis 5:24 And Enoch walked with God: and he [was] not; for God took him.

docs.title: Isaiah 14:12-15 (Demythologized Canaanite Myth)
docs.text:
Isaiah 14:12 How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! [how] art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!

Isaiah 14:13 For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:

Isaiah 14:14 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High.

Isaiah 14:15 Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit.

Note: Isaiah 14 uses imagery that parallels Canaanite mythology about the god Helel (Day Star), but applies it to the king of Babylon and to Satan's fall. This demonstrates the prophetic pattern of using pagan imagery while transforming its meaning.

docs.title: Matthew 22:30 (Jesus on Angels and Marriage)
docs.text: Matthew 22:30 For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven.

Key Observations: - Paul calls Epimenides ἴδιος αὐτῶν προφήτης ("their own prophet") -- using the SAME word (prophetes, G4396) that the NT uses for biblical prophets - This is remarkable: Paul applies the title "prophet" to a PAGAN POET - The word prophetes is applied to Epimenides in the same grammatical form as it would be applied to Isaiah or Jeremiah - Paul affirms the TRUTH of Epimenides' statement (v.13: "this witness is true") without endorsing Epimenides' theology or other writings - PARALLEL TO JUDE: Jude says Enoch "prophesied" (same word family, G4395); Paul says Epimenides is a "prophet" (G4396). Both cite a true statement from a non-canonical source without endorsing everything in that source.

docs.title: Analysis: Second Temple Literature and Genesis 6
Overview
docs.text: This analysis addresses four interconnected questions about the relationship between Second Temple Jewish literature (particularly 1 Enoch) and the biblical text of Genesis 6:1-4, examining whether 1 Enoch preserves original meaning or represents later expansion, whether the angel interpretation was unanimous, whether Jude's quotation endorses 1 Enoch's theology, and whether the Pentateuch naturally supports the angel interpretation.

docs.title: Part 1: The Development Problem -- Genesis 6 to 1 Enoch
The Scale of Expansion
docs.text:
Genesis 6:1-4 consists of exactly four verses containing approximately 100 Hebrew words. This text mentions: - Men multiplying, daughters born (v.1) - "Sons of God" seeing and taking wives (v.2) - God limiting human days to 120 years, calling them "flesh" (v.3) - Giants (nephilim) in the earth, mighty men, men of renown (v.4)

1 Enoch 6-16 (the Book of the Watchers) expands this into eleven chapters containing elaborate narrative with: - Named angels: Semjaza (the leader), Azazel, and 18 other named "Watchers" - An oath-bound conspiracy: The angels swear an oath on Mount Hermon to carry out their plan - Forbidden knowledge teachings: Angels teach metallurgy, cosmetics, enchantments, astrology, weather signs - Giant mythology: Giants 3,000 ells tall who consume all produce, then turn to cannibalism - An intermediary petition: Enoch serves as a go-between, carrying the angels' petition to God - Detailed punishments: Specific punishments assigned to specific named angels - Azazel as scapegoat figure: Azazel bound and cast into darkness

docs.title: The Critical Question: Preservation or Elaboration?
docs.text:
The claim: 1 Enoch preserves original traditions about Genesis 6 that the biblical text abbreviated.

The evidence against:

  1. The expansion pattern matches midrashic elaboration, not historical preservation. Jewish midrash characteristically takes brief biblical texts and expands them with named characters, dialogues, narrative details, and theological commentary. The Dead Sea Scroll commentary tradition (pesharim) does the same thing. 1 Enoch follows this exact pattern.

  2. None of 1 Enoch's distinctive details appear in Scripture. The Bible never mentions:

  3. Named fallen angels (Semjaza, Azazel)
  4. An oath on Mount Hermon
  5. Angels teaching metallurgy or cosmetics
  6. Giants 3,000 ells tall
  7. Enoch as intermediary for angels

  8. Any detail from 1 Enoch's elaborate narrative

  9. The elaboration direction is always one way. Brief text becomes elaborate narrative; elaborate narrative never becomes brief text. If 1 Enoch contained the "original tradition," it would be inexplicable why Moses would strip ALL of it down to four generic verses with no distinctive details preserved.

  10. Other Second Temple texts elaborate differently. Jubilees 5:1-11 tells the story differently from 1 Enoch. The Book of Giants (from Qumran) adds different details still. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds its own elaborations. If these were "preserving original tradition," they would agree with each other. Instead, they diverge -- exactly as independent midrashic expansions would.

  11. The composition dates reveal dependency. 1 Enoch 6-36 is typically dated to the 3rd century BC -- over a millennium after Moses. The Book of Giants is even later. These are Second Temple compositions, not pre-Mosaic traditions.

docs.title: Parallel: Other Midrashic Expansions
docs.text:
The same expansion pattern occurs with other biblical texts: - Genesis 22 (the binding of Isaac) -- The Targums and midrashim add dialogues between Abraham and Isaac, Satan's role, angels weeping, etc. No one argues these "preserve original details." - Exodus 14 (the Red Sea crossing) -- Midrashic literature adds named Egyptian generals, specific numbers, tribal formations. These are recognized as elaborations. - Genesis 3 (the fall) -- Later literature adds extensive dialogues between the serpent and Eve, details about the tree, etc.

The pattern is consistent: brief biblical text generates elaborate midrashic expansion. 1 Enoch's relationship to Genesis 6 fits this pattern exactly.

docs.title: Part 2: Was the Angel Interpretation Unanimous?
The Claim
docs.text: The angel view is often presented as the unanimous understanding of ancient Judaism and early Christianity, supposedly overturned only in modern times.

docs.title: The Evidence: It Was NOT Unanimous
docs.text:
Readings supporting HUMAN identity:

Source Date Genesis 6:2 Rendering Nature Targum Onkelos 2nd cent. AD "sons of nobles/great ones" Human Symmachus (Greek) 2nd cent. AD "sons of kings" Human Standard LXX (Rahlfs) 3rd cent. BC "sons of God" (υἱοί, NOT ἄγγελοι) Neutral -- used for humans in NT Peshitta (Syriac) 2nd cent. AD "sons of God" Neutral Vulgate (Latin) 4th cent. AD "filii Dei" ("sons of God") Neutral

Church fathers supporting HUMAN identity:

Father Date Position Julius Africanus c. 160-240 AD Sethite view John Chrysostom 347-407 AD Sethite view Augustine 354-430 AD Sethite view (City of God XV.23) Cyril of Alexandria 376-444 AD Sethite view Theodoret 393-458 AD Sethite view

Readings supporting ANGEL identity:

Source Date Genesis 6:2 Rendering Nature 1 Enoch 6-16 3rd cent. BC Angels (named "Watchers") Angelic Jubilees 5:1-11 2nd cent. BC Angels Angelic Book of Giants (Qumran) 2nd-1st cent. BC Giants from angel unions Angelic Codex Alexandrinus 5th cent. AD "angels of God" (ἄγγελοι) Angelic (variant) Philo of Alexandria 1st cent. AD Angels Angelic Justin Martyr c. 100-165 AD Angel view Angelic

docs.title: Critical Observations from Prior Studies
docs.text:
From septuagint-genesis-6-translation study: - The standard critical text of the LXX (Rahlfs-Hanhart) reads "sons of God" (υἱοί), NOT "angels of God" (ἄγγελοι) in Genesis 6:2 - The same LXX translators who used "angels" in Job 1:6, 2:1, and 38:7 deliberately chose "sons" for Genesis 6 - The "angels" reading in Codex Alexandrinus (5th century) is a later scribal variant - This distinction shows the translators SAW a contextual difference

From genesis-6-lxx-nt-comparison study: - The LXX Genesis 6:2 uses identical Greek terminology (υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ) to the NT's phrase for human believers (Rom 8:14, 19; Gal 3:26) - Linguistically, the LXX Genesis 6 phrase is FULLY compatible with human reference

docs.title: Conclusion on Unanimity
docs.text: The angel interpretation was widespread but not unanimous. Ancient Jewish sources like Targum Onkelos explicitly chose human readings. The standard LXX translators distinguished Genesis 6 from Job. Major church fathers held the Sethite view. The claim of unanimity is historically false.

docs.title: Part 3: Does Jude's Quotation of 1 Enoch Endorse Its Theology?
The Argument
docs.text: "Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 in Jude 14-15, calling Enoch's words a 'prophecy.' This validates 1 Enoch and, by extension, its angel interpretation of Genesis 6."

docs.title: The Biblical Pattern: Quoting a Source Does Not Endorse Its Entire Theology
docs.text:
Paul quotes three pagan sources:

Passage Source Quoted Pagan Author What Paul Calls Him Acts 17:28a "In him we live and move and have our being" Epimenides of Crete "your own poets" (ποιητῶν) Acts 17:28b "For we are also his offspring" Aratus of Soli (Phaenomena) "your own poets" Titus 1:12 "Cretians are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies" Epimenides of Crete "a prophet of their own" (προφήτης) 1 Cor 15:33 "Evil communications corrupt good manners" Menander (Thais) (no title given)

Critical parallels between Paul and Jude:

  1. Paul calls Epimenides "a prophet" (prophetes, G4396). This is the same Greek word used for Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Jesus. Yet no one argues that Paul thereby endorses Epimenides' theology, his other writings, or his Cretan religious system.

  2. Jude says Enoch "prophesied" (propheteuo, G4395). This is the verb form of the same word Paul uses for Epimenides. Jude attributes the prophecy to the MAN Enoch ("the seventh from Adam"), identifying him historically, not validating the BOOK attributed to him.

  3. Paul affirms the TRUTH of the specific statement (Titus 1:13: "This witness is true"), not the truth of everything Epimenides wrote or believed.

  4. Jude affirms the TRUTH of the specific prophecy (God coming in judgment against the ungodly), not the truth of everything in 1 Enoch.

docs.title: What Jude 14-15 Actually Quotes
docs.text:
The content of Jude's quotation from 1 Enoch 1:9 is: - The Lord comes with ten thousands of His saints - To execute judgment upon all - To convict the ungodly of their ungodly deeds and hard speeches

What this content is about: Universal eschatological judgment against the ungodly.

What this content is NOT about: Angels, Genesis 6, Watchers, named fallen angels, giant offspring, forbidden knowledge, or any distinctive 1 Enoch theology.

Jude quotes a statement about final judgment -- a truth thoroughly established throughout Scripture (Deut 33:2; Dan 7:10; Zech 14:5; Matt 25:31; 2 Thess 1:7-8; Rev 19:14). The specific statement Jude quotes would be TRUE regardless of whether 1 Enoch existed.

docs.title: The Logical Error
docs.text:
The argument "Jude quotes 1 Enoch, therefore 1 Enoch's angel interpretation of Genesis 6 is validated" commits a logical fallacy:

  1. Jude quotes statement X from 1 Enoch
  2. 1 Enoch also contains interpretation Y of Genesis 6
  3. Therefore Jude endorses interpretation Y

This is a non sequitur. Quoting one true statement from a source does not validate every other statement in that source. Paul's quotation of Epimenides does not validate Epimenides' claim that Zeus was born in Crete. Paul's quotation of Aratus does not validate Stoic pantheism. Jude's quotation of 1 Enoch's judgment prophecy does not validate 1 Enoch's Watcher narrative.

docs.title: Additional Evidence: Jude's Context
docs.text:
From jude-6-7-angels-sin study: - Jude 6 describes angelic rebellion (leaving their position, cast from heaven -- parallel to Rev 12) - Jude 6 does NOT describe angels taking human wives - Jude 7 describes Sodom's sin as homosexuality ("strange flesh") - "In like manner" connects surrounding cities to Sodom, not angels to sexual sin - Jude gives THREE examples of judgment (Israel, angels, Sodom) -- three SEPARATE illustrations, not one connected narrative

Even in the immediate context of Jude's letter, the angel reference (v.6) does not match 1 Enoch's narrative of angel-human intermarriage.

docs.title: Part 4: The Pentateuch Without Second Temple Imports
Reading Genesis 1-6 on Its Own Terms
docs.text:
If a reader approached Genesis 1-6 with no knowledge of 1 Enoch, Jubilees, or Second Temple angel traditions, what would the text naturally communicate?

Genesis 4: Establishes Cain's ungodly line (murder, arrogance, polygamy -- Lamech) Genesis 4:26: Marks Seth's line: "then began men to call upon the name of the LORD" Genesis 5: Traces Seth's godly line through Enoch ("walked with God") and Noah Genesis 6:1-2: "Sons of God" take "daughters of men" as wives Genesis 6:3: God says: "My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh" Genesis 6:5-7: God sees human wickedness and resolves to judge

The natural reading in context: The godly line (sons of God, identified by calling on the LORD's name) intermarried with the ungodly line (daughters of men, Cain's descendants). This mixed marriage led to spiritual decline. God's response addresses HUMAN flesh, not angelic transgression.

docs.title: The Critical Verse: Genesis 6:3
docs.text:
"My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh."

God identifies the "sons of God" as: 1. "Man" (adam) -- a human term 2. "Flesh" (basar) -- a human description 3. Subject to limited "days" -- human mortality

If angels were the problem, why would God: - Address His response to "man"? - Call the offenders "flesh"? - Limit human lifespan as the consequence? - Focus judgment entirely on the human race (flood)?

From genesis-6-sons-of-god_2 study: God's own words in Gen 6:3 identify the "sons of God" as "man" and "flesh." This is the single most decisive textual indicator.

docs.title: Moses's Vocabulary Patterns
docs.text:
From moses-angel-terminology study (existing research): - Moses uses "malak" (H4397, angel/messenger) for celestial beings 28+ times throughout the Pentateuch - Moses NEVER uses "bene elohim" (sons of God) for angels - In Genesis 19:1, when Moses means angels, he writes "angels" (malakhim) - If Moses intended angels in Genesis 6:2, why did he use completely different terminology?

From moses-human-god-relationship-terms study: - Moses calls Israel "children of the LORD your God" (Deut 14:1) -- humans as "children of God" - Moses uses "my people," "holy nation," "sons" for godly humans

docs.title: Part 5: Moses Strips Pagan Mythology from Genesis
The Pattern: Moses Systematically Strips Divine Status from Pagan Mythological Entities
docs.text:
The Pentateuch was written in a world saturated with pagan mythology. Surrounding cultures had rich mythologies about divine beings interacting with the physical world. Moses's response to this cultural context is consistent and systematic: he strips divine status from the elements that pagan cultures worshipped.

Pagan Myth Moses's Text What Moses Does Sun = Shamash (deity) Gen 1:16: "the greater light" Strips divine identity; it is a "light" (maor), not a god Moon = Sin (deity) Gen 1:16: "the lesser light" Strips divine identity; it is a "light," not a god Stars = divine beings Gen 1:16: "the stars also" Dismissive aside: "also" -- not divine, just made Sea monsters = Tiamat (divine rival) Gen 1:21: "God created great whales" Created things (bara), not divine rivals Man = from divine blood Gen 2:7: "formed man of the dust" From dust, not divine blood (contra Enuma Elish) Celestial bodies = worthy of worship Deut 4:19: "should be driven to worship them" Explicitly forbids celestial worship Helel/Day Star = deity Isa 14:12: "fallen from heaven" Applied to a mortal king who will "die like men"

docs.title: The Consistency of the Pattern
docs.text:
This pattern is not occasional -- it is systematic and comprehensive:

  1. Creation Day 1: Light is created by God's word, not born from divine union
  2. Creation Day 4: Sun and moon are functional "lights," deliberately unnamed (in pagan cultures, naming conferred divine status)
  3. Creation Day 5: Sea creatures (tanninim) are created by God, not primordial rivals
  4. Creation Day 6: Man from dust, breath from God -- no divine blood component
  5. Post-flood: Rainbow as covenant sign (Gen 9:13-16), not divine weapon
  6. Deuteronomy: Explicit prohibition against celestial worship (Deut 4:19)

docs.title: The Implication for Genesis 6
docs.text:
If the Pentateuch SYSTEMATICALLY strips pagan mythology -- removing divine status from sun, moon, stars, sea monsters, and human origins -- then reading Genesis 6 as "divine beings mating with humans" would be:

  1. A reversal of the established pattern. Every other pagan mythological concept is stripped of divine character. Why would Moses suddenly PRESERVE the most sensational myth of all -- divine beings procreating with humans?

  2. A contradiction of Moses's own theological program. Moses's consistent message is that these "divine" beings of pagan myth are merely created things. Introducing actual divine-human hybridization would undermine his entire program.

  3. An insertion of precisely what Moses elsewhere removes. Pagan cultures (Mesopotamian, Greek, Canaanite) had myths of divine beings mating with humans. Moses removes such concepts everywhere else but supposedly preserves it in Genesis 6?

The human interpretation CONTINUES the pattern. If "sons of God" = godly human line, then Genesis 6 describes human intermarriage and moral decline -- no mythological divine beings involved. This is consistent with everything else Moses writes.

The angel interpretation REVERSES the pattern. If "sons of God" = angels/divine beings who mate with humans, then Moses has introduced the very pagan mythology he systematically strips everywhere else.

docs.title: From the Word Study (04-word-studies.md)
docs.text: H430 (elohim) is translated in the KJV as: - God (the true God): ~87.5% of occurrences - gods (false deities): ~5.2% - the judges: 5 occurrences (Exo 21:6; 22:8, 9; 1 Sam 2:25) - mighty: 2 occurrences (Gen 23:6; Exo 9:28)

docs.title: What This Means for "Sons of God" (bene ha'elohim)
docs.text:
The phrase "sons of God" is built on elohim. Because elohim has a documented range including "judges" and "mighty ones," the phrase "sons of elohim" can mean: - Sons of God (theological/spiritual relationship) - Sons of the mighty/powerful (human rulers) - Sons of the judges (human authorities) - Sons of the gods (divine council -- as in Job)

From psalm-82-gods study: - Psalm 82:6 calls human judges "elohim" and "children of the most High" - Jesus interprets this as referring to humans "unto whom the word of God came" (John 10:34-35) - The parallel Psalm 58 calls the same group "sons of men" - Elohim applied to humans is BIBLICALLY ESTABLISHED

The Targum Onkelos translation "sons of nobles" and Symmachus's "sons of kings" both reflect this legitimate semantic range. These are not distortions of the Hebrew but valid renderings based on documented usage of elohim.

docs.title: Synthesis: The Six Lines of Evidence Converge
docs.text: Question Finding 1. Does 1 Enoch preserve original meaning? No -- the expansion pattern matches midrashic elaboration; none of 1 Enoch's distinctive details appear in Scripture 2. Was the angel view unanimous? No -- Targum Onkelos, Symmachus, standard LXX translators, and major church fathers held the human view 3. Does Jude's quotation endorse 1 Enoch? No -- quoting a true statement does not endorse the source's entire theology (parallel: Paul quoting pagan poets) 4. Does the Pentateuch naturally support the angel view? No -- the immediate context (Gen 4-5), God's words in Gen 6:3, and Moses's vocabulary all favor the human reading 5. Does Moses's treatment of pagan mythology support the angel view? No -- the angel view reverses Moses's pattern of stripping pagan mythology from Genesis 6. Does elohim require "divine beings"? No -- elohim means judges, mighty ones, rulers in documented usage

docs.title: Word Studies: Second Temple Literature and Genesis 6
Lexicon Entry
docs.text:
• Transliteration: 'elohiym
  • Pronunciation: el-o-heem
  • Part of Speech: masculine noun (plural form)
  • Total OT occurrences: 2,685
  • Definition: Plural of eloah; gods in the ordinary sense; but specifically used (especially with the article) of the supreme God; occasionally applied by way of deference to magistrates; and sometimes as a superlative -- angels, exceeding, God (gods)(-dess, -ly), (very) great, judges, mighty.

docs.title: Elohim as "Judges" -- Key Passages
docs.text:
The KJV translates elohim as "the judges" in: - Exodus 21:6 -- "his master shall bring him unto the judges [elohim]" - Exodus 22:8 -- "the master of the house shall be brought unto the judges [elohim]" - Exodus 22:9 -- "the cause of both parties shall come before the judges [elohim]" (twice)

And as "the judge" in: - 1 Samuel 2:25 -- "the judge [elohim] shall judge him"

docs.title: Elohim as "Mighty" -- Key Passages
docs.text:
• Genesis 23:6 -- "a mighty [elohim] prince among us"
  • Exodus 9:28 -- "mighty [elohim] thunderings"

docs.title: Significance for Genesis 6
docs.text:
The wide semantic range of elohim demonstrates that "sons of elohim" (bene ha'elohim) is NOT linguistically limited to "sons of angels" or "sons of divine beings." The phrase could legitimately mean: 1. Sons of God -- godly descendants (Sethite view) 2. Sons of the judges/mighty ones -- sons of rulers or nobles (Targum Onkelos: "sons of nobles") 3. Sons of the gods -- divine beings (angel view)

The Targum Onkelos rendering "sons of nobles/great ones" reflects the elohim = "mighty ones/judges" semantic range. Symmachus translated "sons of kings" -- also reflecting the ruler/judge meaning. Both are linguistically legitimate based on the documented usage of elohim.

  • Pronunciation: prof-ay-tace
  • Part of Speech: masculine noun
  • Total NT occurrences: 134
  • Definition: From a compound of pro (before/forth) and phemi (to speak); a foreteller, prophet; by analogy, an inspired speaker

docs.title: Translation Distribution
docs.text: Translation Count Percentage prophets 69 51.5% prophet 34 25.4% a prophet 12 9.0% A prophet 6 4.5% the prophets 4 3.0% other forms 9 6.7%

docs.title: Key Usage: Titus 1:12
docs.text:
Paul calls Epimenides ἴδιος αὐτῶν προφήτης ("their own prophet") using the identical Greek word (prophetes) used for: - Moses (Acts 3:22: "A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up") - Jesus (Luke 24:19: "a prophet mighty in deed and word") - OT prophets generally (Hebrews 1:1: "God, who at sundry times spake by the prophets")

This is critical for the Jude/1 Enoch question: If Paul can call a pagan Cretan poet "a prophet" (G4396) without endorsing Epimenides' theology, religion, or other writings, then Jude can say Enoch "prophesied" (G4395) without endorsing 1 Enoch's entire theological framework.

docs.title: The Range of Prophetes
docs.text:
The NT use of prophetes extends beyond "inspired canonical author" to include: - Biblical prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, etc. - NT prophets: Agabus, church prophets (1 Cor 12:28; Eph 4:11) - Pagan figures who spoke truth: Epimenides (Titus 1:12) - Historical figures who predicted: Caiaphas unwittingly prophesied (John 11:51)

The word describes the ACT of speaking forth truth, not necessarily the canonical authority of the speaker's entire body of work.

docs.title: Key Usage: Jude 1:14
docs.text:
Ἐπροφήτευσεν (Epropheteusen) -- Aorist Active Indicative 3rd Singular - "And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these..."

Grammatical Analysis: - The aorist tense indicates a completed past action -- Enoch did prophesy - The subject is the MAN Enoch ("the seventh from Adam"), not the BOOK of 1 Enoch - Jude attributes the prophetic act to the historical person, using his genealogical identification - Compare Matthew 7:22 where false prophets claim "have we not prophesied in thy name?" -- the word propheteuo can describe the act of speaking forth without validating the speaker's authority

docs.title: The Jude/Paul Parallel in Word Study
docs.text:
Feature Jude 1:14 Titus 1:12 Source cited 1 Enoch (attributed to Enoch) Epimenides of Crete Verb/Title used ἐπροφήτευσεν (propheteuo, G4395) προφήτης (prophetes, G4396) Word family Same root: prophet- Same root: prophet- Speaker identified as "Enoch, seventh from Adam" "one of themselves, a prophet of their own" Content affirmed Truth about coming judgment Truth about Cretan character Source endorsed? Not the book, but the statement Not Epimenides' religion, but the statement Paul's verdict -- "This witness is TRUE" (v.13)

Conclusion from word study: The propheteuo/prophetes word family is used for speaking truth, not for endorsing an entire corpus. Both Jude and Paul cite a true statement from a non-canonical source using the "prophet" word family, confirming that quoting does not equal endorsing.

docs.title: Summary of Word Study Findings
docs.text:
1. H430 (elohim): The semantic range includes God, gods, judges, mighty ones. "Sons of elohim" is not linguistically limited to "sons of angels." The Targum Onkelos and Symmachus readings reflect legitimate semantic options.

  2. G4396 (prophetes): The word means "one who speaks forth." Paul applies it to a pagan poet (Titus 1:12). This establishes that calling someone a "prophet" or saying they "prophesied" does not canonize their entire body of work.

  3. G4395 (propheteuo): Jude says Enoch "prophesied" using the same word family Paul uses for Epimenides. The act of prophesying affirms the truth of the specific statement, not the theological framework of the source.

docs.title: Conclusion: Second Temple Literature and Genesis 6 -- 1 Enoch, Pagan Context, and Biblical Authority
Question
docs.text: The angel interpretation of Genesis 6:1-4 is documented in Second Temple Jewish literature: 1 Enoch (Book of the Watchers), Jubilees, and the Book of Giants. These texts elaborate Genesis 6's four verses into detailed narratives with named angels, oath-bound conspiracies, forbidden knowledge teachings, and elaborate giant mythology. (1) Does the development from Genesis 6's brief text to 1 Enoch's elaborate narrative suggest preservation of original meaning or later interpretive expansion? (2) Was the angel interpretation unanimous in ancient Judaism, or did alternative readings exist? (3) Does Jude's quotation of 1 Enoch (Jude 14-15) endorse 1 Enoch's theology of Genesis 6? (4) Does the Pentateuch itself, read without importing Second Temple categories, naturally lead to the angel interpretation or the human interpretation?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The evidence examined across six lines of inquiry consistently points in the same direction: 1 Enoch's elaborate Watcher narrative represents later midrashic expansion, not preservation of original meaning. The angel interpretation was not unanimous in ancient Judaism. Jude's quotation of 1 Enoch follows the same pattern as Paul quoting pagan poets -- affirming a true statement without endorsing the source's theology. The Pentateuch, read on its own terms, naturally supports the human interpretation through its immediate context, God's own identification of the "sons of God" as "man" and "flesh" (Gen 6:3), and Moses's systematic stripping of pagan mythology from Genesis.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Genesis 6:2-3 That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose. And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

Jude 1:14-15 And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed, and of all their hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.

Titus 1:12 One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.

Acts 17:28 For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

Genesis 1:16 And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also.

Deuteronomy 4:19 And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven.

docs.title: Question 1: Does 1 Enoch Preserve Original Meaning or Represent Later Expansion?
docs.text:
Answer: Later expansion. The development from Genesis 6's four verses to 1 Enoch's eleven-chapter narrative follows the recognizable pattern of midrashic elaboration, not historical preservation.

Evidence:

  1. The expansion is massive and one-directional. Genesis 6:1-4 contains approximately 100 Hebrew words. 1 Enoch 6-16 expands this into detailed narrative with named angels (Semjaza, Azazel, 18 others), an oath-bound conspiracy on Mount Hermon, angels teaching forbidden knowledge (metallurgy, cosmetics, astrology), giants 3,000 ells tall who turn to cannibalism, and Enoch serving as intermediary. NONE of these details appear anywhere in Scripture.

  2. Multiple Second Temple texts elaborate differently. Jubilees 5:1-11 tells the story differently from 1 Enoch. The Book of Giants adds different details. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan provides yet another elaboration. If these texts preserved a common original tradition, they would agree. Instead, they diverge -- exactly as independent midrashic expansions of a common source text would.

  3. The pattern matches known midrashic expansion. The same phenomenon occurs with Genesis 22 (binding of Isaac), Exodus 14 (Red Sea crossing), and Genesis 3 (the fall). Brief biblical texts generate elaborate extra-biblical narratives. No one argues those expansions "preserve original traditions." 1 Enoch's relationship to Genesis 6 fits the same recognized literary pattern.

  4. If 1 Enoch contained the "original," Moses's abbreviation is inexplicable. Why would Moses, writing under divine inspiration, strip every distinctive detail -- named angels, the oath, forbidden teachings, giant dimensions -- and reduce eleven chapters to four generic verses? The simpler explanation: Genesis 6:1-4 is the original; 1 Enoch is the expansion.

docs.title: Question 2: Was the Angel Interpretation Unanimous?
docs.text:
Answer: No. The angel view was widespread but never universal.

Human-view readings: - Targum Onkelos (2nd cent. AD): "sons of nobles/great ones" -- explicitly human - Symmachus (2nd cent. AD): "sons of kings" -- explicitly human - Standard LXX (Rahlfs-Hanhart critical text): "sons of God" (υἱοί), NOT "angels of God" (ἄγγελοι) -- the same translators who rendered Job 1:6 as "angels" deliberately chose "sons" for Genesis 6 - Major church fathers: Julius Africanus (c. 200 AD), John Chrysostom (c. 400 AD), Augustine (City of God XV.23, c. 426 AD), Cyril of Alexandria, and Theodoret all held the Sethite/human view

The claim that "everyone always understood it as angels until modern times" is historically false. The human interpretation is ancient, Jewish, and well-attested.

From septuagint-genesis-6-translation study: The fact that the LXX translators used ἄγγελοι ("angels") for Job 1:6 but υἱοί ("sons") for Genesis 6:2 is itself interpretive evidence. They saw a contextual difference and translated accordingly.

docs.title: Question 3: Does Jude's Quotation of 1 Enoch Endorse Its Theology?
docs.text:
Answer: No. Jude's quotation follows the established biblical pattern of citing true statements from non-canonical sources without endorsing the source's entire theological framework.

The Paul-Jude parallel is decisive:

Feature Jude 1:14-15 Titus 1:12 Acts 17:28 1 Cor 15:33 Source 1 Enoch 1:9 Epimenides of Crete Aratus of Soli / Epimenides Menander (Thais) Source type Jewish pseudepigraphal Pagan Cretan poet Pagan Greek poets Pagan Greek comedy Title given "prophesied" (G4395) "a prophet of their own" (G4396) "your own poets" (G4163) (none) Content quoted God comes in judgment against ungodly Cretans are liars, beasts, lazy We live/move/have being in God; we are His offspring Evil company corrupts Endorsed? The specific statement The specific statement (v.13: "this witness is true") The specific statement The specific statement Source theology endorsed? No No (Epimenides' religion rejected) No (Stoic pantheism rejected) No (pagan comedy not endorsed)

Greek grammar confirms the parallel: - Jude uses ἐπροφήτευσεν (epropheteusen, G4395) -- "prophesied" (aorist active indicative) - Paul uses προφήτης (prophetes, G4396) -- "prophet" (nominative singular) - These are from the same word family (prophet-). Both apply the "prophet" concept to non-canonical speakers who said something true. - Paul calls a PAGAN poet "a prophet" using the very same Greek word the NT uses for Isaiah and Jeremiah. This establishes beyond doubt that the prophetic vocabulary does not equal canonical endorsement.

What Jude actually quotes: A prophecy about God coming in judgment against the ungodly. This truth is attested throughout Scripture (Deut 33:2; Dan 7:10; Zech 14:5; Matt 25:31; 2 Thess 1:7-8; Rev 19:14). The specific content is about eschatological judgment -- it contains NOTHING about angels, Genesis 6, Watchers, giant offspring, or any distinctive 1 Enoch theology.

The logical fallacy: "Jude quotes 1 Enoch, therefore Jude endorses 1 Enoch's angel interpretation of Genesis 6" commits a non sequitur. Quoting statement X from a source does not validate statement Y from the same source. Paul quoting Aratus does not validate Stoic pantheism. Jude quoting 1 Enoch's judgment prophecy does not validate 1 Enoch's Watcher mythology.

docs.title: Question 4: Does the Pentateuch Naturally Support the Angel or Human Interpretation?
docs.text:
Answer: The human interpretation. Three converging lines of evidence from the Pentateuch itself favor the human reading:

A. The immediate context (Genesis 4-5) establishes the framework: - Genesis 4: Cain's ungodly line (murder, arrogance, polygamy) - Genesis 4:26: Seth's godly line marked: "then began men to call upon the name of the LORD" - Genesis 5: Seth's line traced through Enoch ("walked with God") and Noah - Genesis 6:1-2: "Sons of God" intermarry with "daughters of men" - The narrative flow is godly line merging with ungodly line -- no introduction of supernatural beings required

B. God's own words identify them as human (Genesis 6:3): - "My spirit shall not always strive with man" -- addressing humans - "For that he also is flesh" -- calling them flesh (never used for angels) - "Yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years" -- limiting human lifespan - If angels were the problem, God's response is inexplicably focused on human judgment

C. Moses strips pagan mythology from Genesis everywhere else:

Pagan Mythology Moses's Treatment Result Sun = deity (Shamash) Gen 1:16: "the greater light" Demythologized Moon = deity (Sin) Gen 1:16: "the lesser light" Demythologized Sea monsters = divine rivals (Tiamat) Gen 1:21: "God created great whales" Demythologized Man = from divine blood (Kingu) Gen 2:7: "dust of the ground" Demythologized Celestial bodies = gods Deut 4:19: "shouldest be driven to worship them" Explicitly forbidden Divine beings mate with humans (pagan trope) Gen 6:1-4 ???

The angel interpretation would have Moses PRESERVING the most sensational pagan myth (divine beings procreating with humans) while stripping divine status from sun, moon, sea creatures, and human origins everywhere else. This is a reversal of his entire theological program.

The human interpretation continues the pattern: "sons of God" = godly humans, "daughters of men" = ungodly humans, the problem = spiritual decline through intermarriage. No pagan mythological framework is preserved. The pattern is consistent.

docs.title: The Elohim Semantic Range
docs.text:
H430 (elohim) has 2,685 OT occurrences across a wide semantic range: - God (the true God): ~87.5% - gods (false deities): ~5.2% - judges (human authorities): Exodus 21:6; 22:8, 9 -- 5 occurrences - mighty (superlative): Genesis 23:6; Exodus 9:28 -- 2 occurrences

From psalm-82-gods study: Jesus Himself interprets "gods" (elohim) in Psalm 82 as referring to HUMANS "unto whom the word of God came" (John 10:34-35). The parallel Psalm 58 calls the same group "sons of men." Elohim applied to human authorities is biblically established.

"Sons of elohim" is therefore NOT limited to "sons of divine beings." Targum Onkelos's "sons of nobles" and Symmachus's "sons of kings" reflect legitimate semantic options based on documented elohim usage.

docs.title: What the Evidence Establishes
docs.text:
1. 1 Enoch's Watcher narrative is midrashic expansion. The massive, one-directional elaboration from four verses to eleven chapters, with details found nowhere in Scripture, matches the recognized pattern of later interpretive development.

  2. The angel interpretation was NOT unanimous. Ancient Jewish (Targum Onkelos, Symmachus), Greek (standard LXX translators), and patristic (Augustine, Chrysostom, Julius Africanus) sources held the human interpretation.

  3. Jude quoting 1 Enoch does NOT endorse its angel theology. Paul quotes pagan poets (Epimenides, Aratus, Menander) using the same "prophet" word family, without endorsing their theology. The precedent is clear and the parallel exact.

  4. The Pentateuch without Second Temple imports supports the human reading. Genesis 4-5 establishes the godly/ungodly line contrast. Genesis 6:3 identifies the subjects as "man" and "flesh." Moses's vocabulary uses "malak" for angels, not "bene elohim." Moses strips pagan mythology from Genesis everywhere else -- the angel reading would reverse this pattern.

  5. The elohim semantic range allows the human reading. "Sons of elohim" can legitimately mean "sons of the mighty/nobles/judges" based on documented OT usage of elohim.

  6. The Second Temple literature should be read as interpretation, not source. These texts are valuable for understanding ancient Jewish interpretation, but they are not authoritative for determining what Genesis 6 means. The biblical text must be interpreted from the biblical text.

docs.title: What This Study Does NOT Claim
docs.text:
• That 1 Enoch has no historical or scholarly value
  • That the angel view is impossible to hold
  • That Jude's quotation is insignificant
  • That Second Temple literature should be ignored
  • That all who hold the angel view are wrong-minded

docs.title: What This Study DOES Claim
docs.text:
• That 1 Enoch's elaboration follows midrashic patterns, not historical preservation
  • That the angel interpretation was disputed in antiquity, not unanimous
  • That biblical quotation of non-canonical sources follows a clear pattern that does not equal endorsement
  • That the Pentateuch's own text, context, vocabulary, and theological program favor the human interpretation
  • That importing Second Temple categories into Genesis 6 is an interpretive choice, not a textual necessity

docs.title: Topics Research: Septuagint Translation of Genesis 6:2
Question
docs.text: Does the Septuagint (LXX) translate "sons of God" in Genesis 6:2 as "angels of God"? And if so, what does this mean for interpretation?

docs.title: Important Principle
docs.text:
The Septuagint is a translation, not the inspired original.

The LXX is a Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made by Jewish scholars, primarily in Alexandria, Egypt, beginning around the 3rd century BC. While valuable as an ancient witness to Jewish interpretation, it reflects the interpretive choices of the translators, not the authoritative meaning of the text.

The Hebrew Masoretic Text is the inspired original. Translations (including the LXX, Vulgate, and modern versions) reflect human understanding of that original.

docs.title: ANGEL (a spirit)
docs.text:
A CELESTIAL SPIRIT Called ANGEL OF THE LORD MAT 1:20,24; 2:13,19; 28:2; LUK 1:11; ACT 5:19; 7:30,35; 8:26; 12:7,23 Called MORNING STARS JOB 38:7 ... Do not marry MAT 22:30; MRK 12:25; LUK 20:35 ...

Key observation from Nave's: Angels are described as celestial spirits who "do not marry" (Matt 22:30; Mark 12:25; Luke 20:35). This is relevant to whether "sons of God" in Genesis 6:2 (who took wives) could be angels.

docs.title: ADOPTION (Spiritual)
docs.text:
SPIRITUAL EXO 4:22,23; NUM 6:27; DEU 14:1; 26:18; 27:9; 28:10; 32:5,6... "Ye are the children of the LORD your God" (DEU 14:1)

Key observation: Nave's documents that Scripture calls godly humans "children of God" - this is the language Moses used for Israel (Deut 14:1).

docs.title: Topic 1: Translation Terminology
docs.text:
This study examines how ancient translations rendered the Hebrew phrase בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (bene ha'elohim):

Translation Date Genesis 6:2 Rendering Septuagint (LXX) 3rd cent. BC υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ = "sons of God" Codex Alexandrinus 5th cent. AD ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ = "angels of God" (variant) Peshitta (Syriac) 2nd cent. AD "sons of God" Vulgate (Latin) 4th cent. AD "filii Dei" = "sons of God" Targum Onkelos 2nd cent. AD "sons of nobles" (human) Symmachus (Greek) 2nd cent. AD "sons of the kings" (human)

docs.title: Topic 2: LXX Translator Distinctions
docs.text:
The LXX translators made a notable distinction between how they rendered the same Hebrew phrase in different books:

Passage Hebrew LXX Greek LXX Translation Genesis 6:2 בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ sons of God Genesis 6:4 בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ sons of God Job 1:6 בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ angels of God Job 2:1 בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ angels of God Job 38:7 בְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים ἄγγελοί μου my angels

Critical finding: The same Hebrew phrase was translated differently based on context: - In Genesis 6 (earthly scene of marriage): "sons of God" - In Job (heavenly throne-room with Satan): "angels of God"

docs.text:
Reference Hebrew LXX Greek LXX Translation Context Gen 6:2 bene ha'elohim υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ sons of God Earthly; marriage Gen 6:4 bene ha'elohim υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ sons of God Earthly; marriage Job 1:6 bene ha'elohim ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ angels of God Heavenly throne room Job 2:1 bene ha'elohim ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ angels of God Heavenly throne room Job 38:7 bene elohim ἄγγελοί μου my angels Creation; before humans

docs.title: Verse Analysis: Septuagint Translation of Genesis 6:2
Key Observation
docs.text:
The Septuagint translators made a significant distinction between Genesis and Job, even though the Hebrew phrase is identical:

Book Hebrew Greek Translation Context Genesis 6 bene ha'elohim υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ (huioi tou theou) Earthly marriage scene Job 1, 2, 38 bene ha'elohim ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ (angeloi tou theou) Heavenly throne room

This is remarkable: The LXX translators knew how to write "angels" (ἄγγελοι) in Greek. They used it in Job. But they chose NOT to use it in Genesis 6. Why?

docs.title: Analysis: Why the Distinction?
docs.text:
The LXX translators saw something in the context that led them to make different translation choices:

Genesis 6 Context: - Earthly scene on "the face of the earth" (v. 1) - Men multiplying; daughters born (human reproduction) - "Took them wives" - normal marriage vocabulary - God's response focuses on "man" who is "flesh" (v. 3) - Human lifespan limited to 120 years (v. 3)

Job 1-2 Context: - Heavenly throne-room scene - Beings "present themselves before the LORD" - Satan among them - No marriage, no reproduction, no earthly activity

Job 38:7 Context: - Creation account - Before humans existed - "Morning stars" and "sons of God" together - Clearly celestial beings

docs.title: The Contextual Principle
docs.text:
The LXX translators applied a principle we should also apply: context determines meaning.

The same phrase can have different referents in different settings: - In a heavenly throne room with Satan → angelic beings - In an earthly scene of marriage → humans in relationship with God

docs.title: The Standard Text (Rahlfs-Hanhart)
docs.text:
The critical edition of the Septuagint (Rahlfs-Hanhart) reads:

Genesis 6:2: οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ = "the sons of God"

This is the standard, scholarly text of the LXX.

Source verification: - Blue Letter Bible LXX Genesis 6:2 - Full Greek text: ἰδόντες δὲ οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τὰς θυγατέρας τῶν ἀνθρώπων... - Confirms: υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ (huioi tou theou) = "sons of God" (NOT angeloi)

docs.title: Variant Readings
docs.text:
Some manuscripts have different readings:

Manuscript Date Genesis 6:2 Reading Codex Vaticanus (B) 4th century AD υἱοί ("sons") Codex Alexandrinus (A) 5th century AD ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ ("angels of God")

docs.title: Analysis of Variants
docs.text:
Codex Alexandrinus reading "angels": - This is a later manuscript (5th century) - Likely a scribal harmonization with Job - Not the original LXX reading - Reflects what one scribe (or tradition) believed, not what the text says

Manuscript variants tell us what scribes thought, not what is correct. Later harmonization is common - scribes often "fixed" perceived inconsistencies.

docs.title: Peshitta (Syriac) - 2nd century AD
docs.text: Translates Genesis 6:2 as "sons of God" (bnay Alaha)

docs.title: Vulgate (Latin) - 4th century AD (Jerome)
docs.text: Translates Genesis 6:2 as "filii Dei" = "sons of God"

docs.title: Targum Onkelos (Aramaic) - 2nd century AD
docs.text:
Translates Genesis 6:2 as "sons of nobles" (bene rabrevaya)

Significance: This explicitly interprets "sons of God" as humans - specifically, noble or powerful men.

docs.title: Symmachus (Greek) - 2nd century AD
docs.text:
Translates Genesis 6:2 as "sons of the kings" (huioi ton basileon)

Significance: Another explicit human interpretation - sons of rulers/kings.

docs.title: Summary of Ancient Translation Evidence
docs.text:
Translation Date Genesis 6:2 Rendering Interpretation LXX (standard) 3rd cent. BC "sons of God" Literal Peshitta 2nd cent. AD "sons of God" Literal Vulgate 4th cent. AD "sons of God" Literal Targum Onkelos 2nd cent. AD "sons of nobles" Human Symmachus 2nd cent. AD "sons of the kings" Human Codex Alexandrinus 5th cent. AD "angels of God" Angel (variant)

Finding: The majority of ancient translations render this as "sons of God" (literal). Two translations (Targum Onkelos, Symmachus) explicitly interpret it as humans. Only a later variant (Codex Alexandrinus) has "angels."

docs.title: The Claim
docs.text: "The Septuagint translates Genesis 6:2 as 'angels of God,' proving the angel view."

docs.title: The Reality
docs.text:
1. The standard LXX text says "sons of God," NOT "angels"
  2. The critical edition reads υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ (huioi tou theou)

  3. This is not disputed among scholars

  4. The LXX translators distinguished Genesis 6 from Job

  5. Same Hebrew → different Greek based on context

  6. They knew the word for "angels" and chose not to use it in Genesis 6

  7. The "angels" reading is a later variant

  8. Found in Codex Alexandrinus (5th century)
  9. Likely scribal harmonization with Job

  10. Not the original translation

  11. Other ancient translations support the human view

  12. Targum Onkelos: "sons of nobles"
  13. Symmachus: "sons of the kings"

docs.title: Connection to Moses-Angel-Terminology Study
docs.text:
The prerequisite study found:

"Moses consistently uses 'angel' (malak) when referring to celestial messengers." "Moses did NOT use 'sons of God' for angels anywhere in the Pentateuch."

If Moses meant "angels" in Genesis 6:2, he could have written: - מַלְאֲכֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (mal'ake ha'elohim) = "angels of God" - מַלְאָכִים (mal'akim) = "angels"

Instead, he wrote בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (bene ha'elohim) = "sons of God."

The LXX translators recognized this distinction. They knew how to translate "malak" (as ἄγγελος). They knew Moses didn't use that word in Genesis 6, so they didn't add it.

docs.title: Translations Are Not Authoritative
docs.text:
A translation is the work of human interpreters. It tells us what the translators thought the text meant, not what it actually means.

Even if the entire LXX tradition had "angels of God" in Genesis 6:2 (which it does not): - This would only tell us what the translators believed - It would not determine what the Hebrew text actually means - The question must be answered from the Hebrew original and its context

docs.title: The Question Must Be Answered from Scripture
docs.text:
Doctrinal questions are answered from Scripture, not from translations.

The LXX is valuable as an ancient witness to Jewish interpretation. But it remains a translation - the opinions of translators, not the inspired original.

docs.title: Patterns Identified
docs.text:
1. LXX context-sensitivity: Translators used context to choose between "sons" and "angels"
  2. Genesis 6 = "sons": Standard LXX consistently uses υἱοί in Genesis 6
  3. Job = "angels": LXX translators saw Job's heavenly scenes as requiring ἄγγελοι
  4. "Angels" variant is late: Codex Alexandrinus (5th century) - likely harmonization
  5. Human interpretations exist: Targum Onkelos, Symmachus explicitly chose human readings

docs.title: Moses's Usage of mal'ak
docs.text:
The moses-angel-terminology study documented:

Term Count in Pentateuch malak YHWH (angel of the LORD) 14 occurrences malak elohim (angel of God) 3 occurrences malakim (angels, plural) 4 occurrences malak (angel/his angel/etc.) 7 occurrences

Total: 28+ occurrences of "malak" for celestial beings in the Pentateuch.

Critical finding: Moses NEVER used "bene elohim" (sons of God) to refer to angels. He had a word for angels (malak) and used it consistently.

docs.title: The LXX Translation Choices
docs.text: Finding Evidence Genesis 6: "sons" (υἱοί) Standard LXX text Job 1, 2, 38: "angels" (ἄγγελοι) Same Hebrew, different Greek Context drove the choice Earthly (sons) vs. heavenly (angels) "Angels" in Gen 6 is late variant Codex Alexandrinus, 5th century

docs.title: The Significance
docs.text:
The LXX translators were capable scholars who: 1. Knew the difference between υἱός (son) and ἄγγελος (angel) 2. Chose to use different words based on context 3. Did NOT interpret Genesis 6 as referring to angels 4. Did interpret Job as referring to angels

This contextual distinction is itself evidence that ancient interpreters saw a difference between the Genesis 6 and Job contexts.

docs.title: genesis-6-sons-of-god Word Studies
docs.text: That study established: - "bene ha'elohim" occurs only 5 times in OT - Context differs significantly between Genesis and Job - Genesis 6:3 calls the subjects "flesh" (unusual for angels) - Marriage vocabulary in Genesis 6 is normal human language

docs.title: moses-angel-terminology Study
docs.text:
That study established: - Moses consistently used "malak" for angels (28+ times) - Moses used "cherubim" for specific celestial class - Moses NEVER used "bene elohim" for angels - If Moses meant angels, why use different terminology?

This study confirms: The LXX translators recognized Moses's vocabulary and did not impose "angels" on Genesis 6.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does the Septuagint (LXX) translate "sons of God" in Genesis 6:2 as "angels of God"? And if so, what does this mean for interpretation?

docs.title: Summary Answer
docs.text: The claim that "the Septuagint translates Genesis 6:2 as 'angels of God'" is misleading. The standard critical text of the LXX translates Genesis 6:2 as "sons of God" (υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ), NOT "angels of God." Remarkably, the same LXX translators who translated Job 1:6, 2:1, and 38:7 as "angels of God" chose to translate Genesis 6:2 differently - indicating they saw a contextual distinction. The "angels" reading found in some manuscripts (e.g., Codex Alexandrinus) is a later variant, likely scribal harmonization with Job.

docs.title: Key Verses
docs.text:
Genesis 6:2 (Hebrew): בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (bene ha'elohim) = "sons of God" Genesis 6:2 (LXX): οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ (hoi huioi tou theou) = "sons of God"

Job 1:6 (Hebrew): בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים (bene ha'elohim) = "sons of God" Job 1:6 (LXX): οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ (hoi angeloi tou theou) = "angels of God"

Deuteronomy 14:1: "Ye are the children of the LORD your God..." Moses uses "sons/children of God" language for humans (Israel).

docs.title: 1. The Standard LXX Text Says "Sons of God"
docs.text:
The critical edition of the Septuagint (Rahlfs-Hanhart) reads:

Genesis 6:2: οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ = "the sons of God"

This is not disputed. The standard LXX text does NOT say "angels of God" in Genesis 6.

docs.title: 2. The LXX Translators Made a Deliberate Distinction
docs.text:
The same Hebrew phrase (בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים) was translated differently based on context:

Passage Context LXX Translation Genesis 6:2 Earthly scene, marriage "sons of God" Genesis 6:4 Earthly scene, marriage "sons of God" Job 1:6 Heavenly throne room with Satan "angels of God" Job 2:1 Heavenly throne room with Satan "angels of God" Job 38:7 Creation, before humans existed "my angels"

This distinction is significant. The LXX translators knew Greek words for both "sons" (υἱοί) and "angels" (ἄγγελοι). They chose "sons" for Genesis 6 and "angels" for Job. This reflects an interpretive judgment based on context.

docs.title: 3. The "Angels" Reading Is a Later Variant
docs.text:
The reading "angels of God" (ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ) in Genesis 6:2 appears in: - Codex Alexandrinus (5th century AD)

But NOT in: - Codex Vaticanus (4th century AD) - reads "sons" - Standard critical text (Rahlfs-Hanhart) - reads "sons"

The "angels" reading is likely a scribal harmonization with Job - a later scribe "correcting" what seemed like an inconsistency.

docs.title: 4. Other Ancient Translations Support "Sons" or "Humans"
docs.text:
Translation Date Genesis 6:2 Rendering Peshitta (Syriac) 2nd cent. AD "sons of God" Vulgate (Latin) 4th cent. AD "filii Dei" = "sons of God" Targum Onkelos 2nd cent. AD "sons of nobles" (human) Symmachus (Greek) 2nd cent. AD "sons of the kings" (human)

Notably, Targum Onkelos and Symmachus explicitly interpreted "sons of God" as humans (nobles, kings), not angels.

docs.title: 5. Translations Are Not Authoritative
docs.text:
A translation reflects what the translators believed, not what the text actually means. Even if all ancient translations said "angels" (which they do not), this would only tell us what ancient interpreters thought - not what Moses wrote.

Doctrinal questions must be answered from Scripture itself, not from translations of Scripture.

docs.title: The Claim
docs.text: "The Septuagint translates Genesis 6:2 as 'angels of God,' supporting the angel view."

docs.title: The Reality
docs.text:
1. The standard LXX says "sons of God" - not "angels"
  2. The LXX translators deliberately distinguished Genesis 6 from Job
  3. The "angels" reading is a 5th-century variant - likely scribal harmonization
  4. Other ancient translations support the human view - Targum Onkelos, Symmachus
  5. Translations are not authoritative - they reflect interpreter opinion, not inspired text

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The Septuagint evidence, when examined carefully, actually weakens the angel view argument rather than supporting it:

  1. The standard LXX text says "sons," not "angels" in Genesis 6
  2. The LXX translators saw a contextual difference between Genesis 6 (earthly marriage) and Job (heavenly throne room)
  3. The "angels" variant is late and secondary - likely scribal harmonization
  4. Ancient Jewish translators (Targum Onkelos, Symmachus) explicitly chose human interpretations
  5. Moses never used "bene elohim" for angels - he used "malak" consistently

The fact that the same translators who rendered Job as "angels" chose NOT to render Genesis 6 as "angels" is itself evidence that ancient interpreters saw a difference between these contexts.

Genesis 19:1 And there came two angels to Sodom at even; and Lot sat in the gate of Sodom: and Lot seeing them rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face toward the ground;

Genesis 19:2 And he said, Behold now, my lords, turn in, I pray you, into your servant's house, and tarry all night, and wash your feet, and ye shall rise up early, and go on your ways. And they said, Nay; but we will abide in the street all night.

Genesis 19:3 And he pressed upon them greatly; and they turned in unto him, and entered into his house; and he made them a feast, and did bake unleavened bread, and they did eat.

Genesis 19:4 But before they lay down, the men of the city, even the men of Sodom, compassed the house round, both old and young, all the people from every quarter:

Genesis 19:5 And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.

Genesis 19:6 And Lot went out at the door unto them, and shut the door after him,

Genesis 19:7 And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly.

Genesis 19:8 Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you, and do ye to them as is good in your eyes: only unto these men do nothing; for therefore came they under the shadow of my roof.

Genesis 19:9 And they said, Stand back. And they said again, This one fellow came in to sojourn, and he will needs be a judge: now will we deal worse with thee, than with them. And they pressed sore upon the man, even Lot, and came near to break the door.

Genesis 19:10-11 But the men put forth their hand, and pulled Lot into the house to them, and shut to the door. And they smote the men that were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great: so that they wearied themselves to find the door.

docs.text:
Judges 19:22 Now as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about, and beat at the door, and spake to the master of the house, the old man, saying, Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him.

Judges 19:23 And the man, the master of the house, went out unto them, and said unto them, Nay, my brethren, nay, I pray you, do not so wickedly; seeing that this man is come into mine house, do not this folly.

docs.title: Hebrew Vocabulary Parallel
docs.text:
The Judges 19 narrative uses identical Hebrew vocabulary to Genesis 19:

Hebrew Word Strong's Meaning Genesis 19 Judges 19 יָדַע (yada) H3045 "know" (sexually) 19:5, 19:8 19:22, 19:25 רעע (ra'a) H7489 "wickedly" 19:7 19:23 בַּת (bat) H1323 "daughter(s)" 19:8 19:24 אִישׁ (ish) H376 "man/men" (visitor) 19:5 19:22

docs.title: Key Distinction: "Men" vs "Angels"
docs.text:
Passage Speaker Hebrew Strong's Translation Gen 19:1 Narrator מַלְאָךְ (mal'ak) H4397 "angels" Gen 19:5 Sodomites אִישׁ (ish) H376 "men" Jdg 19:22 Men of Gibeah אִישׁ (ish) H376 "man"

The narrator tells us the visitors were "angels" (מַלְאָכִים), but the Sodomites called them "men" (אִישׁ) - the same word used in Judges 19. Both mobs thought they were pursuing "men."
