docs.title: The Interpretive Question
docs.text:
What does Jude mean by σαρκὸς ἑτέρας ("strange flesh" / "flesh of a different kind")?

Two interpretations have been proposed: 1. Homosexual relations - flesh "different" from natural design 2. Angelic flesh - flesh of a categorically different order

docs.title: The Critical Distinction
docs.text:
Greek has two words commonly translated "another/other":

Word Strong's Meaning Nuance ἕτερος (heteros) G2087 other, different Different in KIND or nature ἄλλος (allos) G243 another, other Another of the SAME kind

docs.title: Evidence from NT Usage
docs.text:
Jude uses ἕτερος (G2087) - only translated "strange" once in the entire NT (here in Jude 1:7).

Paul uses ἄλλος (G243) in 1 Corinthians 15:39 when distinguishing flesh types: - "another (ἄλλη) flesh of beasts" - "another (ἄλλη) of fishes" - "another (ἄλλη) of birds"

Paul's usage shows ἄλλος for different types within the same category of flesh.

Romans 1:26-27 uses παρὰ φύσιν ("against nature") for homosexuality - NOT ἕτερος.

docs.title: Linguistic Implication
docs.text:
Jude's choice of ἕτερος suggests flesh that is categorically different - not merely another type within the same category.

If homosexuality: Why not use παρὰ φύσιν like Paul? Human male flesh is not a "different kind" from human female flesh - both are human.

If angelic flesh: ἕτερος precisely describes flesh of a completely different order - angelic vs human.

docs.title: Key Observations
docs.text:
1. The visitors were angels (Gen 19:1, 15) - explicitly stated
  2. They appeared as men (Gen 19:5) - the Sodomites called them "men"
  3. The Sodomites did not know they were angels - they demanded to "know" them as "men"
  4. Lot offered his daughters (Gen 19:8) - female substitute for male visitors
  5. The Sodomites refused the female substitute (Gen 19:9) - their desire was specifically for the male visitors

docs.title: What This Suggests
docs.text:
For interpretation 1 (homosexuality): - The Sodomites wanted males, not females - They refused Lot's daughters - Their sin was homosexual desire

For interpretation 2 (angelic flesh): - The visitors WERE angels, regardless of appearance - If "strange flesh" means angels, it's what they actually were - From God's perspective (who inspired Jude), they were pursuing angelic beings

docs.title: The Parallel in Judges 19
docs.text:
The Gibeah narrative closely parallels Genesis 19, using identical Hebrew vocabulary:

Element Genesis 19 Judges 19 Hebrew "know" (sexual demand) 19:5 19:22 יָדַע (yada) H3045 "wickedly" (host's response) 19:7 19:23 רעע (ra'a) H7489 "daughter(s)" offered 19:8 19:24 בַּת (bat) H1323 "not known man" 19:8 19:24 יָדַע (yada) H3045 "man/men" (visitor) 19:5 19:22 אִישׁ (ish) H376

docs.title: Key Observation: "Men" vs "Angels"
docs.text:
Passage Speaker Hebrew Strong's Translation Gen 19:1 Narrator מַלְאָךְ (mal'ak) H4397 "angels" Gen 19:5 Sodomites אִישׁ (ish) H376 "men" Jdg 19:22 Men of Gibeah אִישׁ (ish) H376 "man"

The narrator in Genesis 19:1 tells us the visitors were מַלְאָכִים (angels), but the Sodomites called them אִישׁ (men) - the same word used in Judges 19. From the mob's perspective, both scenarios involved pursuing "men" (אִישׁ).

Significance: - The linguistic parallel is undeniable - the same Hebrew words describe the same scenario - The Sodomites thought they were pursuing "men" (אִישׁ) - identical to Gibeah - But the narrator (and Jude, with hindsight) knows they were actually "angels" (מַלְאָךְ) - This supports both readings: the subjective sin was the same (homosexual desire for אִישׁ), but the objective reality differed (מַלְאָכִים in Sodom)

docs.title: The Grammatical Question
docs.text:
Jude 1:7 contains the phrase τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις ("in like manner to these").

See related study: jude-1-6-7-in-like-manner for full analysis.

docs.title: Two Readings
docs.text:
Reading A: τούτοις refers to the angels (v6) - Sodom sinned "in like manner to the angels" - Both crossed flesh-categories - Supports interpretation 2 (angelic flesh)

Reading B: τούτοις refers to the inhabitants of the cities (v7) - The surrounding cities sinned "like the people of Sodom" - v6 and v7 are separate examples of judgment - Does NOT connect Sodom's sin to the angels' sin

docs.title: Grammatical Evidence
docs.text:
• τούτοις is masculine plural
  • Cities are feminine
  • Angels (v6) are masculine

However, NT Greek shows constructio ad sensum - cities can take masculine when inhabitants are meant (Acts 8:5, 8:14; Luke 10:13; Matt 23:37).

Conclusion from related study: Grammar alone does not determine the antecedent. Both readings are grammatically defensible.

docs.title: What Jude 6 Says
docs.text:
"The angels which kept not their first estate (arche), but left their own habitation (oiketerion)..."

See related study: ../jude-6-everlasting-chains/ and jude-6-7-angels-sin

docs.title: Key Findings from Related Studies
docs.text:
1. Arche (G746) = position, rank, domain - NOT physical nature
  2. Oiketerion (G3613) = dwelling place - in context, heaven
  3. Jude 6 describes the angelic rebellion (Rev 12 parallel)
  4. The angels were cast out of heaven - NOT that they took human form

docs.title: Does Jude 6 Describe Sexual Sin?
docs.text:
The jude-6-7-angels-sin study concluded: No.

  • "First estate" (arche) refers to position/rank, not nature
  • "Habitation" (oiketerion) most naturally means heaven
  • The parallel in Revelation 12 shows angels cast from heaven
  • Nothing in the vocabulary requires or implies sexual activity

If Jude 6 does NOT describe sexual sin, then "in like manner" (if it connects v6 and v7) would not necessarily connect their sins but perhaps their judgments or some other element.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Element Jude 2 Peter Angels v6: Reserved in chains v4: Cast to hell, chains of darkness Connection "in like manner" No connecting phrase Sodom v7: Fornication, strange flesh v6: Overthrow, example to ungodly

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
2 Peter does NOT include "in like manner" and does NOT describe Sodom's specific sin. Peter treats angels, flood, and Sodom as separate examples of judgment.

If Peter and Jude share a common tradition, the "in like manner" and "strange flesh" are unique to Jude.

docs.title: Interpretation 1: Homosexuality
docs.text:
Supporting Evidence: 1. Genesis 19:4-5 shows men demanding male visitors 2. Genesis 19:8-9 shows refusal of female substitute 3. Judges 19 parallel involves no angels - same sin pattern 4. Romans 1:26-27 connects Sodom's legacy with homosexuality 5. NT terms for homosexuality (arsenokoites) derive from LXX of Lev 18:22; 20:13 6. Ezekiel 16:50 calls Sodom's sin "abomination" (toebah) - same word as Lev 18:22

Challenges: 1. Why use ἕτερος ("different kind") for same-species flesh? 2. Human male flesh is not categorically "different" from human female flesh

docs.title: Interpretation 2: Angelic Flesh
docs.text:
Supporting Evidence: 1. ἕτερος means "different in kind" - angelic flesh is categorically different 2. Genesis 19:1 explicitly states visitors were angels 3. Creates theological parallel with v6 (if "in like manner" connects them)

Challenges: 1. Sodomites didn't know visitors were angels 2. Judges 19 parallel has no angels - same sin described 3. Requires assuming Jude 6 describes sexual sin (not established) 4. 2 Peter parallel does not connect the two

docs.title: The Judges 19 Parallel - What It Proves and Doesn't Prove
docs.text:
The Gibeah narrative (Judges 19) replicates the Genesis 19 scenario using identical Hebrew vocabulary:

Hebrew Word Strong's Genesis 19 Judges 19 יָדַע (yada) H3045 "know" (19:5) "know" (19:22) רעע (ra'a) H7489 "wickedly" (19:7) "wickedly" (19:23) בַּת (bat) H1323 "daughters" (19:8) "daughter" (19:24)

But there are no angels in Gibeah. The visitor was a human Levite.

What this proves: - The same Hebrew vocabulary describes both events - Homosexual mob violence existed as a sin pattern without angels - The narrative structure can occur with purely human actors

What this does NOT prove: - That Jude wasn't highlighting something additional about Sodom's case - That ἕτερος should be understood the same way for both narratives

The Judges 19 parallel is linguistically strong - the same Hebrew words describe the same sin. However, it doesn't prove Jude wasn't also noting the angelic dimension unique to Sodom.

docs.title: The Both/And Reading
docs.text:
A more nuanced reading recognizes that both elements may be true simultaneously:

The Sodomites' perspective (subjective): - They saw "men" (Gen 19:5) - Their intent was homosexual - they wanted males, refused females - Their culpable sin was same-sex lust

Jude's perspective (objective, with hindsight): - The visitors WERE angels (Gen 19:1) - In objective reality, they pursued flesh of a categorically different order - ἕτερος ("different in kind") is precisely accurate - angelic flesh IS categorically different

docs.title: Why This Reading Works
docs.text:
1. Explains ἕτερος - Jude uses "different in kind" because, from his inspired hindsight, that's what the flesh actually was. The word choice reflects the objective reality, not the Sodomites' perception.

  2. Explains the Judges 19 distinction - Gibeah had the same homosexual intent but NOT the same objective reality. Sodom's case was uniquely egregious because they (unknowingly) crossed the human/angel boundary.

  3. Doesn't require the Sodomites to know - The objective nature of the sin doesn't depend on their awareness. Jude, writing with divine perspective, knows what they were actually pursuing.

  4. Maintains the homosexual element - Their culpable intent was homosexual; the angelic dimension adds another layer to what actually occurred.

  5. Explains why Jude chose Sodom over Gibeah - If he just wanted an example of homosexuality, Gibeah was available. He chose the one with angels because that added dimension matters.

docs.title: What This Does NOT Require
docs.text:
This reading does NOT require: - That Jude 6 describes sexual sin (it describes rebellion - leaving position) - That Genesis 6 "sons of God" were angels (a separate question) - That "in like manner" connects the sins of v6 and v7 (grammar is ambiguous)

The connection between v6 and v7 (if any) might be: - Both are examples of divine judgment - Both involve leaving/crossing proper boundaries (position for angels, flesh-categories for Sodom) - But NOT necessarily the same type of sin

docs.title: Consistency with OT
docs.text:
Leviticus 18:22 calls homosexuality תּוֹעֵבָה (toebah - "abomination") Ezekiel 16:50 says Sodom committed "abomination" (same word)

This links Sodom's sin to the Levitical prohibition - confirming the homosexual element was present.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Two readings are viable:

docs.title: Reading 1: Homosexuality Only
docs.text: "Strange flesh" = flesh "different" from the natural counterpart (men pursuing men). The Judges 19 parallel supports this - same sin pattern, no angels. This is the simpler reading.

docs.title: Reading 2: Both/And
docs.text:
The Sodomites' sin was homosexual in intent, AND (from Jude's perspective) they unknowingly pursued angelic flesh. This explains ἕτερος ("different in kind") and why Jude chose Sodom over Gibeah.

What is certain: - The homosexual element is clearly present (Gen 19:4-9; Ezek 16:50) - The visitors were angels (Gen 19:1)

What remains uncertain: - Whether Jude intended to highlight the angelic dimension - The exact referent of τούτοις in "in like manner" (see related study) - Whether Jude intended to connect the angels' sin (rebellion) to Sodom's sin

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Question Reading 1 Reading 2 What is "strange flesh"? Homosexuality Homosexual intent + angelic reality Why "strange" (ἕτερος)? Different from natural Categorically different (angelic) What was their sin? Same-sex lust Same-sex lust (+ angelic dimension) Judges 19 parallel? Decisive - same sin, no angels Proves homosexual element, not the whole picture Question Answer (both readings) Was homosexuality involved? Yes (Gen 19:4-9; Ezek 16:50) Does Jude 6 describe sexual sin? No - rebellion Does Jude connect v6 and v7 sins? Not clearly established

docs.title: The Phrase
docs.text:
Greek: σαρκὸς ἑτέρας (sarkos heteras) KJV: "strange flesh" Literal: "flesh of a different kind"

Context (Jude 1:7): "Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire."

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• Strong's: "of uncertain affinity; (an-, the) other or different"
  • Part of Speech: Adjective
  • NT Occurrences: 99

docs.title: Critical Distinction: ἕτερος vs ἄλλος
docs.text:
Word Strong's Meaning Nuance ἕτερος (heteros) G2087 other, different Different in KIND or nature ἄλλος (allos) G243 another, other Another of the SAME kind

This distinction is significant. When Greek writers wanted to emphasize qualitative difference, they used ἕτερος. When referring to another of the same type, they used ἄλλος.

docs.title: KJV Translation of ἕτερος (G2087)
docs.text:
• "other" (43x)
  • "another" (42x)
  • "else" (4x)
  • "next day" (3x)
  • "strange" (1x) - only in Jude 1:7

Key Observation: The KJV translates ἕτερος as "strange" only once in the entire NT - in Jude 1:7. This suggests the translators recognized something unusual about the "otherness" here.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
• Strong's: "flesh (as stripped of the skin)"
  • Part of Speech: Noun, Feminine
  • NT Occurrences: 147

docs.title: Semantic Range
docs.text:
1. Physical body/flesh - the material of the body
  2. Human nature - humanity in general
  3. Sinful nature - the flesh as opposed to the Spirit
  4. Kinship - "my flesh" = my relatives

docs.title: Comparative Analysis: 1 Corinthians 15:39
docs.text: 1 Corinthians 15:39 "All flesh [is] not the same flesh: but [there is] one [kind of] flesh of men, another [ἄλλη] flesh of beasts, another [ἄλλη] of fishes, [and] another [ἄλλη] of birds."

docs.title: Greek Words Used
docs.text:
English Greek Strong's Meaning "another" (3x) ἄλλη (alle) G243 another of same category

Key Observation: When Paul discusses different categories of flesh (human, animal, fish, bird), he uses ἄλλος (G243) - "another of the same kind." All are flesh; they differ within the category of "flesh."

Contrast with Jude: Jude uses ἕτερος (G2087) - "different in kind." This suggests flesh that is not merely a different type within the same category, but flesh of an entirely different nature or order.

docs.title: Romans 1:26-27 - Different Terminology
docs.text: Romans 1:26-27 "For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature [παρὰ φύσιν]: And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly..."

docs.title: Key Phrase
docs.text:
• Greek: παρὰ φύσιν (para physin)
  • Meaning: "against nature" or "contrary to nature"

Observation: When Paul describes homosexual relations, he does NOT use ἕτερος or σαρκὸς ἑτέρας. He uses παρὰ φύσιν ("against nature"). This is different terminology from Jude's "strange flesh."

Passage Greek Phrase Literal Concept Jude 1:7 σαρκὸς ἑτέρας "flesh of different kind" Different category of flesh Rom 1:26 παρὰ φύσιν "against nature" Contrary to natural function

docs.title: The Visitors Were Angels
docs.text:
Genesis 19:1 "And there came two angels to Sodom at even..."

Genesis 19:5 "And they called unto Lot, and said unto him, Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them."

Genesis 19:10-11 "But the men put forth their hand, and pulled Lot into the house... And they smote the men that were at the door of the house with blindness..."

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
1. The visitors are explicitly called angels (מַלְאָכִים / ἄγγελοι) in v1 and v15
  2. The men of Sodom sought to "know" them (sexual intent, cf. Gen 4:1)
  3. The angels displayed supernatural power (blindness)

If Reading A ("angels" interpretation): The "strange flesh" Sodom pursued was angelic flesh - flesh of a completely different order than human flesh. This would make ἕτερος ("different in kind") highly appropriate.

docs.title: Note on Genesis 6:1-4
docs.text:
Some interpreters connect Jude 1:6-7 to Genesis 6:1-4 ("sons of God" taking human wives), arguing: - v6 = angels pursuing human flesh - v7 = humans pursuing angelic flesh (a "mirror" of the same sin)

However, this connection is NOT established by Jude's text:

  1. Jude 6 describes rebellion, not sexual sin - "first estate" (arche) = position/rank; "habitation" (oiketerion) = heaven. The related study (jude-6-7-angels-sin) concludes this refers to the angelic rebellion (Rev 12 parallel), not Genesis 6.

  2. The Genesis 6 interpretation is a separate question - Whether "sons of God" in Genesis 6 are angels is debated and must be established from Genesis 6 itself, not imported from Jude.

  3. Jude does not mention Genesis 6 - He does not reference wives, offspring, or Nephilim.

This word study does not assume the Genesis 6 connection. The angelic dimension in Jude 1:7 comes from Genesis 19:1 (the visitors were angels), not from Genesis 6.

docs.title: OT Background: Leviticus 18:22-23
docs.text:
Leviticus 18:22 "Thou shalt not lie with mankind, as with womankind: it is abomination [תּוֹעֵבָה - toebah]."

Leviticus 18:23 "Neither shalt thou lie with any beast to defile thyself therewith: neither shall any woman stand before a beast to lie down thereto: it is confusion [תֶּבֶל - tebel]."

docs.title: Hebrew Word Study: תֶּבֶל (tebel) - H8397
docs.text:
• Definition: "mixture, i.e. unnatural bestiality; confusion"
  • Occurrences: 2 (Lev 18:23; 20:12)
  • Concept: Mixing of categories that should not be mixed

Observation: The OT uses different terms for homosexuality (תּוֹעֵבָה - "abomination") versus bestiality (תֶּבֶל - "confusion/mixture"). The concept of תֶּבֶל involves crossing species boundaries - a mixing of different kinds of flesh.

This OT concept of "mixture/confusion" (crossing flesh categories) aligns with ἕτερος ("different in kind") better than with homosexuality.

docs.title: Reading 1: Homosexuality Only
docs.text:
"Strange flesh" = flesh "different" from the natural counterpart (men pursuing men instead of women).

Strengths: - Simpler reading - Judges 19 parallel shows same sin pattern without angels - Ezekiel 16:50 confirms Sodom committed "abomination" (toebah)

Challenge: - Why use ἕτερος ("different kind") rather than παρὰ φύσιν ("against nature") like Paul?

docs.title: Reading 2: Both/And
docs.text:
"Strange flesh" encompasses both: - Subjective: Homosexual intent (they wanted males, refused females) - Objective: Angelic flesh (Jude knows the visitors were angels)

Strengths: - Explains ἕτερος - the flesh WAS categorically different (angelic) - Explains why Jude chose Sodom over Gibeah - Maintains the homosexual element

Challenge: - More complex interpretation

docs.title: Linguistic Conclusion
docs.text:
The word ἕτερος (G2087) specifically denotes qualitative difference - something of a different category or nature, not merely "another" of the same type.

  • ἄλλος (G243): another apple in the basket (same kind)
  • ἕτερος (G2087): an orange instead of an apple (different kind)

Jude's choice of σαρκὸς ἑτέρας ("flesh of a different kind") could mean: - Reading 1: Flesh different from the natural counterpart (same-sex) - Reading 2: Flesh that was objectively of a different order (angelic)

What is certain: The homosexual element is present (Gen 19:4-9; Ezek 16:50).

What is debated: Whether Jude is also highlighting the angelic dimension.

See 03-analysis.md and CONCLUSION.md for full analysis of both readings.

docs.title: Conclusion: What is "Strange Flesh" in Jude 1:7?
The Question
docs.text: What does Jude mean by σαρκὸς ἑτέρας ("strange flesh" / "flesh of a different kind") in Jude 1:7?

docs.title: The Passage
docs.text:
Jude 1:6-7

And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.

docs.title: Reading 1: Homosexuality
docs.text: "Strange flesh" = flesh "different" from the natural counterpart (men pursuing men instead of women)

docs.title: Reading 2: Both/And (Homosexual Intent + Angelic Reality)
docs.text:
"Strange flesh" encompasses both: 1. Subjectively (the Sodomites' intent): Homosexual lust - they wanted males, refused females 2. Objectively (what Jude knows in hindsight): Angelic flesh - the visitors were actually angels

Both readings are defensible. This study presents the evidence for each.

docs.title: The Linguistic Argument
docs.text:
Word Meaning ἕτερος (G2087) different in KIND ἄλλος (G243) another of SAME kind

Jude uses ἕτερος - the KJV translates it "strange" only here in the entire NT.

Why this matters: From Jude's inspired perspective, the flesh WAS categorically different - it was angelic. The word choice reflects the objective reality, not the Sodomites' perception.

docs.title: The Genesis 19 Narrative
docs.text:
What the Sodomites saw What was actually true "Men" (Gen 19:5) Angels (Gen 19:1) Homosexual targets Beings of a different order
  • The Sodomites' intent was homosexual (they refused female substitutes - Gen 19:8-9)
  • The reality was that they pursued angelic beings

docs.title: The Judges 19 Parallel
docs.text:
The Gibeah narrative uses identical Hebrew vocabulary to Genesis 19:

Hebrew Strong's Genesis 19 Judges 19 יָדַע (yada) H3045 "know" (19:5) "know" (19:22) רעע (ra'a) H7489 "wickedly" (19:7) "wickedly" (19:23) בַּת (bat) H1323 "daughters" (19:8) "daughter" (19:24) אִישׁ (ish) H376 "men" (19:5) "man" (19:22)

docs.title: Key Distinction: "Men" vs "Angels"
docs.text:
Passage Speaker Hebrew Translation Gen 19:1 Narrator מַלְאָךְ (mal'ak) H4397 "angels" Gen 19:5 Sodomites אִישׁ (ish) H376 "men" Jdg 19:22 Men of Gibeah אִישׁ (ish) H376 "man"

Both mobs used the same word - אִישׁ (ish) - for the visitor. The Sodomites thought they were pursuing "men," just like Gibeah. But the narrator tells us the visitors were actually מַלְאָכִים (angels).

What this proves: From the mob's perspective, both events were identical - pursuing אִישׁ (men).

What this also shows: The objective reality differed - Sodom's "men" were actually angels, known to the narrator and to Jude.

Key question: Why did Jude choose Sodom over Gibeah? Both used identical vocabulary for the same sin.

docs.title: The OT Confirmation
docs.text:
Ezekiel 16:50 says Sodom committed "abomination" (תּוֹעֵבָה / toebah) - the same term used in Leviticus 18:22 for homosexuality.

This confirms the homosexual element was present.

docs.title: Reading 1 (Homosexuality Only)
docs.text:
Strengths: 1. Judges 19 parallel - identical Hebrew vocabulary (יָדַע, רעע, בַּת), same sin, no angels 2. Genesis 19:8-9 - men refused female substitutes, specifically wanted males 3. Ezekiel 16:50 - Sodom's sin called "abomination" (toebah) - the Levitical term for homosexuality 4. Simpler reading - doesn't require layered interpretation

Challenges: 1. Why use ἕτερος ("different kind") rather than παρὰ φύσιν ("against nature") like Paul? 2. Human male flesh is not categorically "different" from human female flesh

docs.title: Reading 2 (Both/And)
docs.text:
Strengths: 1. Explains ἕτερος - "different in kind" accurately describes what the flesh actually was (angelic) 2. Explains Judges 19 distinction - same homosexual intent, but Sodom had the additional angelic dimension 3. Explains why Jude chose Sodom - the angelic element makes it distinctive 4. Maintains the homosexual element - clearly attested in Genesis 19 and Ezekiel 16:50

Challenges: 1. More complex interpretation 2. Requires distinguishing subjective intent from objective reality

docs.title: What This Does NOT Require
docs.text:
This reading does NOT require:

  • That Jude 6 describes sexual sin - It describes rebellion (leaving position/habitation)
  • That Genesis 6 "sons of God" were angels - That is a separate question not established by Jude 6-7
  • That "in like manner" connects the sins - The grammar is ambiguous (see related study)

The connection between v6 and v7 (if any) might be: - Both are examples of divine judgment - Both involve crossing proper boundaries (position for angels, flesh-categories for Sodom) - But NOT necessarily the same type of sin

docs.title: From jude-6-7-angels-sin
docs.text:
Finding: The angels' sin in Jude 6 was rebellion (leaving their position, cast from heaven) - NOT sexual sin.

  • "First estate" (arche) = position, rank
  • "Habitation" (oiketerion) = heaven
  • Revelation 12 provides the parallel

docs.title: From jude-1-6-7-in-like-manner
docs.text: Finding: The grammar of τὸν ὅμοιον τρόπον τούτοις is ambiguous. Both readings are grammatically defensible.

docs.title: From ../jude-6-everlasting-chains/
docs.text: Finding: "Everlasting chains under darkness" describes spiritual condemnation, not a literal underground prison.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Question Reading 1 Reading 2 What is "strange flesh"? Homosexuality Homosexual intent + angelic reality Why "strange" (ἕτερος)? Different from natural Categorically different (angelic) Did the Sodomites know? N/A No - they thought they were men What was their sin? Same-sex lust Same-sex lust (+ angelic dimension) Question Answer (both readings) Does Jude 6 describe sexual sin? No - it describes rebellion Does Jude connect v6 and v7 sins? Not clearly established Was homosexuality involved? Yes (Gen 19:4-9; Ezek 16:50)

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Both readings are viable:

Reading 1: "Strange flesh" simply means homosexual relations - flesh "different" from the natural counterpart. The Judges 19 parallel supports this, and it's the simpler reading.

Reading 2: "Strange flesh" encompasses both the Sodomites' homosexual intent AND the objective reality (known to Jude) that the visitors were angels. This explains why Jude uses ἕτερος ("different in kind") and why he chose Sodom over Gibeah.

What is certain: The homosexual element is clearly present (Gen 19:4-9; Ezek 16:50). The question is whether Jude is also highlighting the angelic dimension.

The interpreter must weigh: - The significance of ἕτερος vs other terminology - Whether the Judges 19 parallel is decisive - Whether Jude's choice of Sodom (with angels) over Gibeah (without) is significant
